title: RC and RL circuits: from the circuit to the pole-zero form
heading: The method
summary: How to bring a passive circuit with one capacitor or one inductor to the factored form, through the gains at DC and at high frequency and the resistance the component sees, with the circuits grouped by the form they produce.
prereqs: Inverted forms and the sign on the Bode plot
text: Impedances. A capacitor is \(1/(sC)\), and an inductor, \(sL\). A divider, \(Z_2/(Z_1 + Z_2)\), or a series or parallel combination, gives \(N(s)/D(s)\). Normalize. Divide the numerator and the denominator by their constant terms: \(G_0\), the DC gain, is left in front, and each factor becomes \(1 + s/\omega\). With no constant term, factor out \(s\): the factor is in \(\omega/s\), the inverted form, with the high-frequency gain in front.

title: RC and RL circuits: from the circuit to the pole-zero form
heading: The shortcut
summary: How to bring a passive circuit with one capacitor or one inductor to the factored form, through the gains at DC and at high frequency and the resistance the component sees, with the circuits grouped by the form they produce.
prereqs: Inverted forms and the sign on the Bode plot
text: With a single capacitor or inductor, or several that reduce to one with the source zeroed, a shortcut does away with the algebra: Pole: \(\omega_p = 1/\tau\), with \(\tau = R_{eq}C\) or \(\tau = L/R_{eq}\), \(R_{eq}\) being the resistance seen from the capacitor's or inductor's terminals with the source zeroed (voltage sources shorted, current sources open). If the capacitor sees \(R_{eq} = \infty\), or the inductor \(R_{eq} = 0\), the pole goes to the origin: write it with \(G_\infty\) in front, as in (d). Gains at the ends: \(G_0\) at DC and \(G_\infty\) at high frequency, signed dividers of resistors only. Zero: in the form below, with both non-zero, there is a finite zero, \(\omega_z = \omega_p\,G_0/G_\infty\); with opposite signs, as in a bridge with a differential output, \(\omega_z < 0\): a right-half-plane zero (Right-half-plane pole and zero). With \(G_\infty = 0\), there is only the pole; with \(G_0 = 0\), the zero is at the origin: the inverted pole, with \(G_\infty\) in front. \[G(s) = G_0\,\frac{1 + s/\omega_z}{1 + s/\omega_p}\] Six first-order circuits: (a) R in series, C to ground, and (b) L in series, R to ground, pole; (c) R in series, L to ground, inverted pole; (d) input impedance of the series RC, inverted zero; (e) output impedance of R∥C with the source shorted, pole; (f) R1∥C1 in series with R2 to ground, zero below the pole.

title: RC and RL circuits: from the circuit to the pole-zero form
heading: Pole: (a) and (b)
summary: How to bring a passive circuit with one capacitor or one inductor to the factored form, through the gains at DC and at high frequency and the resistance the component sees, with the circuits grouped by the form they produce.
prereqs: Inverted forms and the sign on the Bode plot
text: In (a), \(G_0 = 1\) (capacitor open) and \(G_\infty = 0\) (capacitor shorted); with the source shorted, the capacitor sees \(R_1\). It is the pole: \[G(s) = \frac{1}{1 + s/\omega_p}, \qquad \omega_p = \frac{1}{R_1C_1}\] In (b), the inductor is a short at DC (\(G_0 = 1\)) and open at high frequency (\(G_\infty = 0\)), and it sees \(R_1\): the same form, with \(\omega_p = R_1/L_1\).

title: RC and RL circuits: from the circuit to the pole-zero form
heading: Inverted pole: (c)
summary: How to bring a passive circuit with one capacitor or one inductor to the factored form, through the gains at DC and at high frequency and the resistance the component sees, with the circuits grouped by the form they produce.
prereqs: Inverted forms and the sign on the Bode plot
text: With the resistor and the inductor swapped, \(G_0 = 0\), because the shorted inductor takes the output to ground, and \(G_\infty = 1\): \[G(s) = \frac{1}{1 + \omega_p/s}, \qquad \omega_p = \frac{R_1}{L_1}\] It is the inverted pole, a pure differentiator times the pole: +20 dB per decade up to \(f_p\), 0 dB above.

title: RC and RL circuits: from the circuit to the pole-zero form
heading: Impedances: (d) and (e)
summary: How to bring a passive circuit with one capacitor or one inductor to the factored form, through the gains at DC and at high frequency and the resistance the component sees, with the circuits grouped by the form they produce.
prereqs: Inverted forms and the sign on the Bode plot
text: The input impedance of the series RC (d), seen by a current source, is \[Z_i(s) = R_1 + \frac{1}{sC_1} = R_1\left(1 + \frac{\omega_z}{s}\right)\] with \(\omega_z = 1/(R_1C_1)\): an inverted zero, with \(R_1\), the high-frequency value, in front. The magnitude is plotted in dBΩ. The output impedance of (e), with the source shorted, is \(R_1 \parallel C_1\): \[Z_o(s) = \frac{R_1}{1 + s/\omega_p}, \qquad \omega_p = \frac{1}{R_1C_1}\] a pole, with \(R_1\) as its DC value.

title: RC and RL circuits: from the circuit to the pole-zero form
heading: Zero below the pole: (f)
summary: How to bring a passive circuit with one capacitor or one inductor to the factored form, through the gains at DC and at high frequency and the resistance the component sees, with the circuits grouped by the form they produce.
prereqs: Inverted forms and the sign on the Bode plot
text: In (f), the divider \(G_0 = R_2/(R_1 + R_2)\) is what is left at DC; at high frequency, \(C_1\) shorts \(R_1\), and \(G_\infty = 1\). With the source shorted, \(C_1\) sees \(R_1 \parallel R_2\): \[G(s) = \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}\cdot\frac{1 + s/\omega_z}{1 + s/\omega_p}\] \[\omega_z = \frac{1}{R_1C_1}, \qquad \omega_p = \frac{1}{(R_1 \parallel R_2)\,C_1}\] The zero comes from the shortcut, \(\omega_z = \omega_p\,G_0\). Since \(R_1 \parallel R_2 < R_1\), the zero is always below the pole: the magnitude rises 20 dB per decade between them, from \(G_0\) to 1, and the phase rises and comes back to 0° (Bode by composition: from factored form to asymptote). It is the phase lead network, which comes back as a compensator in classical control.

title: RC and RL circuits: from the circuit to the pole-zero form
heading: Two corners with four resistors
summary: How to bring a passive circuit with one capacitor or one inductor to the factored form, through the gains at DC and at high frequency and the resistance the component sees, with the circuits grouped by the form they produce.
prereqs: Inverted forms and the sign on the Bode plot
text: Two networks with two corners: u reaches y through R1, and node A through C1 (a) or L1 (b); R4 goes from A to ground, R3 from A to y, and R2 from y to ground. In network (a), by the shortcut: DC (\(C_1\) open): \(u\) reaches \(y\) only through \(R_1\), and \(y\) sees \(R_2 \parallel (R_3 + R_4)\): \(G_0 = \dfrac{R_2 \parallel (R_3 + R_4)}{R_1 + R_2 \parallel (R_3 + R_4)}\). High frequency (\(C_1\) shorted): node A becomes \(u\), \(R_1\) and \(R_3\) are in parallel, and \(G_\infty = \dfrac{R_2}{R_2 + R_1 \parallel R_3}\). Pole: with \(u\) shorted, \(C_1\) sees \(R_4\) in parallel with \(R_3\) plus \(R_1 \parallel R_2\): \(\omega_p = \dfrac{1}{[R_4 \parallel (R_3 + R_1 \parallel R_2)]\,C_1}\). Zero: \(\omega_z = \omega_p\,G_0/G_\infty\), which simplifies to \(\omega_z = \dfrac{R_3 + R_4}{R_4\,(R_1 + R_3)\,C_1}\). At high frequency, \(C_1\) opens a second path from \(u\) to \(y\), through \(R_3\), in parallel with \(R_1\): \(G_\infty > G_0\), and the zero comes before the pole. With four 10 kΩ resistors and \(C_1\) = 10 nF, \(G_0 = 0.4\) and \(G_\infty = 0.667\): the zero at \(f_z = 1.59\) kHz and the pole at \(f_p = 2.65\) kHz.

title: Compensating the ×10 probe
heading: Compensating the ×10 probe
summary: The passive ×10 probe as two R∥C in series, with the resistive divider at DC and the capacitive one at an edge; R1C1 = R2C2 puts the zero on the pole, and a square wave shows whether the probe is overcompensated or undercompensated.
prereqs: RC and RL circuits: from the circuit to the pole-zero form
text: A passive ×10 probe puts 9 MΩ in series with the oscilloscope's 1 MΩ input: the resistive divider gives 1/10. The input, however, has capacitance, and so does the cable. With some 200 pF and nothing else, the 900 kΩ of \(R_1 \parallel R_2\) would make a pole at \(1/(2\pi \cdot 900\ \text{k}\Omega \cdot 200\ \text{pF}) = 884\) Hz: the probe would not even pass 1 kHz. The solution is a capacitor \(C_1\) in parallel with the probe's resistor. Frequencies in hertz, with \(\omega = 2\pi f\). The ×10 probe and the oscilloscope's input: in the probe tip, R1 = 9 MΩ in parallel with C1 = 22 pF; on the oscilloscope's side, R2 = 1 MΩ in parallel with C2, which gathers the input, the cable and the trimmer (100 to 300 pF).

title: Compensating the ×10 probe
heading: The transfer function
summary: The passive ×10 probe as two R∥C in series, with the resistive divider at DC and the capacitive one at an edge; R1C1 = R2C2 puts the zero on the pole, and a square wave shows whether the probe is overcompensated or undercompensated.
prereqs: RC and RL circuits: from the circuit to the pole-zero form
text: Each arm is an R∥C: \(Z_1 = R_1/(1 + sR_1C_1)\) and \(Z_2 = R_2/(1 + sR_2C_2)\). With the numerator and the denominator multiplied by both denominators, the divider gives \[G(s) = \frac{R_2\,(1 + sR_1C_1)}{(R_1 + R_2) + sR_1R_2\,(C_1 + C_2)}\] and, dividing by the constant term, the zero and the pole of First-order pole and zero appear: \[G(s) = G_0\,\frac{1 + s/\omega_z}{1 + s/\omega_p}, \qquad G_0 = \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}\] \[\omega_z = \frac{1}{R_1C_1}, \qquad \omega_p = \frac{1}{(R_1 \parallel R_2)(C_1 + C_2)}\] It is network (f) of RC and RL circuits: from the circuit to the pole-zero form with a capacitor in the lower arm too, and that note's shortcut checks the pole: with the source shorted, \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) are in parallel, and they see \(R_1 \parallel R_2\).

title: Compensating the ×10 probe
heading: Two dividers
summary: The passive ×10 probe as two R∥C in series, with the resistive divider at DC and the capacitive one at an edge; R1C1 = R2C2 puts the zero on the pole, and a square wave shows whether the probe is overcompensated or undercompensated.
prereqs: RC and RL circuits: from the circuit to the pole-zero form
text: At DC, the capacitors are open, and the resistors divide: \(G_0 = R_2/(R_1 + R_2) = 0.1\). At a fast edge, the capacitors' impedance is far below the resistors', and the capacitors divide. Since a capacitor's impedance is proportional to \(1/C\), \[G_\infty = \frac{1/C_2}{1/C_1 + 1/C_2} = \frac{C_1}{C_1 + C_2}\] the same as \(G_0\,\omega_p/\omega_z\). The probe is flat when both dividers are equal: \[\frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2} = \frac{C_1}{C_1 + C_2} \iff R_1C_1 = R_2C_2\] The zero falls on the pole, \(\omega_z = \omega_p\), the two factors cancel, and \(G = 0.1\) at every frequency. With \(R_1\) = 9 MΩ, \(R_2\) = 1 MΩ and \(C_1\) = 22 pF, compensation asks for \(C_2 = R_1C_1/R_2 = 198\) pF, and \(f_z = f_p = 804\) Hz.

title: Compensating the ×10 probe
heading: Away from compensation: the Bode plot and the square wave
summary: The passive ×10 probe as two R∥C in series, with the resistive divider at DC and the capacitive one at an edge; R1C1 = R2C2 puts the zero on the pole, and a square wave shows whether the probe is overcompensated or undercompensated.
prereqs: RC and RL circuits: from the circuit to the pole-zero form
text: The zero stays put at 804 Hz; \(C_2\) moves only the pole. Small \(C_2\), overcompensated. With 100 pF, \(f_p = 1.45\) kHz: the zero comes first, and the magnitude rises from −20 dB to \(20\log_{10} 0.180 = -14.9\) dB, with a positive phase between the two, like a phase lead network. At a 1 V edge, the output jumps to 0.180 V and comes down to 0.1 V: each edge overshoots the final level. Large \(C_2\), undercompensated. With 300 pF, \(f_p = 549\) Hz: the pole comes first, the magnitude falls to −23.3 dB, and the phase is negative, like a phase lag network. The edge jumps only to 0.068 V and climbs slowly to 0.1 V: the edges come out rounded. Starting from rest, the response to a step of amplitude \(U\) is \[y(t) = U\left[G_0 + (G_\infty - G_0)\,e^{-t/\tau}\right]\] It starts at the capacitive divider, \(G_\infty = C_1/(C_1+C_2)\), and ends at the resistive one, \(G_0\), with an exponential of \(\tau = 1/\omega_p = (R_1 \parallel R_2)(C_1 + C_2)\). Compensating means making both dividers equal. The figure lets you change \(C_2\); type the exact value in the box, such as 198p or 150 pF. The ×10 probe with R1 = 9 MΩ, C1 = 22 pF and R2 = 1 MΩ: the Bode plot, with the zero (○) and the pole (×), and the response to a 1 kHz square wave from 0 to 1 V. Move C2 between 100 and 300 pF.

title: Compensating the ×10 probe
heading: Which capacitor is adjusted
summary: The passive ×10 probe as two R∥C in series, with the resistive divider at DC and the capacitive one at an edge; R1C1 = R2C2 puts the zero on the pole, and a square wave shows whether the probe is overcompensated or undercompensated.
prereqs: RC and RL circuits: from the circuit to the pole-zero form
text: In most passive ×10 probes, the adjustment screw is a trimmer capacitor in the box next to the BNC connector, in parallel with the oscilloscope's input: it is part of \(C_2\), as in the model. In some models, the adjustment is in the probe's body: there the trimmer is in parallel with \(R_1\) and adjusts \(C_1\), and more capacitance overcompensates. You adjust it watching the oscilloscope's own calibration square wave, usually at 1 kHz, until the edges are square. Each input has its own capacitance, so the probe must be compensated again whenever it is moved to another channel or oscilloscope. Real probes also have high-frequency adjustments and a lossy cable, outside this model.

title: Compensating the ×10 probe
heading: In the converters
summary: The passive ×10 probe as two R∥C in series, with the resistive divider at DC and the capacitive one at an edge; R1C1 = R2C2 puts the zero on the pole, and a square wave shows whether the probe is overcompensated or undercompensated.
prereqs: RC and RL circuits: from the circuit to the pole-zero form
text: On the bench, the buck's ripple and the edges of the switching node are far above \(f_p\), where the probe's gain is \(C_1/(C_1 + C_2)\), not 0.1. With the example probe at 100 pF, the ripple appears 80% larger; at 300 pF, 32% smaller, and an overshoot or a slow edge on the screen may come from the probe, not from the converter. Compensate the probe before comparing the bench measurement with the lab oscilloscope's simulated scenarios. Exercise Another probe. This one has \(R_1\) = 9 MΩ and \(C_1\) = 15 pF. The oscilloscope's input is 1 MΩ in parallel with 20 pF, and the cable adds 80 pF. How much must the trimmer add to \(C_2\), and where are the zero and the pole? Exercise The step away from compensation. With the probe in the text, predict the response to a 1 V step, from rest, with \(C_2\) = 100 pF and with \(C_2\) = 300 pF: the jump at the edge, the final value, \(\tau\) and the value at 0.5 ms, half a period of a 1 kHz wave. Check it in the figure. Back to the converter Bench measurements of the buck and the boost go through a probe: compensate it before comparing with the scenarios of the lab's oscilloscope. The exact cancellation of a zero by a pole, harmless here, has risks inside a loop, in Pole-zero cancellation and its risks.

title: Sallen-Key active filters: the pole pair as a circuit
heading: Sallen-Key active filters: the pole pair as a circuit
summary: An op-amp as a follower, two resistors and two capacitors give the pole pair with f₀ and Q set by the components; the low-pass, the high-pass in the inverted pair's form, the design equations and the sections of a Butterworth cascade.
prereqs: Butterworth: the Q of each section and the order n
Second-order forms: zeros, undamped, inverted and right-half-plane
text: The pole pairs of Butterworth: the Q of each section and the order n need a circuit. A network of only resistors and capacitors has its poles on the real axis, with \(Q < 0.5\). With an op-amp as a voltage follower, the unity-gain Sallen-Key filter reaches any \(Q\), set by the ratio between the components. Ideal op-amp; frequencies in hertz, with \(\omega = 2\pi f\). Unity-gain Sallen-Key: (a) low-pass, R1 and R2 in series to the + input, C1 from the middle node to the output and C2 from the + input to ground; (b) high-pass, with the roles swapped: C1 and C2 in series, R1 from the middle node to the output and R2 to ground.

title: Sallen-Key active filters: the pole pair as a circuit
heading: The low-pass
summary: An op-amp as a follower, two resistors and two capacitors give the pole pair with f₀ and Q set by the components; the low-pass, the high-pass in the inverted pair's form, the design equations and the sections of a Butterworth cascade.
prereqs: Butterworth: the Q of each section and the order n
Second-order forms: zeros, undamped, inverted and right-half-plane
text: The follower puts the output \(y\) at the voltage of the + input. At that input, the current through \(R_2\) charges \(C_2\), and the middle node is at \(v_m = y\,(1 + sR_2C_2)\). At the middle node, the current from \(u\) through \(R_1\) leaves through \(R_2\) and through \(C_1\) to the output: \[\frac{u - v_m}{R_1} = \frac{v_m - y}{R_2} + sC_1\,(v_m - y)\] and, substituting \(v_m\), \[G(s) = \frac{1}{1 + sC_2\,(R_1 + R_2) + s^2R_1R_2C_1C_2}\] the pole pair of Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q. With \(R_1 = R_2 = R\), comparing with \(1 + s/(Q\omega_0) + (s/\omega_0)^2\): \[\omega_0 = \frac{1}{R\sqrt{C_1C_2}}, \qquad Q = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{C_1}{C_2}}\] The feedback through \(C_1\), the capacitor that goes to the output, is what takes \(Q\) above 0.5. Given \(f_0\) and \(Q\), choose \(C_2\) and compute \[C_1 = 4Q^2\,C_2, \qquad R = \frac{1}{2Q\,\omega_0\,C_2}\]

title: Sallen-Key active filters: the pole pair as a circuit
heading: The high-pass
summary: An op-amp as a follower, two resistors and two capacitors give the pole pair with f₀ and Q set by the components; the low-pass, the high-pass in the inverted pair's form, the design equations and the sections of a Butterworth cascade.
prereqs: Butterworth: the Q of each section and the order n
Second-order forms: zeros, undamped, inverted and right-half-plane
text: Swapping the resistors and the capacitors, \[G(s) = \frac{s^2R_1R_2C_1C_2}{1 + sR_1\,(C_1 + C_2) + s^2R_1R_2C_1C_2}\] With \(C_1 = C_2 = C\), dividing everything by the term in \(s^2\): \[G(s) = \frac{1}{1 + \dfrac{\omega_0}{Qs} + \left(\dfrac{\omega_0}{s}\right)^2}\] \[\omega_0 = \frac{1}{C\sqrt{R_1R_2}}, \qquad Q = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{R_2}{R_1}}\] It is exactly the inverted pole pair of Second-order forms: zeros, undamped, inverted and right-half-plane, a double pure differentiator times the ordinary pair: +40 dB per decade up to \(f_0\), 0 dB above. \(R_1\) goes to the output, \(R_2\) to ground. To design, choose \(C\) and compute \(R_1 = 1/(2Q\,\omega_0C)\); or choose \(R_1\) and compute \(C = 1/(2Q\,\omega_0R_1)\). Either way, \(R_2 = 4Q^2R_1\).

title: Sallen-Key active filters: the pole pair as a circuit
heading: Butterworth and Bessel
summary: An op-amp as a follower, two resistors and two capacitors give the pole pair with f₀ and Q set by the components; the low-pass, the high-pass in the inverted pair's form, the design equations and the sections of a Butterworth cascade.
prereqs: Butterworth: the Q of each section and the order n
Second-order forms: zeros, undamped, inverted and right-half-plane
text: In the second-order Butterworth, \(Q = 0.7071\): \(C_1 = 2C_2\) in the low-pass and \(R_2 = 2R_1\) in the high-pass, and the −3 dB corner, \(f_c\), is \(f_0\) itself. The Bessel uses \(Q = 1/\sqrt 3 = 0.577\): it trades the flattest magnitude for the flattest group delay, and its step overshoots its final value by only 0.43%, against 4.3% for the Butterworth. Its magnitude starts falling earlier: \(f_c = 0.786\,f_0\). A Bessel with its corner at \(f_c\) needs \(f_0 = f_c/0.786 = 1.272\,f_c\).

title: Sallen-Key active filters: the pole pair as a circuit
heading: Example: third-order Butterworth low-pass at 1 kHz
summary: An op-amp as a follower, two resistors and two capacitors give the pole pair with f₀ and Q set by the components; the low-pass, the high-pass in the inverted pair's form, the design equations and the sections of a Butterworth cascade.
prereqs: Butterworth: the Q of each section and the order n
Second-order forms: zeros, undamped, inverted and right-half-plane
text: From the table in Butterworth: the Q of each section and the order n, a real pole and a pair with \(Q = 1\), both at \(f_0\) = 1 kHz. Pair. With \(C_2\) = 79.58 nF, \(C_1 = 4C_2\) = 318.3 nF and \(R = 1/(2 \cdot 2\pi \cdot 1\ \text{kHz} \cdot 79.58\ \text{nF})\) = 1.000 kΩ. Real pole. An RC, followed by another follower, so that the load does not move the pole: with \(C_3\) = 100 nF, \(R_3 = 1/(2\pi f_0C_3)\) = 1591.5 Ω. Cascade. Each stage ends at an op-amp output, so the next stage does not load it: the function is the product. Third-order Butterworth low-pass at 1 kHz: the RC's real pole and the Sallen-Key's pair with Q = 1. At 1 kHz, the pair gives 0 dB, and the pole, −3.01 dB. Here \(C_2\) was chosen to give a round \(R\) = 1 kΩ; in practice, the capacitors come from the standard series, and the computation gives the resistors.

title: Sallen-Key active filters: the pole pair as a circuit
heading: In practice
summary: An op-amp as a follower, two resistors and two capacitors give the pole pair with f₀ and Q set by the components; the low-pass, the high-pass in the inverted pair's form, the design equations and the sections of a Butterworth cascade.
prereqs: Butterworth: the Q of each section and the order n
Second-order forms: zeros, undamped, inverted and right-half-plane
text: A real op-amp has a finite bandwidth: in the high-pass, the passband ends there; in the low-pass, above it, the signal leaks through \(C_1\) to the output, whose impedance rises with frequency, and the attenuation stops growing. Choose an op-amp with a bandwidth well above \(f_0\), even more so with a high \(Q\). \(Q\) depends on a ratio of components: with 5% capacitors, \(C_1/C_2\) may be off by 10%, and \(Q\) by about 5%.

title: Sallen-Key active filters: the pole pair as a circuit
heading: In the converters
summary: An op-amp as a follower, two resistors and two capacitors give the pole pair with f₀ and Q set by the components; the low-pass, the high-pass in the inverted pair's form, the design equations and the sections of a Butterworth cascade.
prereqs: Butterworth: the Q of each section and the order n
Second-order forms: zeros, undamped, inverted and right-half-plane
text: The active version of the ADC's measurement filter is this low-pass, Butterworth, with \(f_0\) = 80 kHz: \(R\) = 10 kΩ, \(C_2\) = 141 pF and \(C_1\) = 281 pF (Sensing and anti-aliasing filter). Exercise Fourth-order Butterworth. Design a fourth-order Butterworth low-pass at 1 kHz with two Sallen-Key stages, all resistors 1 kΩ. Compute the capacitors of both sections. Exercise Third-order Butterworth high-pass. At 1 kHz, with all capacitors 100 nF: a Sallen-Key stage with \(Q = 1\) and an RC high-pass with a follower. Compute the resistors. Exercise Three-way crossover. An active loudspeaker splits the signal into bass, midrange and treble outputs, with crossovers at 120 Hz and 1.44 kHz, using fourth-order Linkwitz-Riley filters: each filter is two identical second-order Butterworth Sallen-Key stages in cascade, −6 dB at the corner. Bass: a low-pass at 120 Hz; midrange: a high-pass at 120 Hz times a low-pass at 1.44 kHz; treble: a high-pass at 1.44 kHz. With \(C_2\) = 47 nF (\(C_1\) = 2 × 47 nF in parallel) in the 120 Hz low-pass, 4.7 nF in the 1.44 kHz one, \(C\) = 100 nF in the 120 Hz high-pass and 10 nF in the 1.44 kHz one, compute the resistors and sketch the midrange asymptotes. Why not a single second-order Butterworth Sallen-Key in each output? The midrange output: two inverted pairs at 120 Hz and two pairs at 1.44 kHz, all with Q = 0.7071. Back to the converter The choice between the RC and the Sallen-Key in the measurement filter, by its phase cost in the loop, is in Sensing and anti-aliasing filter.

title: From circuit to transfer function
heading: From circuit to transfer function
summary: The circuits that realize a transfer function: RC and RL networks, the ×10 probe and the Sallen-Key, taken to the factored form and the Bode plot.
text: This trail takes the pole and zero forms to the circuit: given a network of resistors, capacitors and inductors, or an active filter, reach the factored form and the Bode plot without solving the whole network. It needs the From Laplace to Bode trail: the first-order forms, the inverted ones, the second-order pair and the Butterworth. RC and RL circuits: from the circuit to the pole-zero form: circuits with one capacitor or one inductor brought to the factored form, through the gains at DC and at high frequency and the resistance the component sees. Compensating the ×10 probe: the ×10 probe, two R∥C in series, where the zero and the pole cancel when the resistive and the capacitive dividers are equal. Sallen-Key active filters: the pole pair as a circuit: the pole pair as a circuit, with an op-amp as a follower, and the sections of the Butterworth cascade.

title: From circuit to transfer function
heading: End of the trail
summary: The circuits that realize a transfer function: RC and RL networks, the ×10 probe and the Sallen-Key, taken to the factored form and the Bode plot.

The sensing filter in front of the ADC is an RC, or a Sallen-Key in the active version (Sensing and anti-aliasing filter), and the buck's plant comes out of the averaged circuit the same way (The buck's transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\); the method step by step, in From circuit to factored form (reinforcement)). From here, go on to units 2 to 4, in the Closing and compensating the loop trail.

title: Bode by composition: from factored form to asymptote
heading: Bode by composition: from factored form to asymptote

title: Bode by composition: from factored form to asymptote
heading: The asymptotes of each factor
summary: Two tables sum up the first- and second-order forms, and the recipe works both ways, adding up the factors of G(s) into the asymptotic Bode plot and reading G(s) back from it.

The magnitude gives the slopes in dB per decade, with the corner at \(f\); the phase goes from \(\omega \to 0^+\) to \(\omega \to \infty\) along a line from \(f/10\) to \(10 f\). title: Bode by composition: from factored form to asymptote
heading: The phase rule
summary: Two tables sum up the first- and second-order forms, and the recipe works both ways, adding up the factors of G(s) into the asymptotic Bode plot and reading G(s) back from it.
prereqs: Second-order forms: zeros, undamped, inverted and right-half-plane
text: Each factor has a phase of 0° at the end where it tends to 1 (DC in the ordinary and RHP forms, high frequency in the inverted ones). The total phase is the sum of the factors' phases, plus 180° if \(K < 0\); a program may show it shifted by 360°.

title: Bode by composition: from factored form to asymptote
heading: The recipe
summary: Two tables sum up the first- and second-order forms, and the recipe works both ways, adding up the factors of G(s) into the asymptotic Bode plot and reading G(s) back from it.
prereqs: Second-order forms: zeros, undamped, inverted and right-half-plane
text: From the equation to the plot. Write \(G(s)\) as \(K\) times table factors, naming each form. List the corners in increasing order. At low frequency, add the initial slopes (∓20 at the origin, ±20 or ±40 in the inverted forms, zero elsewhere) and find one point of the line. Where all factors are 1, the level is \(20\log_{10}|K|\). With a root at the origin, \(K(s/\omega_a)^{\pm 1}\) is \(20\log_{10}|K|\) dB at \(f_a\), even if \(f_a\) lies outside the range of the corners; carry that point to the first corner with \(\pm 20\log_{10}(f/f_a)\). At each corner, add the factor's change of slope: ±20 for first order, ±40 for a pair. Add up the phase lines, each from the table's initial value to its final one. Mark the error at the corner: 3 dB for a first-order factor, below for the pole and above for the zero; \(20\log_{10} Q\) dB for a pair, above for poles and below for zeros (with \(Q < 1\) the side flips). Corners less than a decade apart When the phase lines overlap, sort the \(f/10\) and \(10f\) points of all factors and, in each interval, add the slopes of the active lines: ±45° per decade for first order, ±90° for a pair.

title: Bode by composition: from factored form to asymptote
heading: Reading back: from the asymptote to the equation
summary: Two tables sum up the first- and second-order forms, and the recipe works both ways, adding up the factors of G(s) into the asymptotic Bode plot and reading G(s) back from it.
prereqs: Second-order forms: zeros, undamped, inverted and right-half-plane
text: At low frequency: 0 dB per decade and 0°, a DC gain, at \(20\log_{10}|K|\); −20 and −90°, a pure integrator or an inverted zero; +20 and +90°, a pure differentiator or an inverted pole; −40 and −180°, a double pure integrator or an inverted zero pair; +40 and +180°, a double pure differentiator or an inverted pole pair. Each change of slope marks a corner: ±20 dB per decade, a first-order factor; ±40, a pair if there is a peak or a dip; a −40 with the curve 6 dB below is two equal real poles (\(Q = 0.5\)). If, at a corner, the magnitude and the phase move in opposite directions, the factor's root is in the right half-plane. Check by the final phase: with all roots on the left, it would be ±90° per first-order factor and ±180° per pair, plus that of the roots at the origin; each 180° less is an RHP zero, and each 360°, an RHP zero pair, even with overlapping ramps. A pair's \(Q\) comes from the real curve at \(f_0\): \(Q = 10^{(\text{curve} - \text{asymptote})/20}\) for a pole pair and \(10^{(\text{asymptote} - \text{curve})/20}\) for a zero pair, if the other corners are more than a decade away. Pure integrators and differentiators do not disturb it: their asymptote is exact.

title: Bode by composition: from factored form to asymptote
heading: Example both ways
summary: Two tables sum up the first- and second-order forms, and the recipe works both ways, adding up the factors of G(s) into the asymptotic Bode plot and reading G(s) back from it.
prereqs: Second-order forms: zeros, undamped, inverted and right-half-plane
text: \[G(s) = \frac{\omega_i}{s}\cdot\frac{1 + s/\omega_1}{1 + s/(5\omega_2) + (s/\omega_2)^2}, \qquad f_i = 200\ \text{Hz},\ f_1 = 1\ \text{kHz},\ f_2 = 10\ \text{kHz}\] Magnitude: −20 dB per decade up to 1 kHz (0 dB at 200 Hz), flat at −14 dB up to 10 kHz and −40 after it. The phase, with overlapping lines: Phase 100 Hz to 1 kHz 1 kHz to 10 kHz 10 kHz to 100 kHz Active lines zero zero and pair pair Slope (° per decade) +45 −45 −90 Phase at the end (−90° at the start) −45° −90° −180° Back, the real curve passes 14 dB above the asymptote at 10 kHz: \(Q = 10^{14/20} = 5\). The example: pure integrator, zero and pole pair with Q = 5, asymptotes and exact curve.

title: Bode by composition: from factored form to asymptote
heading: In the converters
summary: Two tables sum up the first- and second-order forms, and the recipe works both ways, adding up the factors of G(s) into the asymptotic Bode plot and reading G(s) back from it.
prereqs: Second-order forms: zeros, undamped, inverted and right-half-plane
text: The buck's plant at 9 Ω (The buck's transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\)) is a 27.6 dB gain, a pole pair at 4.96 kHz with \(Q = 7.1\) and the ESR zero at 677 kHz: the magnitude is flat up to 4.96 kHz, falls 40 dB per decade up to 677 kHz and 20 after it, and at the peak the real curve is 44.6 dB, \(20\log_{10} 7.1 = 17\) dB above the asymptote. Exercise From the equation to the plot. Draw the asymptotes of \[G(s) = \frac{20\,(1 - s/\omega_2)}{(1 + s/\omega_1)\,\left(1 + s/(2\omega_3) + (s/\omega_3)^2\right)}\] with \(f_1 = 100\) Hz, \(f_2 = 2\) kHz and \(f_3 = 20\) kHz. Where does the phase end? Gain, pole, RHP zero and pole pair. Exercise From the plot to the equation. Write \(G(s)\) from the plot. Read the gain, the corners and the form of each factor. Back to the converter The circuit origin of the buck plant's \(G_0\), \(f_0\) and \(Q\) is in From circuit to factored form (reinforcement). The same product describes a compensator: the PI is an inverted zero (PI, phase lead and the type III).

title: Exercise list: from the equation to the Bode plot
heading: Exercise list: from the equation to the Bode plot
summary: Six functions in factored form, in increasing difficulty, to draw the magnitude and phase asymptotes, with close corners, a pure differentiator's reference, RHP zeros, a Butterworth band-pass and a negative gain.
prereqs: Bode by composition: from factored form to asymptote
text: Six exercises to practice the path from the equation to the plot, from the simplest to the hardest. In each one, draw the magnitude and phase asymptotes on paper: the corners, each segment's slope and level, and the points where the phase changes slope. Only then open the plot, with the "Show the plot" button, and the answer. The figure's switch turns on the exact curve, to check the error at the corners. In the answers, the slopes are in dB per decade and degrees per decade, and the "active lines" are the factors' phase lines in each interval. Exercise 1. Corners a decade apart. Draw the asymptotes of \(G(s) = \dfrac{100\,(1 + s/\omega_3)}{(1 + s/\omega_1)(1 + s/\omega_2)(1 + s/\omega_4)}\), with \(f_1 = 10\) Hz, \(f_2 = 100\) Hz, \(f_3 = 1\) kHz and \(f_4 = 10\) kHz. The phase lines overlap: use Bode by composition: from factored form to asymptote. Three poles and a zero, a decade apart. Exercise 2. The reference above the corners. Draw the asymptotes of \(G(s) = 10\,\dfrac{(s/\omega_i)(1 + s/\omega_1)}{\left(1 + s/(Q\omega_2) + (s/\omega_2)^2\right)(1 + s/\omega_3)}\), with \(f_i = 1\) MHz, \(f_1 = 10\) Hz, \(f_2 = 1\) kHz, \(f_3 = 100\) kHz and \(Q = 10\). The pure differentiator has its reference above all the corners. A pure differentiator with its reference at 1 MHz. Exercise 3. Pure integrator and RHP zero. Draw the asymptotes of \(G(s) = 0.1\,\dfrac{(1 + s/\omega_1)(1 - s/\omega_2)}{(s/\omega_i)(1 + s/\omega_3)}\), with \(f_i = 10\) Hz, \(f_1 = 1\) kHz, \(f_2 = 10\) kHz and \(f_3 = 1\) MHz. A pure integrator, two zeros and a pole. Exercise 4. RHP zero pair and pure integrator. Draw the asymptotes of \(G(s) = \dfrac{\left(1 - s/(Q\omega_1) + (s/\omega_1)^2\right)(1 + s/\omega_2)}{(s/\omega_i)\left(1 + s/(Q\omega_3) + (s/\omega_3)^2\right)}\), with \(f_i = 1\) kHz, \(f_1 = 100\) Hz, \(f_2 = 10\) kHz, \(f_3 = 100\) kHz and \(Q = 10\). Mark the dip and the peak of the exact curve. A pure integrator, an RHP zero pair, a zero and a pole pair. Exercise 5. Butterworth band-pass. A second-order Butterworth high-pass at 100 Hz, cascaded with a third-order Butterworth low-pass at 10 kHz, with a gain of 1 in the band. Which sections, with what \(Q\)? The figure's equation is the answer: cover it, write your own with Butterworth: the Q of each section and the order n, then draw the asymptotes. Second-order high-pass and third-order low-pass. Exercise 6. Negative gain. Draw the asymptotes of \(G(s) = -10\,\dfrac{1 + s/\omega_2}{1 + s/\omega_1}\), with \(f_1 = 100\) Hz and \(f_2 = 10\) kHz. Where does the phase start? A negative gain, a pole and a zero. Back to the converter The Bode plot of the buck's plant (The buck's transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\)) and that of the loop gain (Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins) are drawn this way, factor by factor; the boost's plant brings the RHP zero of The right-half-plane zero. The reverse list is Exercise list: from the Bode plot to the equation.

title: Exercise list: from the Bode plot to the equation
heading: Exercise list: from the Bode plot to the equation
summary: Six asymptotic Bode plots, in increasing difficulty, to read the gain, the corners, each factor's form and the Q and write G(s) in factored form.
prereqs: Bode by composition: from factored form to asymptote
text: Six exercises to practice reading back, as in Bode by composition: from factored form to asymptote, from the simplest to the hardest. In each one, write \(G(s)\) on paper, with the gain, the corners and each factor's form, and only then open the answer. Under each plot, the figure lists the corners and, separately, the 0 dB frequency of each pure integrator or pure differentiator; a pair's \(Q\) is read on the exact curve, which the figure's switch turns on. The "Show the answer" button gives the equation; the answer box, the reasoning. In the answers, the magnitude is in dB per decade, and the phase comes with the intervals of its lines. Exercise 1. Gain, pole, zero and pole. Three corners, two decades apart. Exercise 2. A pure differentiator and two pairs. Turn on the exact curve: the pairs' \(Q\) comes from it. No flat level at low frequency, with a peak and a dip. Exercise 3. Four corners and the final phase. Compare the final phase with the one the corners would give. Two corners raise the magnitude, two lower it. Exercise 4. Pure integrator, dip and peak. Turn on the exact curve. Watch the phase between 1 kHz and 100 kHz, where the lines overlap. A pure integrator and three corners, a decade apart. Exercise 5. A dip with the phase falling. Turn on the exact curve and check each factor's form by the phase. The magnitude rises 40 dB per decade from the dip. Exercise 6. A pair or two poles? The two plots have the same exact curve: turn it on in both. Write \(G(s)\) for each and show that they are the same function. Which asymptote stays closer to the curve? Plot A: one corner of −40 dB per decade. Plot B: two corners of −20 dB per decade. Back to the converter The buck's plant (The buck's transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\)) reads this way: a flat level, a high-\(Q\) pair and the ESR zero. So does the loop gain of Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins, with the compensator's integrator at low frequency. The reverse list is Exercise list: from the equation to the Bode plot.

title: Butterworth: the Q of each section and the order n
heading: Butterworth: the Q of each section and the order n
summary: The maximally flat filter, built as a cascade of pole pairs with the same f₀ and a real pole for odd orders, with the table of Q from n = 2 to 8 and a band-pass by composition.
prereqs: Second-order filters: each one a composition of the forms
text: An order-\(n\) low-pass is Butterworth when its magnitude is as flat as possible below the corner: \[|G(j\omega)| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + (f/f_0)^{2n}}}\] At \(f_0\) the curve is at −3 dB for any \(n\), with no peak, and above it falls \(20n\) dB per decade. With \(n = 2\), it is the low-pass of Second-order filters: each one a composition of the forms with \(Q = 1/\sqrt 2 = 0.707\): the largest \(Q\) with no resonant peak (Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q).

title: Butterworth: the Q of each section and the order n
heading: The poles and the Q of each pair
summary: The maximally flat filter, built as a cascade of pole pairs with the same f₀ and a real pole for odd orders, with the table of Q from n = 2 to 8 and a band-pass by composition.
prereqs: Second-order filters: each one a composition of the forms
text: The poles lie on a circle of radius \(\omega_0\), \(180^\circ/n\) apart and symmetric about the negative real axis. A pair at an angle \(\theta\) from that axis has real part \(-\omega_0\cos\theta\), and since a pair's real part is \(-\omega_0/(2Q)\), each pair has \[Q_k = \frac{1}{2\cos\theta_k}.\] For even \(n\) the angles are \(90^\circ/n\), \(3 \cdot 90^\circ/n\)…; for odd \(n\) one pole sits on the real axis, at \(-\omega_0\), and the pairs are at \(180^\circ/n\), \(2 \cdot 180^\circ/n\)… \(n\) Real pole \(Q_k\) of the pairs At high frequency 2 — 0.7071 −40 dB per decade 3 at \(-\omega_0\) 1.0000 −60 dB per decade 4 — 0.5412, 1.3066 −80 dB per decade 5 at \(-\omega_0\) 0.6180, 1.6180 −100 dB per decade 6 — 0.5176, 0.7071, 1.9319 −120 dB per decade 7 at \(-\omega_0\) 0.5550, 0.8019, 2.2470 −140 dB per decade 8 — 0.5098, 0.6013, 0.9000, 2.5629 −160 dB per decade

title: Butterworth: the Q of each section and the order n
heading: The cascade
summary: The maximally flat filter, built as a cascade of pole pairs with the same f₀ and a real pole for odd orders, with the table of Q from n = 2 to 8 and a band-pass by composition.
prereqs: Second-order filters: each one a composition of the forms
text: The filter is the product of its sections, \(G_n(s) = \prod_k G_k(s)\), all with the same \(f_0\). Each block is a stage of its own, which does not load the next, so the whole function is the product: even orders use pole pairs only, and odd orders add a real pole, which has no \(Q\). Butterworth as a cascade, one block per section, all at the same f₀: order 3, a real pole and a pair with Q = 1.0000; order 4, pairs with Q = 0.5412 and 1.3066; order 5, a real pole and pairs with Q = 0.6180 and 1.6180. The high-\(Q\) sections peak on their own; it is the product that stays flat. At \(f_0\) the cascade's error is the sum of the sections' errors: each pair gives \(20\log_{10} Q_k\) dB, and the real pole −3.01 dB. With \(n = 4\), \(-5.33 + 2.32 = -3.01\) dB; with \(n = 5\), \(-3.01 - 4.18 + 4.18 = -3.01\) dB. The Butterworth high-pass uses the same \(Q_k\) and the same \(f_0\), through the inverted forms: each pair becomes the inverted pole pair, \((s/\omega_0)^2/D_k\), and the real pole the inverted pole, \((s/\omega_0)/(1 + s/\omega_0)\). The asymptote rises \(20n\) dB per decade up to \(f_0\) and is flat above it, and the phase goes from \(+90n\)° to 0°.

title: Butterworth: the Q of each section and the order n
heading: A band-pass by composition
summary: The maximally flat filter, built as a cascade of pole pairs with the same f₀ and a real pole for odd orders, with the table of Q from n = 2 to 8 and a band-pass by composition.
prereqs: Second-order filters: each one a composition of the forms
text: A wide band-pass is a high-pass cascaded with a low-pass with a higher corner. Take a third-order high-pass at \(f_1 = 200\) Hz and a fifth-order low-pass at \(f_2 = 10\) kHz: \[G(s) = G_{\mathrm{HP}}(s)\,G_{\mathrm{LP}}(s)\] \[G_{\mathrm{HP}}(s) = \frac{1}{1 + \omega_1/s} \cdot \frac{1}{1 + \omega_1/s + (\omega_1/s)^2}\] \[\begin{aligned} G_{\mathrm{LP}}(s) = {} & \frac{1}{1 + s/\omega_2} \cdot \frac{1}{1 + \frac{s}{0.618\,\omega_2} + \left(\frac{s}{\omega_2}\right)^2} \\ & \cdot \frac{1}{1 + \frac{s}{1.618\,\omega_2} + \left(\frac{s}{\omega_2}\right)^2} \end{aligned}\] These are five known forms: the inverted pole and the inverted pair with \(Q = 1\) in the high-pass; the pole, the pair with \(Q = 0.618\) and the pair with \(Q = 1.618\) in the low-pass. Butterworth band-pass: third-order high-pass at 200 Hz and fifth-order low-pass at 10 kHz. Magnitude. +60 dB per decade up to 200 Hz, 0 dB between 200 Hz and 10 kHz, −100 dB per decade above. At 1 Hz, \(-60\log_{10} 200 = -138\) dB. Corners. The exact curve passes at −3.01 dB at both: at 200 Hz, −3.01 dB from the inverted pole and 0 dB from the pair with \(Q = 1\); at 10 kHz, −3.01 − 4.18 + 4.18 dB. Phase. Each factor is 0° where it tends to 1, so the phase starts at +270° (the high-pass), and ends at −450° (the low-pass). In the middle of the band the exact curve passes close to 0° (+4.5° at 1 kHz); the asymptote gives about +41° there, because the phase lines of the two halves overlap from 1 to 2 kHz. A program may show the same curve shifted by a multiple of 360°, from −90° to −810° for instance: it is the same complex number.

title: Butterworth: the Q of each section and the order n
heading: In the converters
summary: The maximally flat filter, built as a cascade of pole pairs with the same f₀ and a real pole for odd orders, with the table of Q from n = 2 to 8 and a band-pass by composition.
prereqs: Second-order filters: each one a composition of the forms
text: The buck's ideal lossless LC pair would only be Butterworth with \(R\sqrt{C/L} = 0.707\): with 22 µH and 47 µF, a 0.48 Ω load, 19 A at 9 V. At 9 Ω the lossless pair would have \(Q = 13.2\); the 7.1 of The buck's transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\) includes the losses. The plant is never flat, and it is the loop that damps it. The measurement filter in front of the ADC, on the other hand, is a design choice, and in its active version it is a Butterworth with \(n = 2\) (Sensing and anti-aliasing filter). Exercise From the specification to the plot. A band-pass is the cascade of a second-order Butterworth high-pass at 50 Hz with a fourth-order Butterworth low-pass at 5 kHz. Identify in the figure's equation the sections and their \(Q\), and draw the magnitude and phase asymptotes, with the slope in each band and the phase from low to high frequency. From the specification to the plot: second-order high-pass and fourth-order low-pass. Back to the converter The lab's Butterworth measurement filter is in Sensing and anti-aliasing filter. The sum of forms that builds any cascade is in Bode by composition: from factored form to asymptote.

title: Feedback and margins
heading: Feedback and margins
summary: How the loop closes, what the sensitivity 1/(1 + T) says, and why the phase and gain margins bound the peak of |S|.
prereqs: Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q
text: On its own, the buck regulates poorly: a step in the duty cycle makes the output overshoot by 80 % of the jump and ring for 1.7 ms (Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q), and the gain changes with input and load. Feedback measures the output, compares it with the reference and corrects the duty cycle. One trip around the loop passes through the controller, the modulator, the plant and the sensor: \[T(s) = \beta\,G_c(s)\,G_m\,G_{vd}(s)\] Call \(A = G_c\,G_m\,G_{vd}\) the forward path. With feedback \(\beta\), the closed loop is \(G_x = A/(1 + T)\), and the poles of \(G_x\) are the roots of \(1 + T(s) = 0\); how they move as the gain rises is in Root locus (qualitative reading). In this course's converters, the ADC reads the output voltage itself, and \(\beta = 1\).

title: Feedback and margins
heading: What the loop buys: the sensitivity
summary: How the loop closes, what the sensitivity 1/(1 + T) says, and why the phase and gain margins bound the peak of |S|.
prereqs: Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q
text: \[S(s) = \frac{1}{1 + T(s)}, \qquad \frac{T(s)}{1 + T(s)} = 1 - S(s)\] Where \(|T|\) is large, a disturbance at the output comes out divided by \(|1 + T|\), and the output follows the reference. Where \(|T|\) is small, \(S \approx 1\): the loop does not act. Near the crossover, \(|1 + T|\) can be less than 1, and the loop amplifies the disturbance. That is the price of bandwidth.

title: Feedback and margins
heading: Crossover and margins
summary: How the loop closes, what the sensitivity 1/(1 + T) says, and why the phase and gain margins bound the peak of |S|.
prereqs: Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q
text: Crossover frequency \(f_c\): the last frequency at which \(|T|\) equals 1. A loop with an integrator can cross 1 more than once, and the margin is read at the last crossing. In order of magnitude, it is the loop's bandwidth. Phase margin (MF): \(180^\circ + \angle T\) at \(f_c\). Gain margin (MG): at \(f_{180}\), the frequency at which the phase of \(T\) reaches −180°, how much \(|T|\) can rise before it equals 1. In dB, \(\mathrm{MG} = -20\log_{10}|T(f_{180})|\). The MF measures how far \(T\) is from the point −1 at the crossover; the MG, at the point where the curve crosses the negative real axis. Read another way, the MF is the extra delay the loop tolerates, \(\Delta t = \mathrm{MF}/(360^\circ f_c)\), and the MG is the extra gain it tolerates.

title: Feedback and margins
heading: Stability of the closed loop
summary: How the loop closes, what the sensitivity 1/(1 + T) says, and why the phase and gain margins bound the peak of |S|.
prereqs: Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q
text: The loop is stable when \(1 + T(s) = 0\) has no roots in the right half-plane. This is the closed-loop criterion, and it does not reduce to the plant's poles. In open loop, stability depends only on the poles, as Transfer function and factored form showed; in closed loop, phase counts. A right-half-plane zero of \(G_{vd}\) creates no unstable pole, but it enters \(T\) as a phase lag, and that lag falls right near the crossover. The phase margin shrinks. With more gain, the crossover rises to where the zero takes away more phase, and the loop can oscillate. That is why Right-half-plane zero: the effect on the loop limits the crossover. When the open-loop plant is stable, as the buck and the boost are in this course, the Nyquist criterion says the same: the curve of \(T\) must not wind around −1.

title: Feedback and margins
heading: How much sensitivity: the peak Ms
summary: How the loop closes, what the sensitivity 1/(1 + T) says, and why the phase and gain margins bound the peak of |S|.
prereqs: Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q
text: The largest value of \(|S|\) over all frequencies is the peak sensitivity, \(M_s = \max|S|\). It is the worst amplification of a disturbance. The margins are local measures, at \(f_c\) and at \(f_{180}\), and \(M_s\) is global. The two are tied together by inequalities that follow from \(|S| \le M_s\): Phase margin. At \(f_c\), \(|T| = 1\) and \(T = -e^{j\,\mathrm{MF}}\), so \(|1 + T| = |1 - e^{j\,\mathrm{MF}}| = 2\,\sin(\mathrm{MF}/2)\). Hence \(|S(f_c)| = 1/\big(2\,\sin(\mathrm{MF}/2)\big) \le M_s\), and \[\mathrm{MF} \ge 2\arcsin\frac{1}{2M_s}\] Gain margin. At \(f_{180}\), \(T = -a\), with \(a = |T(f_{180})|\) real. Then \(|S| = 1/|1 - a| \le M_s\), or \(|1 - a| \ge 1/M_s\). If \(a < 1\), the usual case, \(a \le 1 - 1/M_s\), and the margin as a factor, \(1/a\), is at least \(M_s/(M_s - 1)\). If \(a > 1\), the margin is in reducing the gain, and \(a \ge 1 + 1/M_s\). In any case, the margin as a factor is at least \(1 + 1/M_s\): \[\mathrm{MG} \ge 1 + \frac{1}{M_s}\] With \(M_s = 1.61\), the general bound gives 4.2 dB. In the common case \(a < 1\), which is the buck's, the bound \(M_s/(M_s - 1) = 2.63\) gives 8.4 dB, the value used in From margin to damping: the ζ ≈ MF/100 rule and where it fails. These are worst-case inequalities. A large margin does not guarantee a small \(M_s\), but a small \(M_s\) guarantees the margins.

title: Feedback and margins
heading: A delay is not a pole
summary: How the loop closes, what the sensitivity 1/(1 + T) says, and why the phase and gain margins bound the peak of |S|.
prereqs: Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q
text: \[\varphi_d(f) = -360^\circ\, f\, t_d, \qquad t_d = (1 + D)\,T_s\] A pure delay, \(e^{-s t_d}\), has a magnitude of 1 and a phase that falls in a straight line with \(f\), without limit. A pole changes the magnitude, and its phase stops at −90°. The delay is not a × in the s-plane, but it eats more margin the higher the crossover. The buck's loop gain with the 2p2z: read the crossover, the phase margin and the gain margin, and move the crossover to watch the margins fall.

title: Feedback and margins
heading: In the converters
summary: How the loop closes, what the sensitivity 1/(1 + T) says, and why the phase and gain margins bound the peak of |S|.
prereqs: Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q
text: In the buck, with the first 2p2z design, \(f_c\) = 8 kHz, with MF of 41° and MG of 13.9 dB (Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins). Averaged model, 24 V → 9 V, 9 Ω, with the delay \((1 + D)\,T_s\). In it, \(|T|\) crosses 1 three times: near 1 kHz, falling; near 2.35 kHz, rising; and at 8 kHz, falling. The last is the \(f_c\). At 8 kHz, \(|S| = 1.42\) (+3 dB), the value the MF of 41.3° gives in the formula: there the loop amplifies a disturbance instead of damping it. The worst point is 9.8 kHz, where \(|1 + T| = 0.62\), so \(M_s = 1.61\). The inequalities above ask for an MF of at least 36° and, since the phase crossing sits below −1 (\(a = 0.20\)), an MG of at least 8.4 dB. The design, with 41° and 13.9 dB, meets both without touching them. Extra delay tolerated: \(41^\circ/(360^\circ \cdot 8\,\text{kHz}) = 14.2\) µs, about 2.8 periods of 200 kHz. The delay the loop already has, \((1 + D)T_s = 6.875\) µs, uses 19.8° at 8 kHz (Computation and PWM delay). Extra gain tolerated: 13.9 dB, or 4.95 times. What the 41° margin means for the load step, and why the practical damping rule misses here, is in From margin to damping: the ζ ≈ MF/100 rule and where it fails. Exercise A communication interruption starts delaying the duty-cycle write by a full period, 5 µs. What happens to the MF of the 2p2z? How many more periods could the loop take before it oscillates? From the author's handbook Modelagem de Conversores Chaveados: do modelo à bancada virtual: the phase and gain margins in the measured response. Back to the converter With these concepts, go back to Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins, which shows the margins of the buck's four controllers, and to Computation and PWM delay, which counts where the firmware's delay comes from.

title: First-order pole and zero
heading: First-order pole and zero
summary: A real pole drops the magnitude at −20 dB per decade and lags the phase down to −90°; a zero does the opposite. The asymptote is 3 dB off at the pole frequency, where the real phase is −45°.
text: The first-order factors are the blocks \(1 + s/\omega\) of the factored form. This note covers the two simplest forms, the real pole and the real zero, both in the left half-plane, and how each becomes two straight lines on the Bode plot, one for the magnitude and one for the phase. The other first-order forms come in the next notes: at the origin (Pole and zero at the origin: pure integrator and pure differentiator), in the right half-plane (Right-half-plane pole and zero) and inverted (Inverted forms and the sign on the Bode plot). The two forms of this note: pick the form and move the corner. Beside it, the s-plane, with the pole (×) or the zero (○) at −ω.

title: First-order pole and zero
heading: The pole
summary: A real pole drops the magnitude at −20 dB per decade and lags the phase down to −90°; a zero does the opposite. The asymptote is 3 dB off at the pole frequency, where the real phase is −45°.
text: \[G(s) = \frac{1}{1 + s/\omega_p}, \qquad |G(j\omega)| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + (\omega/\omega_p)^2}}, \qquad \angle G(j\omega) = -\arctan\frac{\omega}{\omega_p}\] On the Bode plot, a pole is drawn with two lines, the asymptotes: the magnitude stays at 0 dB up to the pole frequency, \(f_p\), and then falls 20 dB per decade; the phase stays at 0° up to \(f_p/10\), falls 45° per decade, and reaches −90° at \(10 f_p\). The real curve departs from the asymptotes only near the corner: at \(f_p\), the magnitude is \(1/\sqrt 2\), or −3.01 dB. The asymptote gives 0 dB there: the error is 3 dB; one decade below or above, the error falls to 0.04 dB; the real phase is exactly −45° at \(f_p\). The phase line also gives −45° at the corner, so it is right there. At the edges it is off by 5.7°: the real phase is −5.7° at \(f_p/10\) and −84.3° at \(10 f_p\). −3 dB is not half At \(f_p\), the magnitude is \(0.707\). Half, \(0.5\), is −6 dB, and that happens at \(\sqrt 3\,f_p\). In time, the pole gives an exponential: the response to a unit step is \(y(t) = 1 - e^{-t/\tau}\), with \(\tau = 1/\omega_p\). It reaches 63 % of the final value at \(\tau\), 95 % at \(3\tau\) and 98 % at \(4\tau\). The settling time is the instant from which the response stays within a band around the final value: \(4\tau\) for the 2 % band (the exact calculation gives \(\tau \ln 50 = 3.9\tau\)) and \(4.6\tau\) for 1 %; at \(5\tau\), 0.7 % is left (99.3 %). The higher the pole, the faster the response.

title: First-order pole and zero
heading: The zero
summary: A real pole drops the magnitude at −20 dB per decade and lags the phase down to −90°; a zero does the opposite. The asymptote is 3 dB off at the pole frequency, where the real phase is −45°.
text: The zero, \(1 + s/\omega_z\), sits at \(s = -\omega_z\) and is the mirror of the pole: the magnitude rises 20 dB per decade above \(f_z\), the phase rises from 0° at \(f_z/10\) to +90° at \(10 f_z\), and the corner is also the point of +45° and 3 dB above the asymptote. On its own, the zero is improper: the gain would grow without limit, and the step response would contain an impulse, because \(s\) is a derivative. In a circuit, every zero comes with poles that limit the high-frequency gain. Together with a pole, \((1 + s/\omega_z)/(1 + s/\omega_p)\), the pair is realizable. The phase of each factor Each factor has 0° of phase at the end of the frequency axis where it tends to 1, and the phase is continuous from there. For the pole and the zero, that end is DC: the phase starts at 0° and goes to ∓90°. In a product, the total phase is the sum of the factors' phases; a negative gain adds +180°. The next notes use the same rule.

title: First-order pole and zero
heading: In the converters
summary: A real pole drops the magnitude at −20 dB per decade and lags the phase down to −90°; a zero does the opposite. The asymptote is 3 dB off at the pole frequency, where the real phase is −45°.
text: The ESR zero is a real zero, and it is the only first-order factor in the buck's plant: \[f_{\mathrm{ESR}} = \frac{1}{2\pi\,R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\,C}\] In the buck, with 47 µF and 5 mΩ, it sits at 677 kHz. It adds 0.7° of phase at 8 kHz and 8.4° at 100 kHz, half the switching frequency. In the boost, with 100 µF and 10 mΩ, it sits at 159 kHz. Exercise From the plot to the equation. Write \(G(s)\) in factored form from the magnitude and phase asymptotes. Give the DC gain, the corners and the high-frequency level. A gain, a zero and a pole: read the level, the corners and the slopes. Exercise From the equation to the plot. Draw the asymptotes of \(G(s) = \dfrac{50}{(1 + s/\omega_1)(1 + s/\omega_2)}\), with \(f_1 = 200\) Hz and \(f_2 = 50\) kHz. Mark the slopes, the corners and the phase values. At what frequency does the magnitude asymptote cross 0 dB? Two real poles, 2.4 decades apart. Exercise A calculation tool returns the function \(\dfrac{s + 12566}{s + 376991}\), with \(s\) in rad/s. Write it in factored form, with its DC gain, and give the zero and pole frequencies in hertz. In the author's handbook Modelagem de Conversores Chaveados: do modelo à bancada virtual (in Portuguese): how to obtain poles and zeros from a measured frequency response. Back to the converter The ESR zero is this first-order zero: go back to The ESR zero, which applies it to the buck's plant. The next step is the factors with no corner, the pure integrator and the pure differentiator: Pole and zero at the origin: pure integrator and pure differentiator.

title: Inverted forms and the sign on the Bode plot
heading: Inverted forms and the sign on the Bode plot
summary: A factor written in ω/s is 1 at high frequency and is a pure integrator or a pure differentiator times the ordinary form, sometimes with a minus sign; with that decomposition and the ±180° rule, factor by factor, the four inverted forms are drawn by asymptotes.
prereqs: Pole and zero at the origin: pure integrator and pure differentiator
text: The factored form writes each factor as \(1 + s/\omega\), which is 1 at DC. The same factor can be written the other way round, in \(\omega/s\): \[\text{inverted pole: } \frac{1}{1 + \omega_p/s}, \quad \text{inverted zero: } 1 + \frac{\omega_z}{s}, \quad \text{RHP: } \frac{1}{1 - \omega_p/s}, \quad 1 - \frac{\omega_z}{s}\] These are the inverted forms: the factor is 1 at high frequency, and the gain in front is the high-frequency gain. None needs to be memorized: they all reduce to the forms of the previous notes. The four inverted forms: pick one and move the corner. In the s-plane, each has one root at the origin and the other at −ω, or at +ω in the RHP forms.

title: Inverted forms and the sign on the Bode plot
heading: A pure differentiator or a pure integrator times the ordinary form
summary: A factor written in ω/s is 1 at high frequency and is a pure integrator or a pure differentiator times the ordinary form, sometimes with a minus sign; with that decomposition and the ±180° rule, factor by factor, the four inverted forms are drawn by asymptotes.
prereqs: Pole and zero at the origin: pure integrator and pure differentiator
text: Factoring out \(\omega/s\): \[\frac{1}{1 + \omega_p/s} = \frac{s/\omega_p}{1 + s/\omega_p}, \qquad 1 + \frac{\omega_z}{s} = \frac{\omega_z}{s}\left(1 + \frac{s}{\omega_z}\right)\] The inverted pole is a pure differentiator times an ordinary pole, with the same \(\omega\): the differentiator's line rises +20 dB per decade and crosses 0 dB at \(f_p\), exactly where the pole starts falling −20 dB per decade. Added, the two lines give +20 dB per decade up to \(f_p\) and 0 dB after. In phase, the differentiator gives +90°, and the pole, from 0° to −90°: the sum goes from +90° to 0°. The inverted zero is the mirror: a pure integrator times an ordinary zero, −20 dB per decade up to \(f_z\), and the phase from −90° to 0°. That is why the inverted pole brings a zero at the origin, and the inverted zero, a pole at the origin (Pole and zero at the origin: pure integrator and pure differentiator). With the root in the right half-plane, a minus sign appears: \[\frac{1}{1 - \omega_p/s} = -\frac{s/\omega_p}{1 - s/\omega_p}, \qquad 1 - \frac{\omega_z}{s} = -\frac{\omega_z}{s}\left(1 - \frac{s}{\omega_z}\right)\] Adding the lines, with the sign rule below, gives the four forms; the brackets give \([\omega \to 0^+;\ \omega \to \infty]\): Factor Magnitude Phase Inverted pole, \(1/(1 + \omega_p/s)\) +20 dB per decade up to \(f_p\), then 0 dB \([+90^\circ;\,0^\circ]\) Inverted zero, \(1 + \omega_z/s\) −20 dB per decade up to \(f_z\), then 0 dB \([-90^\circ;\,0^\circ]\) Inverted RHP pole, \(1/(1 - \omega_p/s)\) that of the inverted pole \([-90^\circ;\,0^\circ]\) Inverted RHP zero, \(1 - \omega_z/s\) that of the inverted zero \([+90^\circ;\,0^\circ]\) As in Right-half-plane pole and zero, the RHP forms differ from the others only in the phase.

title: Inverted forms and the sign on the Bode plot
heading: The minus sign: ±180°, factor by factor
summary: A factor written in ω/s is 1 at high frequency and is a pure integrator or a pure differentiator times the ordinary form, sometimes with a minus sign; with that decomposition and the ±180° rule, factor by factor, the four inverted forms are drawn by asymptotes.
prereqs: Pole and zero at the origin: pure integrator and pure differentiator
text: The phase rule is that of First-order pole and zero: each factor has 0° of phase at the end where it tends to 1, and its phase is continuous from there. In the inverted forms, that end is high frequency. A minus sign adds +180° or −180°, which give the same complex number; choose, for each factor, the one that brings its phase to 0° at high frequency. In the inverted RHP zero: the pure integrator gives −90°; the RHP zero, from 0° to −90°. At high frequency the sum is −180°, and the sign enters as +180°: the phase goes from \(-90^\circ + 0^\circ + 180^\circ = +90^\circ\), below \(f_z/10\), to 0°, above \(10 f_z\). In the inverted RHP pole, the pure differentiator gives +90° and the RHP pole, from 0° to +90°: the sign enters as −180°, and the phase goes from −90° to 0°. To check, evaluate the dominant term at low frequency: \(1 - \omega_z/s \approx -\omega_z/(j\omega) = +j\,\omega_z/\omega\), a positive imaginary number, +90°. In the whole function, the total phase is the sum of the factors' phases, and a negative gain adds +180°. A calculation tool may show the same curve shifted by 360°: the complex number is the same. By hand, in four steps Factor out \(\omega/s\) in each inverted factor. Replace each term with a pure integrator, a pure differentiator, a pole or a zero, on either side. Add the magnitude and phase lines. Correct each minus sign with ±180°, by the end where the factor tends to 1, and check with the dominant term.

title: Inverted forms and the sign on the Bode plot
heading: In the converters
summary: A factor written in ω/s is 1 at high frequency and is a pure integrator or a pure differentiator times the ordinary form, sometimes with a minus sign; with that decomposition and the ±180° rule, factor by factor, the four inverted forms are drawn by asymptotes.
prereqs: Pole and zero at the origin: pure integrator and pure differentiator
text: In the buck's 2p2z, the pure integrator and the first zero, at 2 kHz, form an inverted zero, \(1 + \omega_z/s\): below 2 kHz the magnitude falls 20 dB per decade; above, the factor tends to 1, and the phase rises toward 0°. At 8 kHz it is \(-\arctan(2/8) = -14.0^\circ\). It is the form in which the PI and the lag compensator are usually written (PI, phase lead and the type III, The phase-lag compensator). Exercise From the plot to the equation. Write \(G(s)\) from the asymptotes, using an inverted form. A flat band between two slopes. Exercise From the equation to the plot. Draw the asymptotes of \(G(s) = 4\,\dfrac{1 - \omega_1/s}{1 + s/\omega_2}\), with \(f_1 = 100\) Hz and \(f_2 = 20\) kHz. Which sign enters the inverted factor, +180° or −180°? An inverted right-half-plane zero and an ordinary pole. Exercise A function has a zero at \(f_1 = 2\) kHz, a pole at \(f_2 = 60\) kHz and a high-frequency gain \(C_\infty = 30\). With \(\omega_1 < \omega_2\), it has two forms: \[C(s) = C_0\,\frac{1 + s/\omega_1}{1 + s/\omega_2} = C_\infty\,\frac{1 + \omega_1/s}{1 + \omega_2/s}\] (a) What is \(C_0\)? (b) Does the phase reach +90°? (c) Which form shows the low-frequency gain, and which the high-frequency one? Back to the converter The inverted zero is in the buck's 2p2z, in The 2p2z compensator. With the first-order forms complete, the next step is the second-order pair, in Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q; the table of all the forms is in Bode by composition: from factored form to asymptote.

title: The phase-lag compensator
heading: The phase-lag compensator
summary: A pole followed by a higher zero, well below the crossover, multiplies the low-frequency gain by the factor α and costs a few degrees of margin; with no pole at the origin, it reduces the step error but does not zero it.
prereqs: PI, phase lead and the type III
text: Phase lead solves the margin: it puts phase at the crossover. The steady-state error is another problem: it asks for gain at low frequency, far from the crossover. The integrator gives infinite gain there, but costs −90° and accumulates the error when the duty cycle saturates (Anti-windup and duty saturation). The phase-lag compensator gives finite gain, multiplied by a factor, and leaves the crossover nearly where it was.

title: The phase-lag compensator
heading: The form
summary: A pole followed by a higher zero, well below the crossover, multiplies the low-frequency gain by the factor α and costs a few degrees of margin; with no pole at the origin, it reduces the step error but does not zero it.
prereqs: PI, phase lead and the type III
text: \[G_c(s) = \alpha\,\frac{1 + s/\omega_z}{1 + s/\omega_p}, \qquad \alpha = \frac{\omega_z}{\omega_p} > 1\] It is phase lead with the zero and the pole swapped: the same ratio \(\alpha\), now with the pole below. At low frequency, the gain is \(\alpha\). Between the pole and the zero, the magnitude falls 20 dB per decade. Above the zero, the gain is \(\alpha\,\omega_p/\omega_z = 1\). The same function, written in the inverted form, shows this directly: \[G_c(s) = \frac{1 + \omega_z/s}{1 + \omega_p/s}\] Taking \(\omega/s\) out of each factor, the inverted zero's integrator and the inverted pole's differentiator cancel, and the ratio of the gains is left, \(\omega_z/\omega_p = \alpha\). The factor \(\alpha\) in front is what keeps the gain at 1 above the zero. Without it, the block would attenuate \(\alpha\) times at the crossover, and the crossover already designed would move down. The phase is the mirror of lead's hill: a valley, with its bottom at the geometric mean \(\sqrt{f_z\,f_p}\) and the same formula, with the sign flipped: \[\sin|\varphi_{\min}| = \frac{\alpha - 1}{\alpha + 1}\] With \(\alpha = 4\), the valley reaches −36.9°; with \(\alpha = 9\), −53.1°, the values in the lead table. This valley has to stay far from the crossover.

title: The phase-lag compensator
heading: Where to put it: a decade below the crossover
summary: A pole followed by a higher zero, well below the crossover, multiplies the low-frequency gain by the factor α and costs a few degrees of margin; with no pole at the origin, it reduces the step error but does not zero it.
prereqs: PI, phase lead and the type III
text: At \(f_c\), the block's phase is \[\varphi(f_c) = \arctan\frac{f_c}{f_z} - \arctan\frac{f_c}{f_p}\] With the zero a decade below, \(f_z = f_c/10\), and \(\alpha = 4\), it is \(\arctan 10 - \arctan 40 = 84.3^\circ - 88.6^\circ = -4.3^\circ\). With a larger \(\alpha\), the second term approaches 90°, and the cost approaches \(90^\circ - \arctan 10 = \arctan(1/10) = 5.7^\circ\). It is a ceiling: with the zero a decade below, the block never takes more than 5.7° at the crossover, whatever \(\alpha\). The magnitude there is +0.04 dB, and the crossover barely moves. The recipe has four steps: \(\alpha\) is the ratio between the \(K_p\) required and the one the loop already has. The zero goes a decade below the crossover, \(f_z = f_c/10\). The pole goes at \(f_p = f_z/\alpha\). Check the margin. If the cost is more than acceptable, move the pair down. "A decade" is the minimum. With the zero four times below \(f_c\) and \(\alpha = 4\), the cost is already \(\arctan 4 - \arctan 16 = -10.5^\circ\). The block also leaves a tail. It creates a closed-loop pole between its pole and its zero. That pole sits near the zero only when the loop gain there is high. Part of the error fades slowly, with a time constant of the order of \(1/(2\pi f_z)\). In the buck below, with \(K_p = 0.4\), the pole is at −351 Hz, with \(\tau = 0.45\) ms, and carries 30 % of the step. Moving the pair down lengthens the tail: with the zero at 80 Hz, \(\tau = 4.3\) ms.

title: The phase-lag compensator
heading: It does not zero the error
summary: A pole followed by a higher zero, well below the crossover, multiplies the low-frequency gain by the factor α and costs a few degrees of margin; with no pole at the origin, it reduces the step error but does not zero it.
prereqs: PI, phase lead and the type III
text: The block's pole is not at the origin, and the loop's type does not change. On a type 0 plant, the block multiplies \(K_p\) by \(\alpha\), and the step error goes from \(1/(1 + K_p)\) to \(1/(1 + \alpha K_p)\). It shrinks, but does not go to zero. And it shrinks \(\alpha\) times only when \(K_p\) is large: the ratio is \((1 + \alpha K_p)/(1 + K_p)\), which tends to \(\alpha\) with \(K_p \gg 1\) and stays well below it with \(K_p\) near 1. The PI is the block's limit: with the pole taken to the origin, \(f_p \to 0\), the factor \(\alpha\) goes to infinity, and the block becomes an integrator with a zero. Phase lag PI Pole at \(f_p > 0\) at the origin Loop type unchanged up by one Step error, type 0 plant \(1/(1 + \alpha K_p)\) zero Phase at \(f_c\), zero at \(f_c/10\) down to −5.7° −5.7° Saturated duty cycle the block's state stays bounded the integrator accumulates without limit

title: The phase-lag compensator
heading: In the converters
summary: A pole followed by a higher zero, well below the crossover, multiplies the low-frequency gain by the factor α and costs a few degrees of margin; with no pole at the origin, it reduces the step error but does not zero it.
prereqs: PI, phase lead and the type III
text: Buck. A type 0 compensator: a gain and the 2p2z's lead, with the zero at 2 kHz and the pole at 60 kHz, with no integrator. With the crossover at 8 kHz, the gain is \(K = 0.0166\), and the phase margin is 57.4° (continuous prototype, with the delay). But \(K_p = 0.0166 \times 23.9 = 0.396\), and the step error is \(1/1.396 = 72\) %. With the phase lag, \(\alpha = 4\), zero at 800 Hz and pole at 200 Hz, the crossover goes to 8.02 kHz and the margin falls 4.3°, to 53.0°. \(K_p\) becomes 1.58, and the error \(1/2.58 = 39\) %: 1.85 times smaller, not 4, because \(K_p\) was below 1. With \(\alpha = 10\) and the pole at 80 Hz, the margin is 52.2°, and the error 20 %. No finite \(\alpha\) zeroes the error. The 2p2z, which swaps this block for an integrator, zeroes the error with 41.3° of margin. Exercise Predict the cost. In the buck's loop, which crosses at 8 kHz, a phase lag with \(\alpha = 4\) goes in with the zero at 800 Hz. How much phase does it take at the crossover? And with the zero at 2 kHz and the pole at 500 Hz? Exercise In the buck with the type 0 compensator above, \(K_p = 0.396\). Does the phase lag with \(\alpha = 4\) zero the step error? What is it before and after? What would zero it? Exercise A phase lead and a phase lag both have \(\alpha = 9\). What is the peak of one and the valley of the other? Where does each go, relative to the crossover? Back to the converter The converters' 2p2z uses the integrator, not the phase lag: zero error is worth more than the degrees of margin. Its design is in The 2p2z compensator, and the integrator under saturation in Anti-windup and duty saturation.

title: From margin to damping: the ζ ≈ MF/100 rule and where it fails
heading: From margin to damping: the ζ ≈ MF/100 rule and where it fails
summary: How the phase margin turns into damping and overshoot, over what range the ζ ≈ MF/100 rule holds, and why it misses in the buck with the 2p2z.
prereqs: Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q
text: The phase margin says how far the loop is from oscillating (Feedback and margins). What the oscilloscope shows, though, is the step: how far it overshoots the target and for how long it rings. This note bridges the two, and shows in the buck where the bridge gives way.

title: From margin to damping: the ζ ≈ MF/100 rule and where it fails
heading: From margin to step
summary: How the phase margin turns into damping and overshoot, over what range the ζ ≈ MF/100 rule holds, and why it misses in the buck with the 2p2z.
prereqs: Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q
text: Consider the loop of an integrator followed by a pole, \(T = \omega_n^2/[s\,(s + 2\zeta\omega_n)]\), which is this note's reference model. Closed, it is exactly a second-order pair, with \(\omega_0 = \omega_n\) and \(Q = 1/(2\zeta)\). In this loop, the phase margin depends only on the damping: \[\mathrm{MF} = \arctan\left(\frac{2\zeta}{\sqrt{\sqrt{1 + 4\zeta^4} - 2\zeta^2}}\right)\] \(\zeta\) \(Q\) MF MF/100 Overshoot 0.2 2.5 22.6° 0.23 53 % 0.4 1.25 43.1° 0.43 25 % 0.6 0.83 59.2° 0.59 9.5 % 0.7 0.71 65.2° 0.65 4.6 % 0.8 0.63 69.9° 0.70 1.5 % Hence the rule \(\zeta \approx \mathrm{MF}/100\), with MF in degrees. For the integrator-plus-pole loop, it is off by less than 10 % between 37° and 67° of margin, and by less than 15 % at any margin up to 71°; the error vanishes at 57.4°. Below that, the rule promises a bit more damping than there is; above it, a bit less. This range belongs to the model loop, not to any loop. The overshoot comes from the standard form of the pair, \(M_p = e^{-\pi\zeta/\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}}\), the same as Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q with \(\zeta = 1/(2Q)\). The pair's equation, with both forms, is this one: \[G(s) = \frac{1}{1 + \dfrac{s}{Q\,\omega_0} + \dfrac{s^2}{\omega_0^2}}, \qquad s_{1,2} = -\frac{\omega_0}{2Q} \pm j\,\omega_0\sqrt{1 - \frac{1}{4Q^2}}, \qquad Q = \frac{1}{2\zeta}\] A real loop has more poles. The pair near the crossover is dominant when the others are at least five times farther from the \(j\omega\) axis (ten, to trust the numbers) and no zero sits near it: then the step rings near \(f_c\) with the overshoot of the table. When a pole lies closer to the axis than the pair, that pole governs the slow response.

title: From margin to damping: the ζ ≈ MF/100 rule and where it fails
heading: In the converters
summary: How the phase margin turns into damping and overshoot, over what range the ζ ≈ MF/100 rule holds, and why it misses in the buck with the 2p2z.
prereqs: Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q
text: In the buck, with the 2p2z, the loop crosses at 8 kHz with an MF of 41° (Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins). Damping. Predict: with an MF of 41°, the rule gives \(\zeta \approx 0.41\), \(Q \approx 1.2\) and about 25 % overshoot. Check: the closed-loop model gives a pair at 7.2 kHz with \(\zeta = 0.31\) (\(Q \approx 1.6\), overshoot of 36 %): the rule promises a third more damping than there is. In QSPICE, the load step from 1 to 2 A drops the output to 8.59 V, and it comes back to 9.14 V (The 2p2z compensator): the return is 35 % of the dip, which is what \(\zeta \approx 0.31\) predicts. Why the rule misses here. It assumes two things, and the buck meets neither. First, that the loop near the crossover is an integrator followed by a pole; the buck's is the plant near −180°, plus the compensator's lead and the firmware's delay. Not even the exact formula of the table gets it right: at 41.3°, it gives \(\zeta = 0.38\). Second, that the pair is dominant. The buck's closed loop has, besides the pair, a real pole near 470 Hz, closer to the \(j\omega\) axis than the pair: by the criterion above, the pair is not dominant. The rule still gives the order of magnitude of the ringing near \(f_c\), but not the number, and it says nothing about the slow pole. The slow pole shows in the load step as a tail: by the model, a tail of 5 to 6 mV remains after the ringing, with a time constant of about 0.34 ms, and it stays above 1 mV for about 1 ms after the step. In QSPICE, that tail is lost in the tens of millivolts of fluctuation of the simulated output. In the reference step, the same pole dominates: the output has no overshoot, and it takes more than 1 ms to reach 5 V. In QSPICE, it is still 0.46 V above 5 V 600 µs after the start of the ramp, and 0.14 V at 1 ms (5 µs averages). Reference ramp from 9 to 5 V with the 2p2z: the slow descent is the 470 Hz pole. Load step from 1 to 2 A with the aggressive design, MF of 16°: compare the ringing with the 2p2z's, on the oscilloscope. Exercise Predict, then check on the figure. The aggressive design has an MF of 16° at 18 kHz. Before looking at the step: by the rule, what is the estimated \(\zeta\), the overshoot of the pair and the period of the ringing? Back to the converter With these concepts, go back to The 2p2z compensator, where the QSPICE load step is, and to Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins, which shows the margins of the buck's four controllers.
