title: Transfer function and factored form
heading: Transfer function and factored form
summary: The transfer function is a ratio of polynomials. Written in factored form, the DC gain stands alone in front, and each pole and zero marks a frequency on the Bode plot.
text: This note opens the From Laplace to Bode trail. It teaches one skill: write a converter's plant in factored form, and recognize in each factor a frequency of the Bode plot. The starting equation is the buck's plant (The buck's transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\)): \[G_{vd}(s) = \frac{\hat v_o(s)}{\hat d(s)} = G_0\;\frac{1 + s/\omega_{\mathrm{ESR}}}{1 + \dfrac{s}{Q\,\omega_0} + \dfrac{s^2}{\omega_0^2}}, \qquad G_0 = V_{in}\,\frac{R}{R + R_s}\] It has three parts: a gain, a zero and a pair of poles. This note teaches you to name them.

title: Transfer function and factored form
heading: A ratio of polynomials
summary: The transfer function is a ratio of polynomials. Written in factored form, the DC gain stands alone in front, and each pole and zero marks a frequency on the Bode plot.
text: In a linear, time-invariant system at rest at time zero, the ratio between the transform of the output and that of the input is a fixed function of the system: \[G(s) = \frac{Y(s)}{U(s)} = \frac{N(s)}{D(s)}\] In the buck, the input is the small variation of the duty cycle, \(\hat d\), and the output is the small variation of the output voltage, \(\hat v_o\), around the operating point (The averaged switch model). The polynomials have real coefficients, and their roots have names: zeros are the roots of \(N(s)\): there, \(G(s) = 0\); poles are the roots of \(D(s)\): there, \(G(s)\) goes to infinity; the order is the degree of \(D(s)\). The buck is second order, because it stores energy in two elements, the inductor and the capacitor. In a circuit, the order does not exceed the number of these elements. Since the degree of \(N(s)\) does not exceed that of \(D(s)\), the function is proper: the gain does not grow without limit at high frequency. Circuits built from resistors, inductors and capacitors always give proper functions.

title: Transfer function and factored form
heading: The factored form
summary: The transfer function is a ratio of polynomials. Written in factored form, the DC gain stands alone in front, and each pole and zero marks a frequency on the Bode plot.
text: Each real root becomes a factor \(1 + s/\omega\), which equals 1 at \(s = 0\). A pair of complex roots becomes \(1 + s/(Q\omega_0) + s^2/\omega_0^2\), the second-order form. Putting it together, with \(\omega = 2\pi f\): \[G(s) = G_0\,\frac{\prod_i \left(1 + \dfrac{s}{\omega_{z,i}}\right)\prod_k \left(1 + \dfrac{s}{Q_k\,\omega_k} + \dfrac{s^2}{\omega_k^2}\right)}{\prod_j \left(1 + \dfrac{s}{\omega_{p,j}}\right)\prod_m \left(1 + \dfrac{s}{Q_m\,\omega_m} + \dfrac{s^2}{\omega_m^2}\right)}, \qquad G_0 = G(0)\] This is the form the course uses, and it has two advantages: the DC gain, \(G_0 = G(0)\), stands alone in front, because every factor equals 1 at \(s = 0\); each \(\omega\) is the frequency at which that factor starts to act: that is where it shows up on the Bode plot. With the form \(K/(s + a)\), the DC gain, \(K/a\), is hidden in the denominator. That is why the course writes everything factored, like \(G_{vd}\) above, where \(G_0 = V_{in}R/(R+R_s)\) is in plain sight. A root in the right half-plane enters with its sign changed, \(1 - s/\omega\). It has the magnitude of the ordinary form: only the phase differs (Right-half-plane pole and zero). Pole or zero frequency The root at \(s = -\omega\) corresponds to the frequency \(\omega\), in rad/s, or \(f = \omega/2\pi\), in Hz: the pole or zero frequency. The figures in this course mark the s-plane axes in hertz, \(s/2\pi\).

title: Transfer function and factored form
heading: The s-plane
summary: The transfer function is a ratio of polynomials. Written in factored form, the DC gain stands alone in front, and each pole and zero marks a frequency on the Bode plot.
text: Each root is a point in the complex plane. The real part says how the response decays: the further left of the \(j\omega\) axis, the faster. The imaginary part says whether the response oscillates, and at what frequency. A pole in the right half-plane would make the response grow without limit. In open loop, therefore, stability depends only on the poles. A proper rational function, with no canceled factors, is BIBO stable (bounded-input, bounded-output: every bounded input gives a bounded output) if and only if all the poles lie strictly left of the \(j\omega\) axis. A zero in the right half-plane does not make the plant unstable, but it has an effect on the loop, which the note on the right-half-plane zero explains. Poles and zero of the buck's plant, from the averaged model: the complex pair near 5 kHz and the ESR zero far to the left, out of view. Change the load and the ESR and watch the roots move.

title: Transfer function and factored form
heading: In the converters
summary: The transfer function is a ratio of polynomials. Written in factored form, the DC gain stands alone in front, and each pole and zero marks a frequency on the Bode plot.
text: In the buck, with 24 V input, 9 Ω load, 30 mΩ inductor, 10 mΩ switch and 5 mΩ ESR, the series resistance \(R_s\) is 40 mΩ, and the averaged model gives: a DC gain of 23.9, or 27.6 dB; a real zero at \(-2\pi \cdot 677\) kHz, the ESR zero; a pair of complex poles at \(s/2\pi = -351 \pm j\,4947\) Hz, that is, \(f_0 \approx 4.96\) kHz and \(Q = 7.1\). In the boost, from 12 V to 48 V with 48 Ω, the DC gain is 190 (45.6 dB), the pole pair sits at 690 Hz, and a zero appears on the right, at \(+14.1\) kHz (Transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\) of the boost). Exercise Predict, then check on the figure. With 9 Ω of load, move the load control to 4.5 Ω (2 A). Before you touch it: do the poles move closer to or further from the \(j\omega\) axis? Does the DC gain change much? Exercise A colleague computes the roots of \(D(s)\) of the buck's plant, gets \(+351 \pm j\,4947\) Hz and concludes that the open-loop converter is unstable. Where is the likely error? In the author's handbook Modelagem de Conversores Chaveados: do modelo à bancada virtual (in Portuguese): how to obtain poles and zeros from a measured frequency response. Back to the converter With these names, reread the buck's transfer function and the boost's: DC gain, pole pair and zeros, one at a time.

title: The averaged switch model
heading: The averaged switch model
summary: Replacing the switch pair by its average over one period turns the buck into a continuous circuit; perturbed and linearized, it gives the small-signal model.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
From the boost to the digital loop
text: To design the control we need a transfer function, but the switch turns on and off every \(T_s\) and has none. The way out is to look at the average of each quantity over one period, which varies slowly. This note does the derivation for the buck; the result is the plant of the next note.

title: The averaged switch model
heading: Step 1: the switched circuit
summary: Replacing the switch pair by its average over one period turns the buck into a continuous circuit; perturbed and linearized, it gives the small-signal model.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
From the boost to the digital loop
text: Let \(q(t) \in \{0, 1\}\) be the state of the high-side switch. The switching-node voltage is \(v_{sw} = q\,v_{in}\), and the current drawn from the input is \(i_{in} = q\,i_L\). On the inductor, with \(R_s = R_L + R_{on}\) (in CCM there is always one switch in series with it): \[L\,\frac{di_L}{dt} = q\,v_{in} - v_o - R_s\,i_L\]

title: The averaged switch model
heading: Step 2: the average over one period
summary: Replacing the switch pair by its average over one period turns the buck into a continuous circuit; perturbed and linearized, it gives the small-signal model.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
From the boost to the digital loop
text: Define the moving average \(\langle x \rangle_{T_s}(t) = \frac{1}{T_s}\int_{t - T_s}^{t} x(\tau)\,d\tau\). The average of \(q\) is the duty ratio \(d\). If \(v_{in}\) and \(i_L\) barely change within one period (small ripple), the average of the product is the product of the averages, and the switch pair becomes the averaged switching cell: \[\langle v_{sw} \rangle_{T_s} = d\,\langle v_{in} \rangle_{T_s}, \qquad \langle i_{in} \rangle_{T_s} = d\,\langle i_L \rangle_{T_s}\] Averaged switch model The averaged cell is an ideal transformer of ratio \(1 : d\), with a variable \(d\): the voltage comes out multiplied by \(d\), and the input current is the inductor's multiplied by \(d\). Power is conserved: \(\langle v_{in}\rangle\langle i_{in}\rangle = \langle v_{sw}\rangle\langle i_L\rangle\). Replacing the cell in the circuit, the inductor equation becomes \[L\,\frac{d\langle i_L\rangle}{dt} = d\,\langle v_{in}\rangle - \langle v_o\rangle - R_s\,\langle i_L\rangle\] and the capacitor, the ESR and the load stay as before, with the averaged quantities. The ripple vanishes by construction.

title: The averaged switch model
heading: Step 3: the operating point
summary: Replacing the switch pair by its average over one period turns the buck into a continuous circuit; perturbed and linearized, it gives the small-signal model.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
From the boost to the digital loop
text: In steady state, the derivatives vanish: \(\langle i_L\rangle = I_L = V_o/R\) and \(D\,V_{in} = V_o + R_s I_L\), that is, \(D = \frac{V_o}{V_{in}}\cdot\frac{R + R_s}{R}\), the duty ratio with losses.

title: The averaged switch model
heading: Step 4: perturbation
summary: Replacing the switch pair by its average over one period turns the buck into a continuous circuit; perturbed and linearized, it gives the small-signal model.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
From the boost to the digital loop
text: Write each quantity as its operating point plus a small perturbation: \(d = D + \hat d\), \(v_{in} = V_{in} + \hat v_{in}\), \(i_L = I_L + \hat i_L\), \(v_o = V_o + \hat v_o\). The only nonlinear term is the product \(d\,v_{in}\): \[d\,v_{in} = D V_{in} + V_{in}\,\hat d + D\,\hat v_{in} + \hat d\,\hat v_{in}\]

title: The averaged switch model
heading: Step 5: linearization
summary: Replacing the switch pair by its average over one period turns the buck into a continuous circuit; perturbed and linearized, it gives the small-signal model.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
From the boost to the digital loop
text: The term \(\hat d\,\hat v_{in}\) is the product of two small perturbations and is neglected. Subtracting the operating point leaves a linear equation: \[L\,\frac{d\hat i_L}{dt} = V_{in}\,\hat d + D\,\hat v_{in} - \hat v_o - R_s\,\hat i_L\] The switching node becomes a source \(\hat v_{sw} = V_{in}\hat d + D\hat v_{in}\) that drives the LC filter. With a constant \(V_{in}\) (\(\hat v_{in} = 0\)), the buck is linear in \(d\) and the linearization is exact: the plant \(\hat v_o/\hat d\) is \(V_{in}\) times the filter's transfer function, which leads to (2) in The buck's transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\). \[G_{vd}(s) = \frac{\hat v_o(s)}{\hat d(s)} = G_0\;\frac{1 + s/\omega_{\mathrm{ESR}}}{1 + \dfrac{s}{Q\,\omega_0} + \dfrac{s^2}{\omega_0^2}}, \qquad G_0 = V_{in}\,\frac{R}{R + R_s}\] Why the boost is different In the boost, the cell multiplies the state variables: \(\langle v_{sw}\rangle = d'\,\langle v_o\rangle\) and the current delivered to the output is \(d'\,\langle i_L\rangle\). Linearization leaves terms \(V_o\hat d\) and \(I_L\hat d\), and the second one creates the right-half-plane zero. The resulting plant is in Transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\) of the boost.

title: The averaged switch model
heading: Where averaging stops being valid
summary: Replacing the switch pair by its average over one period turns the buck into a continuous circuit; perturbed and linearized, it gives the small-signal model.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
From the boost to the digital loop
text: The averaged model assumes two things, and each has a limit. Small ripple. The average of a product is only the product of the averages if \(\Delta i_L\) and \(\Delta v_o\) are small next to the averages. The model does not see the ripple, but the ADC does: it samples at a fixed point of the waveform and reads a constant offset (see Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM). Slow variations. The average only describes perturbations much slower than the switching. A perturbation near \(f_s/2\) creates, at the switching node, a component at \(f_s - f\) of almost the same frequency, which the filter lets through and which is confused with it by sampling. In practice, the model holds up to a fraction of \(f_s/2\), and the loop's crossover stays well below that. The model also does not know the control is digital: the sample, the computation and the PWM delay the response by \((1 + D)T_s\), the computation delay, which enters as a factor \(e^{-s(1+D)T_s}\) multiplying the plant. DCM and diode emulation In DCM, the current rests at zero for part of the period and the averaged cell changes: the plant loses one of the LC poles. The synchronous buck stays in forced CCM and does not have this problem, unless the firmware turns the low-side switch off on negative current.

title: The averaged switch model
heading: In the converters
summary: Replacing the switch pair by its average over one period turns the buck into a continuous circuit; perturbed and linearized, it gives the small-signal model.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
From the boost to the digital loop
text: In the lab's buck (24 V → 9 V, 200 kHz), \(R_s\) = 30 mΩ + 10 mΩ = 40 mΩ, and at 1 A the duty ratio with losses is \((9 + 0.04)/24 = 0.377\), against 0.375 ideal. The averaged model with the \((1+D)T_s\) delay was checked in QSPICE by adding a small sine to the duty inside the firmware: it stayed within 0.3 dB and 0.7° of the switched circuit from 500 Hz to 15 kHz, across the resonance. At 30 kHz, already almost a third of \(f_s/2\) = 100 kHz, the magnitude still matches, but the phase is 3.9° off and the point fails the linearity check (Measuring the loop gain by injecting into the duty). The 2p2z's crossover, at 8 kHz, lies in the region where the model is reliable. In the boost and the buck-boost, with the right-half-plane zero, the same method gave 0.2 dB and 1.4° and 0.4 dB and 1.9°, from 300 Hz to 7 kHz. Exercise With the buck at 24 V, how much does the average switching-node voltage change for a duty step \(\hat d = 0.01\)? And for an input step from 24 to 18 V, with \(D\) fixed at 0.375? Exercise The 2p2z's crossover is 8 kHz. What fraction of \(f_s/2\) is that, and why does the design not push the crossover up to near 50 kHz? In the author's handbook Modelagem de Conversores Chaveados: do modelo à bancada virtual (in Portuguese): the moving average and the averaged model, step by step.

title: The boost's crossover window
heading: The boost's crossover window
summary: Between a floor of three times the resonance and a ceiling at a fraction of the right-half-plane zero; without losses, the ratio of the two is the plant's Q, and the 1/3 window exists only with Q above 9.
prereqs: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: The right-half-plane zero puts a ceiling on the crossover: rules of thumb ask for \(f_c\) below \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}/3\), or below \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}/5\) in the worst case. There is also a floor. In the type III compensator recipe, the two zeros go on the resonance \(f_0\) and the crossover sits above \(3f_0\). The floor is consistent with that recipe: three times above the zeros, they already give \(2\arctan 3 = 143^\circ\) of lead against the \(-180^\circ\) of the pole pair. The two limits together make a window: \[3 f_0 < f_c < \frac{f_{\mathrm{RHP}}}{3}\] When the ceiling falls below the floor, the window is empty, and the recipe has no solution.

title: The boost's crossover window
heading: The ratio of the limits is Q
summary: Between a floor of three times the resonance and a ceiling at a fraction of the right-half-plane zero; without losses, the ratio of the two is the plant's Q, and the 1/3 window exists only with Q above 9.
prereqs: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: Without losses, \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}} = R D'^2/(2\pi L)\) (equation Right-half-plane zero of the boost) and \(f_0 = D'/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})\) (Transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\) of the boost). The ratio is \[\frac{f_{\mathrm{RHP}}}{f_0} = R\,D'\sqrt{\frac{C}{L}} = Q\] the quality factor of the lossless boost: the buck's \(R\sqrt{C/L}\), with the inductor seen as \(L/D'^2\). The 1/3 window exists when \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}/f_0 > 9\), that is, \(Q > 9\). The 1/5 window needs \(Q > 15\). A heavy load and a low input bring down \(R\) and \(D'\) together. The worst corner of the range is also the one with the lowest \(Q\), and that is where the window closes. It is the lossless Q The losses damp the peak, but hardly move the ratio. At 12 V and 2 A, the exact \(Q\) is 3.6, and \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}/f_0\) = 10.0, close to the lossless \(Q\), 10.3. The \(Q\) read from the peak of the Bode plot gives the wrong answer. In the four-switch buck-boost, the zero carries the factor \((V_{in} + V)/V = 1/D\) (equation Right-half-plane zero of the buck-boost), and the ratio becomes \(Q/D\). With \(D\) near 0.5, the window opens with \(Q\) near 4.5.

title: The boost's crossover window
heading: Where the 2p2z crosses
summary: Between a floor of three times the resonance and a ceiling at a fraction of the right-half-plane zero; without losses, the ratio of the two is the plant's Q, and the 1/3 window exists only with Q above 9.
prereqs: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: The \(3f_0\) floor assumes the zeros at \(f_0\). The boost's 2p2z puts both zeros at 500 Hz, below the lowest resonance of the range (570 Hz, at 10 V). At 1.5 kHz, three times above them, they have already given the same 143°. That is why it crosses at about \(2.2\,f_0\), below the floor, with 35° to 46° of margin. Zeros below \(f_0\) lower the floor: what counts is the distance between the crossover and the zeros. At the two 2 A corners, the crossover lies between the two ceiling rules: \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}/4.6\) at 12 V and \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}/3.7\) at 10 V. The boost's pole pair and right-half-plane zero: lower the input and raise the load, and watch the zero move towards the resonance.

title: The boost's crossover window
heading: From 1/3 to 1/5 by the gain alone
summary: Between a floor of three times the resonance and a ceiling at a fraction of the right-half-plane zero; without losses, the ratio of the two is the plant's Q, and the 1/3 window exists only with Q above 9.
prereqs: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: With the window empty, lowering the crossover looks like the way out. At the worst corner, 10 V and 2 A, the zero is at 4.66 kHz. With the 2p2z's zeros and pole fixed, a new gain takes the crossover from \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}/3\) = 1553 Hz to \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}/5\) = 932 Hz: Term Phase at 1553 Hz Phase at 932 Hz Difference Right-half-plane zero −18.4° −11.3° +7.1° Delay and sample −5.4° −2.6° +2.8° Averaged plant without the zero −171.4° −161.7° +9.7° Compensator +50.5° +31.3° −19.2° Phase margin 35.2° 35.6° +0.4° The zero, the delay and the resonance give back 19.6°, and the compensator loses 19.2°, because the zeros at 500 Hz are close to the new crossover. Only the gain margin improves, from 10.0 to 18.0 dB. With the zeros moved down to 300 Hz together with the crossover, the model gives 56.4° and 17.1 dB.

title: The boost's crossover window
heading: In the converters
summary: Between a floor of three times the resonance and a ceiling at a fraction of the right-half-plane zero; without losses, the ratio of the two is the plant's Q, and the 1/3 window exists only with Q above 9.
prereqs: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: Boost. From 12 V to 48 V, with 33 µH and 100 µF. The averaged model with losses gives, at the four corners: Point \(f_0\) \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}\) \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}/f_0\) 1/3 window 1/5 window 2p2z \(f_c\) 12 V, 1 A 690 Hz 14.1 kHz 20.5 2.07–4.70 kHz 2.07–2.82 kHz 1.50 kHz 12 V, 2 A 687 Hz 6.87 kHz 10.0 2.06–2.29 kHz empty 1.49 kHz 10 V, 1 A 574 Hz 9.68 kHz 16.9 1.72–3.23 kHz 1.72–1.94 kHz 1.27 kHz 10 V, 2 A 570 Hz 4.66 kHz 8.2 empty empty 1.26 kHz At the nominal 2 A point, the 1/3 window is only 230 Hz wide. At 10 V, it closes. The 2p2z passes at all four corners with 35.5° to 46.2° (Robust design across the operating range), because it does not follow the recipe: zeros below \(f_0\) and the crossover below \(3f_0\). Buck-boost. From 9 to 15 V and from 1 to 3 A, with \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}/f_0 \approx Q/D\). The 1/3 window opens at 1 A across the range; at 2 A, at 9, 12 and 15 V (at 9 V, by 50 Hz); at 3 A, only at 15 V. The 1/5 window opens only at 1 A and at 15 V and 2 A. The 2p2z, with its zeros at 1 kHz, crosses between \(1.7\,f_0\) and \(1.9\,f_0\); at 3 A, at \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}/3.6\) (9 V), \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}/4.6\) (12 V) and \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}/5.5\) (15 V), with 39° to 44° of margin (Four-switch buck-boost, Four-switch buck-boost 8–16 V → 12 V: worked example). Buck. Without a right-half-plane zero, the ceiling comes from the digital delay (Computation and PWM delay), and the 2p2z crosses at \(1.6\,f_0\) (Synchronous buck 24 V → 9 V: worked example). Exercise With \(D' = 0.248\) and 48 Ω, compute the lossless \(Q\) of the boost at 12 V and 1 A. Do the 1/3 and 1/5 windows exist? Exercise In the buck-boost at 9 V and 3 A, \(D' = 0.417\) and \(R\) = 4 Ω, with 22 µH and 100 µF. Does the 1/3 window exist? Exercise Add up the differences in the table "From 1/3 to 1/5 by the gain alone". Why does the phase margin hardly change?

heading: Synchronous boost 12 V → 48 V: worked example
summary: The lab's boost, from the specifications to the firmware, with the numbers of every step, the right-half-plane zero that holds the crossover at 1.5 kHz and the fifteen scenarios simulated in QSPICE.
text: This is the converter of the From the boost to the digital loop trail: a synchronous boost controlled by a microcontroller, simulated in QSPICE with the same C code as the Synchronous buck 24 V → 9 V: worked example, in floating point; the scenarios start in steady state, and the Q15 version was not simulated. Each step below points to the note that explains the theory and shows the number it gives for this boost. The lab's synchronous boost: the main switch below (G1), the synchronous rectifier on top (G2), the lossy inductor and capacitor, and the resistive load.

title: Synchronous boost 12 V → 48 V: worked example
heading: Specifications
summary: The lab's boost, from the specifications to the firmware, with the numbers of every step, the right-half-plane zero that holds the crossover at 1.5 kHz and the fifteen scenarios simulated in QSPICE.
text: Quantity Value Input / output 12 V → 48 V Switching 100 kHz, dead time of 100 ns Inductor 33 µH, resistance of 15 mΩ Capacitor 100 µF, ESR of 10 mΩ Switches \(R_{on}\) = 10 mΩ Load 48 Ω (1 A) and 24 Ω (2 A) ADC 12 bits, full scale of 60 V Duty ratio from 0 to 0.85 Design summary. Voltage-mode control, with one ADC sample and one controller update per period, as in the buck. The default compensator is a 2p2z with crossover at 1.5 kHz, two zeros at 500 Hz (below the resonance, at 690 Hz) and a pole at 30 kHz. The crossover is low because of the right-half-plane zero, which comes down to 6.9 kHz at 2 A. The numbers below come from the validated model, at 12 V, at 1 A and at 2 A.

title: Synchronous boost 12 V → 48 V: worked example
heading: The example, step by step
summary: The lab's boost, from the specifications to the firmware, with the numbers of every step, the right-half-plane zero that holds the crossover at 1.5 kHz and the fifteen scenarios simulated in QSPICE.
text: Steady state. The volt-second balance of Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM, applied to the boost, gives \(D = 1 - 12/48 = 0.75\); with the losses, 0.752 at 1 A and 0.754 at 2 A. The inductor current is \(I_o/D'\): 4.03 A and 8.14 A. The ripple is \(\Delta i_L = V_{in} D T_s/L = 2.73\) A (2.71 A in QSPICE), and the capacitor's, \(I_o D T_s/C = 75\) mV at 1 A; with the ESR steps, the simulated output has 102 mV peak to peak. Sizing L and C. The capacitor is set by the load step: \(1\,\text{A}/(2\pi\cdot 1.5\,\text{kHz}\cdot 100\,\text{µF}) = 1.06\) V. In the simulation with the 2p2z, the output falls from 47.95 to 46.89 V: 1.06 V. With the boost's low crossover, the capacitor has to be large. The averaged switch model. The boost's averaged cell multiplies the state variables: \(d'\,v\) and \(d'\,i_L\). \(R_l\) = 15 mΩ + 10 mΩ = 25 mΩ. The site's model is the sampled-data one of Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost, derived from the switched circuit, with no fitted factor. It stayed within 0.2 dB and 1.4° of QSPICE from 300 Hz to 7 kHz, at 12 V and 48, 24 and 12 Ω (1, 2 and 4 A), measured as in Measuring the loop gain by injecting into the duty. Transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\) of the boost. DC gain of 190 (45.6 dB), about \(V/D'\); resonance at 690 Hz, with \(Q\) = 4.4 at 1 A and 3.6 at 2 A; at 1.5 kHz, the plant is 34.1 dB. From the input to the output, \(G_{vg}(0) = 4.00\), about \(1/D'\), with no right-half-plane zero (\(G_{vg}\), \(Z_{out}\) and the three ports of the plant). The right-half-plane zero. The right-half-plane zero lies at 14.1 kHz at 1 A and 6.9 kHz at 2 A. At 1.5 kHz, it takes 6.1° and 12.3° of phase. The ESR zero (The ESR zero) lies at 159 kHz and gives only 0.5°. Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost. The sample, just before G1 turns on, sits about 50 mV above the average: with the samples at 48 V, the average is 47.95 V. In the plant the ADC sees, the right-half-plane zero rises to 22.1 kHz at 1 A and 8.4 kHz at 2 A, and the margin gains 1.6°. Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins. With the 2p2z, the crossover is at 1.5 kHz, with a phase margin of 46.2° and a gain margin of 17.9 dB at 1 A (the phase crosses −180° at 8.5 kHz); at 2 A, 41.5° and 13.7 dB (6.1 kHz). Computation and PWM delay. The firmware's delay is \((1 + D)\,T_s = 17.5\) µs. The switched response behaves, to first order, like a shorter delay, \((1 + D/2)\,T_s = 13.8\) µs (Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost), which costs \(360^\circ\cdot 1.5\,\text{kHz}\cdot 13.8\,\text{µs} = 7.4^\circ\). With \(f_s\) = 100 kHz (Sampling and the zero-order hold (ZOH)), the crossover sits at \(f_s/67\): here the limit is the zero, not the delay. Robust design across the operating range. The 1.5 kHz crossover sits at \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}/4.6\) at 2 A. With the input at 10 V and 2 A, the zero comes down to 4.7 kHz, the crossover to 1.26 kHz, and the margin to 35.5°. There the window between \(3f_0\) and \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}/3\) is empty (The boost's crossover window). The bilinear (Tustin) transform and prewarping. Without prewarping, Tustin would take 1.5 kHz to 1.499 kHz, but the 30 kHz pole to 24.1 kHz (−20 %). The 2p2z was discretized by matched poles and zeros. The 2p2z compensator. The zeros go to \(e^{-2\pi\cdot 500\cdot 10\,\text{µs}} = 0.9691\) and the pole to \(p = 0.1518\): \(b_0 = 0.1648\), \(b_1 = -0.3194\), \(b_2 = 0.1548\), \(a_1 = -1.1518\) and \(a_2 = 0.1518\). At 1.5 kHz, the compensator attenuates 34.1 dB and gives back 49.5° of phase. The equivalent PID has \(K_P\) = 0.0117, \(K_I\) = 18.6 s⁻¹, \(K_D\) = 1.82 µs and \(T_F\) = 5.31 µs. ADC quantization. \(q = 60\,\text{V}/4095 = 14.65\) mV; the 48 V are exactly code 3276, and the output ripple spans 7 steps. DPWM resolution and limit cycles. With the HRTIM at 400 MHz, a period has 4000 counts (12.0 bits). One count moves the output \(190/4000 = 47.5\) mV, 3.2 ADC steps: the DPWM is still coarser than the ADC. Q15 fixed point. \(b_0\), \(b_1\), \(b_2\) and \(a_2\) fit in Q15; \(a_1 = -1.15\) does not, as in the buck. The PID in velocity form has \(a_1 = -1.443\). Anti-windup and duty saturation and Derivative kick and derivative on the measurement. The duty goes from 0 to 0.85. On the reference steps without a slew, the derivative kick takes the duty to one of the limits, and the integrator clamp and the velocity form behave very differently. The 2p2z in C, in the interrupt. At 100 kHz, the interrupt has 10 µs, or 4000 cycles of a 400 MHz core.

title: Synchronous boost 12 V → 48 V: worked example

title: Synchronous boost 12 V → 48 V: worked example

title: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
heading: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
summary: In steady state, the volt-second balance on the inductor gives the buck's duty ratio, and the triangular current gives the current and voltage ripple.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: The buck connects the switching node to the input, then to ground, and the LC filter delivers the average of that square wave to the load. This note computes the duty ratio and the ripple in steady state. It is the first step of the digital buck trail. Synchronous buck: the high-side switch conducts for D·Tₛ and the low-side switch for the rest of the period.

title: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
heading: Volt-second balance
summary: In steady state, the volt-second balance on the inductor gives the buck's duty ratio, and the triangular current gives the current and voltage ripple.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: In steady state, the inductor current ends each period at the value it started with. Since \(v_L = L\,di_L/dt\), the area of the inductor voltage over one period is zero: \[(V_{in} - V_o)\,D T_s + (-V_o)(1 - D)\,T_s = 0\] With the high-side switch closed, the inductor sees \(V_{in} - V_o\); with it open (and the low-side switch closed), it sees \(-V_o\). Solving: \[D = \frac{V_o}{V_{in}}\] Duty ratio The duty ratio \(D\) is the fraction of the switching period \(T_s = 1/f_s\) during which the high-side switch conducts. We write \(D' = 1 - D\) for the rest of the period. The resistive losses (\(R_s = R_L + R_{on}\), in series with the inductor) call for slightly more \(D\), because part of the voltage drops across them. In closed loop this does not matter: the controller finds the \(D\) that gives \(V_o\) on its own.

title: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
heading: Inductor current ripple
summary: In steady state, the volt-second balance on the inductor gives the buck's duty ratio, and the triangular current gives the current and voltage ripple.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: During \(DT_s\), the current rises with slope \((V_{in} - V_o)/L\); during \(D'T_s\), it falls with slope \(V_o/L\). The peak-to-peak ripple is \[\Delta i_L = \frac{(V_{in} - V_o)\,D}{L\,f_s} = \frac{V_o\,(1 - D)}{L\,f_s}\] The average of \(i_L\) is the load current \(I_o = V_o/R\), because in steady state the capacitor accumulates no charge. The peak, \(I_o + \Delta i_L/2\), is what saturates the core and what the switches must withstand (Thermal design and part selection for the buck).

title: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
heading: The boundary of continuous conduction
summary: In steady state, the volt-second balance on the inductor gives the buck's duty ratio, and the triangular current gives the current and voltage ripple.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: Continuous conduction mode (CCM) In CCM, the inductor current never rests at zero during the period. The boundary is \(I_o = \Delta i_L/2\): below it, the valley of the triangular wave would reach zero. In a buck with a diode, below the boundary the diode blocks and the converter enters discontinuous conduction (DCM), with another duty ratio and other dynamics. The synchronous buck is different: the low-side switch conducts in both directions, the current goes negative in the valley and the converter stays in CCM, called forced CCM. The equations of this note hold at any load. Negative current in the synchronous buck At light load, or in a downward reference step, the negative current returns energy to the input. A bench supply that cannot sink current may see its voltage rise. Controllers with "diode emulation" turn the low-side switch off when the current reaches zero, and the converter then enters DCM again.

title: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
heading: Output voltage ripple
summary: In steady state, the volt-second balance on the inductor gives the buck's duty ratio, and the triangular current gives the current and voltage ripple.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: The capacitor absorbs the AC part of \(i_L\), a triangle of \(\pm\Delta i_L/2\). The charge it receives in the positive half is the area of a triangle, \(\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{T_s}{2}\cdot\frac{\Delta i_L}{2}\), and the capacitive part follows from it. The capacitor's series resistance adds a part proportional to the current itself: \[\Delta v_C = \frac{\Delta i_L}{8\,C\,f_s}, \qquad \Delta v_{\mathrm{ESR}} = R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\,\Delta i_L\] The two parts are out of phase: the ESR's follows the current, and the capacitive one is its integral, with peaks a quarter period apart. The total ripple lies between the larger one and their sum. The next step, Sizing L and C, uses these equations backwards: from the ripple specifications to L and C.

title: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
heading: In the converters
summary: In steady state, the volt-second balance on the inductor gives the buck's duty ratio, and the triangular current gives the current and voltage ripple.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: The lab's buck goes from 24 V to 9 V at 200 kHz, with L = 22 µH and C = 47 µF (ESR 5 mΩ). \(D = 9/24 = 0.375\). \(\Delta i_L = (24 - 9)\cdot 0.375 / (22\,\text{µH}\cdot 200\,\text{kHz}) = 1.28\) A. With the 9 Ω load (1 A), the current goes from 0.36 A to 1.64 A; with 4.5 Ω (2 A), the peak reaches 2.64 A. The CCM boundary is at \(I_o = 0.64\) A, that is, a load above 14.1 Ω. \(\Delta v_C = 1.28/(8\cdot 47\,\text{µF}\cdot 200\,\text{kHz}) = 17.0\) mV and \(\Delta v_{\mathrm{ESR}} = 5\,\text{m}\Omega\cdot 1.28\,\text{A} = 6.4\) mV. Adding the waveforms with the right phase, the total is 17.6 mV peak to peak, not 23.4 mV. In the QSPICE simulation, before the load step, each period shows \(\Delta i_L \approx 1.28\) A and about 18 mV of output ripple. The ADC samples at the start of the period, in the current's valley. With ideal waveforms, that point sits about 6 mV below the average; in the simulation it is about 5 mV, one ADC step (see Sampling and the zero-order hold (ZOH) and ADC quantization). Load step from 1 to 2 A: measure the ripple before the step Exercise In the input scenario, \(V_{in}\) drops from 24 to 18 V with the output at 9 V. Compute \(D\), \(\Delta i_L\) and the capacitive part of the output ripple. Exercise With 18 V at the input, above what load resistance does the current's valley go negative? In the author's handbook Modelagem de Conversores Chaveados: do modelo à bancada virtual (in Portuguese): the volt-second balance and the triangular inductor current of the buck, derived step by step.

title: Losses of the synchronous buck
heading: Losses of the synchronous buck
summary: The conduction, switching, dead-time, gate, inductor and capacitor losses of the lab's buck, added up into a budget and an efficiency-versus-load curve.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
RMS current in the buck's capacitors
text: The buck's averaged model treats the losses as one series resistance, \(R_s = R_L + R_{on}\) (The averaged switch model). That is enough for the loop, but not to say how hot the converter gets. This note splits the losses by mechanism, with the formulas the author's synchronous buck loss model uses, and adds everything up for the lab's buck.

title: Losses of the synchronous buck
heading: The mechanisms
summary: The conduction, switching, dead-time, gate, inductor and capacitor losses of the lab's buck, added up into a budget and an efficiency-versus-load curve.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
RMS current in the buck's capacitors
text: Conduction in the switches. The high-side switch conducts during \(D\), the low-side one during \(1 - D\). With \(I_{L,\mathrm{rms}} = \sqrt{I_o^2 + \Delta i_L^2/12}\), \[P_{\mathrm{cond}} = I_{L,\mathrm{rms}}^2\,D\,R_{on} + I_{L,\mathrm{rms}}^2\,(1 - D)\,R_{on}\] High-side switching. When it switches, the high-side switch has voltage and current at the same time. In the linear-overlap model, it turns on at the valley current and turns off at the peak: \[P_{\mathrm{sw}} = \tfrac12\,V_{in}\,(I_{\mathrm{valley}}\,t_r + I_{\mathrm{peak}}\,t_f)\,f_s\] The low-side switch turns on with its body diode already conducting, at almost zero voltage, and has no such loss (Dead time and switching in the synchronous buck). Output capacitance and reverse recovery. Every period, the high-side switch charges the node's capacitance and removes the charge stored in the low-side switch's diode; both losses land in it: \[P_{C_{oss}} \approx Q_{oss}\,V_{in}\,f_s, \qquad P_{Q_{rr}} = Q_{rr}\,V_{in}\,f_s\] \(Q_{oss}\) is the switch's output charge at the working voltage; the form \(\tfrac12\,C_{oss}\,V_{in}^2\,f_s\) underestimates twice over: it counts only the switch's own energy, not the charge of the other one (with constant \(C\), \(Q V f_s = C V^2 f_s\)), and it uses the \(C_{oss}\) at 30 V, smaller than at low voltages: below, 30.0 against 105.6 mW. \(Q_{rr}\) grows with the current the diode was carrying. Dead time. In the two dead times of each period, the current flows through the body diode, with a drop \(V_{SD}\) much larger than \(I\,R_{on}\): \[P_{dt} = V_{SD}\,(I_{\mathrm{valley}} + I_{\mathrm{peak}})\,t_{dt}\,f_s\] Gate drive. The driver charges and discharges each switch's gate once per period: \(P_g = 2\,Q_g\,V_{GS}\,f_s\). It goes mostly to the driver and the gate resistors; the part in the switch's internal resistance heats the package. Inductor and capacitors. The inductor's copper dissipates \(I_{L,\mathrm{rms}}^2 R_L\), the core loses a power that depends only on the ripple (The buck inductor: core losses, Dowell and saturation), and each capacitor dissipates \(I_{\mathrm{rms}}^2 R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\) (RMS current in the buck's capacitors). The efficiency is \(\eta = P_o/(P_o + \sum P)\).

title: Losses of the synchronous buck
heading: In the converters
summary: The conduction, switching, dead-time, gate, inductor and capacitor losses of the lab's buck, added up into a budget and an efficiency-versus-load curve.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
RMS current in the buck's capacitors
text: The lab's buck has \(R_{on}\) = 10 mΩ, a dead time of 50 ns, and switches at 200 kHz. The lab model uses ideal switches; for the switches, the numbers are from Alpha & Omega's 60 V AO4262E MOSFET (data sheet Rev.1.0, January 2016): \(R_{DS(on)}\) of 5.2 mΩ typical and 6.5 mΩ maximum at 25 °C with 10 V on the gate; \(Q_g\) = 30 nC; \(C_{oss}\) = 520 pF at 30 V, and about 22 nC of \(Q_{oss}\) up to 24 V, from the \(C_{oss}\) curve; \(Q_{rr}\) = 60 nC at 16.5 A and 500 A/µs; \(t_r\) = 5 ns and \(t_f\) = 7 ns, measured at 30 V, with a 1.8 Ω load (about 16.7 A) and 3 Ω on the gate. Conduction uses the typical \(R_{DS(on)}\) at 25 °C; the lab's \(R_{on}\), a parameter of the averaged model, is close to the switch's maximum at 125 °C (10.5 mΩ). The body diode gives 0.71 V at the valley and 0.73 V at the peak. The inductor is the one chosen in The buck inductor: core losses, Dowell and saturation: 40.5 mΩ at 60 °C plus the effect of the ripple, and 24.4 mW in the core; with the lab's \(R_L\), the copper would give 124.1 mW. The input capacitor's ESR is an assumption: 5 mΩ, like the output's. Budget at 2 A (\(I_{\mathrm{valley}}\) = 1.36 A, \(I_{\mathrm{peak}}\) = 2.64 A, \(I_{L,\mathrm{rms}}\) = 2.03 A), computed with the loss functions of the author's model: Loss Power Share Conduction (8.1 + 13.4 mW) 21.5 mW 3.7 % High-side switching (16.3 + 44.3 mW) 60.7 mW 10.5 % \(C_{oss}\) 105.6 mW 18.2 % \(Q_{rr}\) (estimated) 23.8 mW 4.1 % Dead time 22.6 mW 3.9 % Gate (10 V) 120.0 mW 20.7 % Inductor copper 196.5 mW 33.8 % Core 24.4 mW 4.2 % ESR, output and input 5.6 mW 1.0 % Total 580.6 mW At 18 W output, \(\eta\) = 96.88 %. Two terms need care: \(Q_{rr}\): the high-side switch recovers the low-side diode, which carries the valley current, 1.36 A; scaling the charge, \(60\cdot 1.36/16.5 = 4.9\) nC, or 23.8 mW. The data sheet's 60 nC give 288.0 mW, an upper bound: a total of 844.9 mW and \(\eta\) = 95.52 %. Switching and dead time: the high-side turn-off, \(\tfrac12 V_{in} I_{\mathrm{peak}} t_f f_s\), is an upper bound (the node's capacitance holds the voltage while the channel closes). In the dead time, the node takes about 17 ns to fall, and the diode conducts for the rest (Dead time and switching in the synchronous buck); without that fall, it would be 29.0 mW. Checked in QSPICE with the AO4262E's VDMOS model from the simulator's library, 3 Ω on each gate, the lab's inductor (30 mΩ, no core) and 9 V at 2 A. The budget in the table uses the same assumptions and the model's charges, measured in the simulator: \(Q_{oss}\) = 12.5 nC up to 24 V and \(Q_{rr}\) = 6.4 nC. Term Budget QSPICE High-side turn-on (\(t_r\), \(C_{oss}\), \(Q_{rr}\)) 107.0 mW 98.4 mW High-side turn-off 44.3 mW 7.4 mW Conduction 21.5 mW 24.4 mW Diode in the dead time (low-side windows) 25.4 mW 15.1 mW Gate 120.0 mW 106.0 mW Copper and ESR 124.8 mW 125.0 mW Total (\(\eta\)) 443.0 mW (97.60 %) 376.3 mW (97.96 %) The turn-on and the conduction agree. The budget overestimates the turn-off, almost at zero voltage in the simulator; the diode, because each switch's turn-off delay, about 20 ns, eats part of the dead time; and the low-side gate, which turns on without the Miller plateau (24.3 nC, against 28.1 nC). The VDMOS model has less \(C_{oss}\) than the data sheet (330 against 520 pF at 30 V). Load Losses (\(Q_{rr}\) estimated) \(\eta\) \(\eta\) with the \(Q_{rr}\) bound 1 A 379.2 mW 95.96 % 93.16 % 2 A 580.6 mW 96.88 % 95.52 % The fixed losses (\(C_{oss}\), gate and core) add up to 250.0 mW and dominate at light load; so \(\eta\) rises with the load. Below 0.64 A, the valley goes negative and the switching formulas no longer hold. Exercise If the dead time went from 50 ns to 100 ns, how much would the diode loss and the efficiency change at 2 A? Exercise Does driving only the low-side switch at 4.5 V instead of 10 V pay off? Use \(Q_g\) = 15 nC and a typical \(R_{DS(on)}\) of 6.6 mΩ at 4.5 V (against 5.2 mΩ at 10 V), at 2 A.

heading: Synchronous buck 24 V → 9 V: worked example
summary: The lab's buck, from the specifications to the firmware, with the numbers of every step of the trail and the four controllers simulated in QSPICE.
text: This is the converter that runs through the From the analog buck to the digital loop trail: a synchronous buck controlled by a microcontroller, simulated in QSPICE with the firmware in C. Each step below points to the note that explains the theory and shows the number it gives for this buck. The lab's synchronous buck: two complementary switches with dead time, a lossy LC filter and a resistive load.

title: Synchronous buck 24 V → 9 V: worked example
heading: Specifications
summary: The lab's buck, from the specifications to the firmware, with the numbers of every step of the trail and the four controllers simulated in QSPICE.
text: Quantity Value Input / output 24 V → 9 V Switching 200 kHz, dead time of 50 ns Inductor 22 µH, resistance of 30 mΩ Capacitor 47 µF, ESR of 5 mΩ Switches \(R_{on}\) = 10 mΩ Load 9 Ω (1 A) and 4.5 Ω (2 A) ADC 12 bits, full scale of 20 V Duty ratio from 0 to 0.9 Design summary. Voltage-mode control, with one ADC sample and one controller update per period. The default compensator is a 2p2z with crossover at 8 kHz, two zeros at 2 kHz (below the LC resonance, at 5 kHz) and a pole at 60 kHz. The computed duty applies in the next period, with trailing-edge PWM.

title: Synchronous buck 24 V → 9 V: worked example
heading: The example, step by step
summary: The lab's buck, from the specifications to the firmware, with the numbers of every step of the trail and the four controllers simulated in QSPICE.
text: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM. \(D = 9/24 = 0.375\); \(\Delta i_L = 1.28\) A; output ripple of 17.6 mV peak to peak (17.0 mV from the capacitor and 6.4 mV from the ESR, out of phase). The CCM boundary is at 14.1 Ω, but the synchronous buck stays in forced CCM above it. Sizing L and C. The ripple is 64 % of 2 A, and the peak reaches 2.64 A; the capacitor's RMS current is 0.37 A. The 47 µF capacitor is set by the load step: \(1\,\text{A}/(2\pi\cdot 8\,\text{kHz}\cdot 47\,\text{µF}) \approx 0.42\) V of dip. The averaged switch model. \(R_s = R_L + R_{on}\) = 40 mΩ. The averaged model with delay stayed within 0.3 dB and 0.7° of QSPICE from 500 Hz to 15 kHz, measured as in Measuring the loop gain by injecting into the duty. The buck's transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\). DC gain of 27.6 dB; \(f_0\) = 4.96 kHz; \(Q\) = 7.1 at 9 Ω and 4.6 at 4.5 Ω; at 8 kHz the plant is 23.4 dB. The ESR zero. \(f_{\mathrm{ESR}}\) = 677 kHz, above the switching frequency: it gives 0.7° at 8 kHz, that is, nothing. Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins. With the 2p2z, the crossover is at 8.0 kHz, with a phase margin of 41° and a gain margin of 13.9 dB (the phase crosses −180° at 23 kHz). At 4.5 Ω, 46° and 14.1 dB. Between 1 and 2.4 kHz, where the compensator's zeros are, the loop gain dips slightly below 0 dB (down to −1.1 dB), but there the phase is far from −180°. Sampling and the zero-order hold (ZOH). Sampling at 200 kHz: the Nyquist limit is 100 kHz, and the crossover is at \(f_s/25\). Computation and PWM delay. The delay is \((1 + D)T_s = 1.375\cdot 5\,\text{µs} = 6.875\,\mu\)s, which costs \(360^\circ\cdot 8\,\text{kHz}\cdot 6.875\,\text{µs} = 19.8^\circ\) of phase at crossover. The bilinear (Tustin) transform and prewarping. Without prewarping, Tustin would move 8 kHz to 7.96 kHz (−0.5 %), but the 60 kHz pole to 48 kHz (−20 %). The default 2p2z was discretized by pole-zero matching. The 2p2z compensator. In the form \(\frac{b_0 + b_1 z^{-1} + b_2 z^{-2}}{1 + a_1 z^{-1} + a_2 z^{-2}}\), the default 2p2z's coefficients are \(b_0 = 0.2311\), \(b_1 = -0.4341\), \(b_2 = 0.2038\), \(a_1 = -1.1518\) and \(a_2 = 0.1518\), with the integrator at \(z = 1\) and the pole at \(p = a_2\). ADC quantization. One ADC step is \(20\,\text{V}/4095 = 4.884\) mV; the output ripple spans 3.6 steps. DPWM resolution and limit cycles. With the HRTIM at 400 MHz counting up, one period has \(400\,\text{MHz}/200\,\text{kHz} = 2000\) counts (11.0 bits). One duty step moves the output by \(24\,\text{V}/2000 = 12.0\) mV, 2.5 ADC steps: the DPWM is coarser than the ADC, and there is a risk of limit cycles. With the centered pulse, each half period has 1000 steps, from the 2000 counts per period. Q15 fixed point. The default 2p2z's coefficients \(b_0\), \(b_1\), \(b_2\) and \(a_2\) fit in Q15, which goes from −1 to almost 1; \(a_1 = -1.15\) does not, and the velocity form stores only \(a_2\). Those of the aggressive design (\(b_1 = -1.58\)) and of the unstable one (\(b_1 = -2.17\)) do not, and call for another scaling. Anti-windup and duty saturation and Derivative kick and derivative on the measurement. The duty ratio is limited from 0 to 0.9. In the reference step without slew, the PID's derivative kick drives the duty to zero for one period, and the integrator must be held back. The 2p2z in C, in the interrupt. At 200 kHz, the interrupt has 5 µs, or 2000 cycles of a 400 MHz core, to read the ADC, compute and write the PWM compare register. \(G_{vg}\), \(Z_{out}\) and the three ports of the plant and Input feedforward. From the input to the output, \(G_{vg}(0) = V_o/V_{in} = 0.375\); the output impedance goes from 39.8 mΩ at DC to 4.8 Ω at the resonance. When the input drops from 24 to 18 V, the output sags 1.1 V with the 2p2z; with input feedforward, \(d = u \cdot 24\,\text{V}/v_{in}\), less than 0.1 V.

title: Synchronous buck 24 V → 9 V: worked example
heading: The power stage
summary: The lab's buck, from the specifications to the firmware, with the numbers of every step of the trail and the four controllers simulated in QSPICE.
text: The loop sees only \(R_s\); the board needs the losses, the temperatures and the parts. These notes do the sums for the buck at 2 A, with real 60 V switches in place of the model's ideal ones: RMS current in the buck's capacitors. The input capacitor carries 0.99 A RMS (1.02 A with the input at 18 V), almost three times the output capacitor's 0.37 A. Losses of the synchronous buck. 581 mW of losses and 96.88 % efficiency; with the upper bound of the reverse recovery, 845 mW and 95.52 %. QSPICE, with the switch's model, confirms the turn-on and shows the turn-off almost free of loss. Dead time and switching in the synchronous buck. The high-side switch switches with loss at both edges, and the low-side one turns on at zero voltage. The 50 ns of dead time cost 23 mW in the body diode and take 0.25 V off the node's average voltage. The buck inductor: core losses, Dowell and saturation. A powdered-iron core made for 200 kHz loses 24 mW, against 474 mW for a general-purpose material. Thermal design and part selection for the buck. The high-side switch, which carries the switching, \(C_{oss}\) and reverse recovery losses, sits at 55 °C, and the low-side one at 43 °C, with a 40 °C ambient, with only the board's copper.

text: The margins come from the validated model, at 9 Ω; each link opens the simulation in the oscilloscope. Controller Crossover Phase margin Gain margin Original PID 8.9 kHz 25° 11.6 dB 2p2z 8.0 kHz 41° 13.9 dB Aggressive 18 kHz 16° 2.7 dB Unstable 25 kHz −18° −3.2 dB Original PID: load step from 1 to 2 A 2p2z: load step from 1 to 2 A Aggressive: the same step, with damped ringing Unstable: the loop oscillates near 23 kHz before any step The original PID has no derivative filter and crosses over with only 25° of margin. The 2p2z crosses a little lower, with 41°. The aggressive design pushes the crossover to 18 kHz, where the delay already eats 44.6°. The unstable one crosses at 25 kHz, beyond the frequency where the phase crosses −180°, and oscillates. Loop gain of the 2p2z: crossover at 8 kHz, phase margin of 41° and gain margin of 13.9 dB. title: Synchronous buck 24 V → 9 V: worked example
heading: In the converters
summary: The lab's buck, from the specifications to the firmware, with the numbers of every step of the trail and the four controllers simulated in QSPICE.
text: In the simulation with the 2p2z, the load step from 1 to 2 A pulls the output down to 8.59 V, close to the 0.42 V estimate of step 2. With the PID, the minimum is 8.66 V, and with the aggressive design, 8.73 V: crossing over higher dips less, but the smaller phase margin shows up as ringing. What changes in the boost The lab's Synchronous boost 12 V → 48 V: worked example (12 V → 48 V, 100 kHz) has a right-half-plane zero: at 14 kHz at 1 A and at 7 kHz at 2 A. This zero removes phase like a delay and forces the crossover to stay low, at 1.5 kHz in the boost's 2p2z, against 8 kHz here. The buck has no such zero, because the duty ratio multiplies no state variable. The four-switch buck-boost has the zero too and, besides, a plant that changes with the input. title: Four-switch buck-boost 8–16 V → 12 V: worked example
heading: Four-switch buck-boost 8–16 V → 12 V: worked example
summary: The lab's buck-boost, from the specifications to the firmware, with a 2p2z that works from 9 to 15 V and from 1 to 3 A, and the thirteen scenarios simulated in QSPICE.
text: This converter steps the voltage of an 8 to 16 V battery down or up to a 12 V bus. It runs in buck-boost mode, with all four switches commutating, and is simulated with the same C code as the Synchronous buck 24 V → 9 V: worked example and the Synchronous boost 12 V → 48 V: worked example, in floating point; the scenarios start in steady state, and the Q15 version was not simulated. The new difficulty is that the plant changes with the input, and a single compensator has to work across the whole range. Each step below points to the note that explains the theory and shows the number it gives here. The lab's four-switch buck-boost: G1 turns on Q1 and Q4, and the inductor receives the input; G2 turns on Q2 and Q3, and the inductor discharges into the output.

On the step from 1 to 3 A, \(2\,\text{A}/(2\pi\cdot 3\,\text{kHz}\cdot 100\,\text{µF}) = 1.06\) V. In the simulation with the 2p2z, the output falls from 11.98 to 10.90 V: 1.08 V. The averaged switch model. \(R_l\) = 15 mΩ + 2 × 10 mΩ = 35 mΩ: the inductor and the two switches always in series with it. The site's model is the sampled-data one of Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost, derived from the switched circuit, with no fitted factor. It stayed within 0.2 dB and 0.7° of QSPICE from 300 Hz to 7 kHz, at 12 V and 1 A, 12 V and 2 A, and 9 V and 3 A, measured as in Measuring the loop gain by injecting into the duty. Transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\) of the boost. The plant has the boost's form, with \(V_{in} + V\) in place of \(V\). DC gain of about 47 (33.4 dB) across the range; resonance at 1.70 kHz at 12 V, from 1.45 to 1.89 kHz from 9 to 15 V. The right-half-plane zero. The right-half-plane zero lies at 20.9 kHz at 12 V and 2 A, 13.7 kHz at 3 A, and comes down to 8.5 kHz at 9 V and 3 A. Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost. The sample sits about 50 mV above the average (11.95 V with the samples at 12 V). In the plant the ADC sees, the zero rises to 28.9 kHz at 2 A, and the margin gains 1.2°. Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins. At the nominal point, the 2p2z crosses at 3.0 kHz, with a phase margin of 42.6° and a gain margin of 13.8 dB (the phase crosses −180° at 9.5 kHz). Computation and PWM delay. The firmware's delay is \((1 + D)\,T_s = 15.1\) µs. To first order, the switched response behaves like \((1 + 0.506/2) \cdot 10\,\text{µs} = 12.5\) µs (Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost), which costs 13.5° at 3 kHz. The crossover sits at \(f_s/33\) (Sampling and the zero-order hold (ZOH)). Robust design across the operating range. From 9 to 15 V and from 1 to 3 A, the phase margin stays between 39.1° (9 V, 3 A) and 43.9° (15 V, 1 A), and the gain margin above 11.7 dB. At the specification's extreme, 8 V and 3 A, the margin falls to 37.2°. At 3 A, the window between \(3f_0\) and \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}/3\) opens only at 15 V, and the 2p2z crosses below \(3f_0\) (The boost's crossover window). The bilinear (Tustin) transform and prewarping. Without prewarping, Tustin would take 3 kHz to 2.99 kHz, but the 40 kHz pole to 28.6 kHz (−28 %). The 2p2z was discretized by matched poles and zeros. The 2p2z compensator. The zeros go to \(e^{-2\pi\cdot 1000\cdot 10\,\text{µs}} = 0.9391\) and the pole to \(p = 0.0810\): \(b_0 = 0.2198\), \(b_1 = -0.4129\), \(b_2 = 0.1939\), \(a_1 = -1.0810\) and \(a_2 = 0.0810\).
