title: RMS current in the buck's capacitors
heading: RMS current in the buck's capacitors
summary: The buck's input capacitor carries a pulsed current of RMS value IoD(1-D), much larger than the output capacitor's, which sees only the inductor's triangular ripple.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
text: A capacitor heats up with the current through it, not with the voltage across it. The loss is \(I_{\mathrm{rms}}^2 R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\), and the manufacturer gives an RMS current limit for each temperature. So, after choosing the capacitance for the voltage ripple, the current still has to be checked. In the buck, the two capacitors carry very different currents.

title: RMS current in the buck's capacitors
heading: The output capacitor
summary: The buck's input capacitor carries a pulsed current of RMS value IoD(1-D), much larger than the output capacitor's, which sees only the inductor's triangular ripple.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
text: The inductor is in series with the output, and the current reaching the output node is already continuous, with a triangular ripple. The load takes the average, \(I_o\), and the output capacitor takes only the triangular part. The output capacitor's RMS current equation, which Sizing L and C uses in step 3, gives \(\Delta i_L/\sqrt{12}\). It does not depend on the load: with the same \(\Delta i_L\), the RMS current is the same at 0.5 A or at 2 A.

title: RMS current in the buck's capacitors
heading: The input capacitor
summary: The buck's input capacitor carries a pulsed current of RMS value IoD(1-D), much larger than the output capacitor's, which sees only the inductor's triangular ripple.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
text: On the input side, the high-side switch carries the inductor current during \(DT_s\) and nothing for the rest of the period. The current drawn from the input is a train of pulses of height \(I_o\). The source, with its cables and filter, has inductance and delivers only the average, \(I_{in} = D\,I_o\). The difference comes from the input capacitor: during \(DT_s\), the capacitor supplies \(I_o - D I_o = (1 - D)\,I_o\); during \((1 - D)\,T_s\), the source recharges it with \(D\,I_o\). The two charges are equal, \((1 - D)\,I_o\,D T_s\), so the capacitor's average current is zero. The square of the RMS current is the mean of the square: \[I_{C_{in},\mathrm{rms}}^2 = D\,(1 - D)^2 I_o^2 + (1 - D)\,D^2 I_o^2 = D\,(1 - D)\,I_o^2\,[(1 - D) + D]\] and so \[I_{C_{in},\mathrm{rms}} = I_o\,\sqrt{D\,(1 - D)}\] The current is proportional to the load, unlike the output capacitor's. The factor \(\sqrt{D(1-D)}\) peaks at 0.5 at \(D = 0.5\): the worst case is an input voltage equal to twice the output. The equation ignores the ripple of \(i_L\) during \(DT_s\). With it, the pulse becomes a trapezoid, and the exact sum is \[I_{C_{in},\mathrm{rms}}^2 = D\,I_{L,\mathrm{rms}}^2 - (D\,I_o)^2, \qquad I_{L,\mathrm{rms}}^2 = I_o^2 + \frac{\Delta i_L^2}{12}\] The first term is the square of the RMS current in the high-side switch, and the second removes the DC part, which comes from the source.

title: RMS current in the buck's capacitors
heading: The input capacitance
summary: The buck's input capacitor carries a pulsed current of RMS value IoD(1-D), much larger than the output capacitor's, which sees only the inductor's triangular ripple.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
text: The same charge gives the voltage ripple at the input. The capacitor loses \((1 - D)\,I_o\,D T_s\) during the pulse, so \[\Delta v_{in} = \frac{D\,(1 - D)\,I_o}{f_s\,C_{in}}, \qquad C_{in} \ge \frac{D\,(1 - D)\,I_o}{f_s\,\Delta v_{in}}\] with the ESR part, \(R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\,I_{\mathrm{peak}}\), with the inductor's peak current, added on top. The sum assumes all the AC current stays in the capacitor; if the source has a low impedance at the switching frequency, part of it goes into the cables, and that is what an input filter prevents. The lab has no input capacitor In the buck's netlist, the input is an ideal source: it supplies the whole pulses, with no ripple. On a board, the pulse current flows in the loop formed by the input capacitor and the two switches. That capacitor sits right next to the switches, because the inductance of that loop produces the voltage spike at each commutation (Dead time and switching in the synchronous buck).

title: RMS current in the buck's capacitors
heading: In the converters
summary: The buck's input capacitor carries a pulsed current of RMS value IoD(1-D), much larger than the output capacitor's, which sees only the inductor's triangular ripple.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
text: The lab's buck has L = 22 µH, C = 47 µF with an ESR of 5 mΩ, and switches at 200 kHz. The RMS currents below come from the steady-state functions of the author's synchronous buck sizing model; the exact one was checked by numerically sampling the waveform. \(V_{in}\) \(D\) \(C_o\): \(\Delta i_L/\sqrt{12}\) \(C_{in}\), 1 A \(C_{in}\), 2 A \(C_{in}\), 2 A, exact 24 V 0.375 0.37 A 0.48 A 0.97 A 0.99 A 18 V 0.5 0.30 A 0.50 A 1.00 A 1.02 A The input carries almost three times the output's current at 2 A: 0.99 A against 0.37 A. With an ESR of 5 mΩ, the same as the model's output capacitor (an assumption, since the lab has no input capacitor), the loss would be 4.9 mW at the input and 0.7 mW at the output. The worst case is 18 V, in the input scenario that falls from 24 to 18 V: \(D\) reaches 0.5, and the RMS current, \(I_o/2\). The capacitance, from the charge balance: for 1 % ripple, \(\Delta v_{in}\) = 0.24 V at 24 V and 2 A, \(C_{in} \ge 0.375\cdot 0.625\cdot 2/(200\,\text{kHz}\cdot 0.24) = 9.8\) µF; at 18 V, with 1 % of 18 V (0.18 V), 13.9 µF. The form without \((1 - D)\), \(D\,I_o/(f_s\,\Delta v_{in})\), is a conservative bound: here, 60 % more. In the Synchronous boost 12 V → 48 V: worked example, the roles swap: the inductor is at the input, which sees only the triangular ripple, and the output receives the pulses from the diode or the switch. In the four-switch buck-boost, both capacitors receive pulses, each in the mode where its side switches. Exercise With the input at 18 V and the load at 2 A, compare the RMS current in the input capacitor from the (1) and from the exact sum. Exercise How much input capacitance keeps the ripple at 0.1 V at 24 V and 2 A, without counting the ESR?

title: Dead time and switching in the synchronous buck
heading: Dead time and switching in the synchronous buck
summary: What happens at the switch node during the dead time, why the high-side switch switches with loss and the low-side one does not, and how to choose the dead time between shoot-through and body-diode loss.
text: In the synchronous buck, the two switches must never conduct together: that would short the input. The driver turns one switch off and waits a dead time before turning the other on. In that interval, the inductor current does not stop, and the path it finds decides who switches with loss.

title: Dead time and switching in the synchronous buck
heading: The two body diodes
summary: What happens at the switch node during the dead time, why the high-side switch switches with loss and the low-side one does not, and how to choose the dead time between shoot-through and body-diode loss.
text: Body diode The body diode is the drain-to-source junction every power MOSFET has, in parallel with the channel. It conducts from source to drain whenever the voltage across the switch goes negative, with a drop \(V_{SD}\) between 0.7 and 1 V. With the inductor current positive at both edges, the period runs in this sequence: The high-side switch turns off at the peak current. The inductor discharges the node's capacitances, and the node falls from \(V_{in}\) to zero. While the channel closes, the switch still has voltage and current: that is the turn-off loss. The low-side switch's body diode conducts until the end of the dead time, with the node at \(-V_{SD}\). The low-side switch turns on with almost zero volts across it. There is no switching loss: this is zero-voltage switching (ZVS). The low-side switch turns off at the valley. The current, still positive, goes back into the body diode. The high-side switch turns on against the conducting diode. It must take over the valley current, charge the node from zero to \(V_{in}\) and remove the charge stored in the diode. Reverse recovery A junction diode that has conducted holds charge. To block, it conducts in reverse until that charge is removed. The removed charge is \(Q_{rr}\), and the reverse recovery costs \(Q_{rr} V_{in}\) per period, dissipated in the switch that turns on. That is why the high-side switch switches with loss at both edges, and the low-side one at neither. The losses of Losses of the synchronous buck follow this picture. Light load. With \(I_o < \Delta i_L/2\), the current's valley goes negative, and the synchronous buck stays in CCM. In step 4, the current flows from the output into the node, charges the capacitances up to \(V_{in}\) and puts the high-side switch's body diode into conduction. If the dead time is long enough for that, the high-side switch also turns on at zero voltage. The time needed is the node's charge divided by the valley current.

title: Dead time and switching in the synchronous buck
heading: Choosing the dead time
summary: What happens at the switch node during the dead time, why the high-side switch switches with loss and the low-side one does not, and how to choose the dead time between shoot-through and body-diode loss.
text: Minimum. The dead time must cover the delay mismatch between the driver's two channels, the fall time of the switch turning off and a margin. With less, both switches conduct together every period. Maximum. Every extra nanosecond is diode time, with \(V_{SD}\) in place of \(I R_{on}\), and a diode that conducts longer accumulates more charge for the reverse recovery. The dead time also changes the node's average voltage. At the edge where the high-side switch turns on, the node sits at \(-V_{SD}\) instead of \(V_{in}\), and the average loses \((V_{in} + V_{SD})\,t_{dt}\,f_s\); at the other, it sits at \(-V_{SD}\) instead of \(-I R_{on}\), almost nothing.

title: Dead time and switching in the synchronous buck
heading: The edges
summary: What happens at the switch node during the dead time, why the high-side switch switches with loss and the low-side one does not, and how to choose the dead time between shoot-through and body-diode loss.
text: The current the switch interrupts changes in a loop with parasitic inductance: the input capacitor, the two switches and the traces between them (RMS current in the buck's capacitors). The rate \(di/dt\) in that inductance adds a spike to the voltage across the switch, \(L_{par}\,di/dt\), and the same inductance rings with \(C_{oss}\), at a frequency \(1/(2\pi\sqrt{L_{par} C_{oss}})\).

title: Dead time and switching in the synchronous buck
heading: In the converters
summary: What happens at the switch node during the dead time, why the high-side switch switches with loss and the low-side one does not, and how to choose the dead time between shoot-through and body-diode loss.
text: The lab's buck has a dead time of 50 ns. The netlist uses ideal switches and a body diode with no stored charge: in QSPICE, there is no \(Q_{rr}\), node capacitance or spike. The numbers below use the AO4262E of Thermal design and part selection for the buck, with a diode of 0.71 V at the valley and 0.73 V at the peak, and its model in QSPICE (Losses of the synchronous buck). The node's fall, in step 1, at 2 A: each switch has about 22 nC of \(Q_{oss}\) up to 24 V, so the node swaps 44 nC, and \(44\,\text{nC}/2.64\,\text{A} \approx 17\) ns; for the rest of the dead time, the diode conducts. In QSPICE, the high-side switch only starts to turn off 19.5 ns after the command, and the node falls in 8 ns: the diode conducts for 24 ns at that edge and 35 ns at the other, where the low-side switch is also slow to turn off. The minimum, by the rule of the author's dead-time model: mismatch between two drivers (15 ns, from Infineon's 1ED3321MC12N, a single-channel part and the catalog's only driver) + \(t_f\) (7 ns) + 30 ns of margin = 52 ns, above the lab's 50 ns; the rule recommends 72 ns. It does not count \(t_{d(off)} - t_{d(on)} = 29 - 6 = 23\) ns (data sheet, 3 Ω on the gate), which raise the minimum to about 75 ns. The 50 ns only work with matched drivers, a half-bridge driver: in QSPICE, the high side starts to turn off 19.5 ns after the command, the node falls in 8.3 ns and about 22 ns remain; with a 15 ns mismatch, 7 ns would remain. At lower current, the Miller plateau is lower, and the real \(t_{d(off)}\) can exceed 29 ns. The cost in the diode, at 2 A, without and with the node's fall at the turn-off edge; QSPICE gives 15.1 mW at 50 ns, adding up the low side's dead-time windows: Dead time Without the fall With the fall 25 ns 14.5 mW 8.1 mW 50 ns 29.0 mW 22.6 mW 100 ns 58.0 mW 51.6 mW 200 ns 116.1 mW 109.6 mW The average voltage: the high-side switch turns on 50 ns after the pulse starts, so the dead time comes out of its on time. At 2 A, \((24 + 0.71)\cdot 50\,\text{ns}\cdot 200\,\text{kHz} = 0.25\) V, plus 7 mV at the other edge: 2.8 % of the 9 V, which the loop makes up with \(D\) about 1.1 points larger. In QSPICE, 9 V at 2 A take \(D\) = 0.3842, 0.9 points above 0.375: the turn-off delay gives part of the time back. Light load: at 0.25 A, the valley is −0.39 A, and the high-side switch only turns on at zero voltage with about \(44\,\text{nC}/0.39\,\text{A} = 113\) ns of dead time, more than twice the present one. The edges: the author's transient model, with 17 nH of parasitic inductance in the loop and \(t_f\) = 7 ns, gives \(di/dt\) = 0.38 A/ns at turn-off at 2.64 A, a spike of 6.4 V above the 24 V, and ringing at 54 MHz with a \(C_{oss}\) of 520 pF. Exercise At a 1 A load, does the high-side switch turn on at zero voltage with the 50 ns dead time? Exercise If the power loop's inductance fell from 17 to 5 nH, with the same \(di/dt\), what would the voltage spike across the switch be?

title: The ESR zero
heading: The ESR zero
summary: The output capacitor's series resistance adds a zero to the plant; with electrolytics it helps the loop, with ceramics it lies above the switching frequency and does not count.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: A real capacitor has an equivalent series resistance (ESR). In the buck's plant, it appears as the factor \(1 + s/\omega_{\mathrm{ESR}}\) in the numerator of (1): a real zero in the left half-plane. \[G_{vd}(s) = \frac{\hat v_o(s)}{\hat d(s)} = G_0\;\frac{1 + s/\omega_{\mathrm{ESR}}}{1 + \dfrac{s}{Q\,\omega_0} + \dfrac{s^2}{\omega_0^2}}, \qquad G_0 = V_{in}\,\frac{R}{R + R_s}\] \[f_{\mathrm{ESR}} = \frac{1}{2\pi\,R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\,C}\]

title: The ESR zero
heading: Where the zero comes from
summary: The output capacitor's series resistance adds a zero to the plant; with electrolytics it helps the loop, with ceramics it lies above the switching frequency and does not count.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: The impedance of the capacitor with its ESR is \[Z_C(s) = R_{\mathrm{ESR}} + \frac{1}{sC} = \frac{1 + s R_{\mathrm{ESR}} C}{sC}\] Below \(f_{\mathrm{ESR}}\), \(1/sC\) dominates, and the capacitor filters. Above it, \(R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\) dominates, and the capacitor becomes a resistor: the current ripple now produces a proportional voltage ripple, the \(R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\Delta i_L\) part of equation Output voltage ripple of the buck. ESR zero The ESR zero is the frequency at which the two parts of the capacitor's impedance have equal magnitude. Above it, the buck's plant falls 20 dB per decade instead of 40, and the phase rises by up to 90° relative to the pole pair alone.

title: The ESR zero
heading: What the zero does on the Bode plot
summary: The output capacitor's series resistance adds a zero to the plant; with electrolytics it helps the loop, with ceramics it lies above the switching frequency and does not count.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: A left-half-plane zero lifts the phase: \(\arctan(f/f_{\mathrm{ESR}})\), which is 45° at \(f_{\mathrm{ESR}}\) and almost nothing a decade below. If the zero is near the crossover \(f_c\), it supplies for free part of the phase boost the compensator would have to give. That was the case in older bucks with electrolytic capacitors, whose ESR is tens of milliohms: with them, a type II compensator was enough. With ceramic capacitors, the ESR drops to a few milliohms, and the zero moves up to hundreds of kHz, above \(f_s/2\). There it does not help: the digital loop does not even see frequencies above \(f_s/2\) (see Sampling and the zero-order hold (ZOH)), and the compensator must give all the phase boost, with two zeros, like the The 2p2z compensator. Do not count on the ESR An electrolytic's ESR varies with temperature (it may double in the cold) and grows with aging. A design that relies on the ESR zero for its phase margin may lose it in winter or after a few years. And putting a ceramic in parallel, to lower the ripple, moves the zero and changes the whole plant. ESR on purpose A resistor is sometimes added in series with the capacitor just to create the zero. It works, but the cost shows in the output ripple and in the load-step response, which gains an instantaneous jump of \(\Delta I\cdot R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\).

title: The ESR zero
heading: In the converters
summary: The output capacitor's series resistance adds a zero to the plant; with electrolytics it helps the loop, with ceramics it lies above the switching frequency and does not count.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: In the lab's buck, C = 47 µF with an ESR of 5 mΩ: \[f_{\mathrm{ESR}} = \frac{1}{2\pi\cdot 5\,\text{m}\Omega\cdot 47\,\text{µF}} = 677\ \text{kHz}\] That is 3.4 times the 200 kHz switching frequency. At 8 kHz, the 2p2z's crossover, the zero gives 0.7° of phase; even at \(f_s/2\) = 100 kHz it gives only 8.4°. For the loop, the capacitor is ideal, and the compensator does all the work. In the boost and the buck-boost, C = 100 µF with an ESR of 10 mΩ, and the zero lies at 159 kHz, also above the 100 kHz switching frequency. There the ESR shows up another way: the ADC samples just before switch G1 turns on, when the capacitor carries the whole inductor current, and reads \(R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\) times that current above the average. The model validated in QSPICE includes this term (Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost). Exercise What ESR would put the buck's zero at 8 kHz, on the crossover? How large would the ESR part of the output ripple be? Exercise A 220 µF electrolytic has an ESR of 80 mΩ at 25 °C. Where is the zero? And if the ESR doubles in the cold? In the author's handbook Modelagem de Conversores Chaveados: do modelo à bancada virtual (in Portuguese): the effect of the ESR among the real plant's parasitics.

title: Four-switch buck-boost
heading: Four-switch buck-boost
summary: Two legs and one inductor that step the voltage down or up; the buck, boost and buck-boost modes, the plant that changes with the input and the mode the lab uses.
prereqs: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: An 8 to 16 V battery feeding a 12 V bus must step the voltage down and up. The four-switch buck-boost does both with a single inductor, without inverting the output: a buck leg at the input (Q1 on top, Q2 below, node A) and a boost leg at the output (Q3 on top, Q4 below, node B), with the inductor between the two nodes. The lab's four-switch buck-boost: the input leg (Q1, Q2) and the output leg (Q3, Q4), with the inductor between nodes A and B.

title: Four-switch buck-boost
heading: Three modes
summary: Two legs and one inductor that step the voltage down or up; the buck, boost and buck-boost modes, the plant that changes with the input and the mode the lab uses.
prereqs: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: Buck. Q3 stays on and Q4 off; only the input leg switches. It is a buck: \(V = D\,V_{in}\), the inductor current is the load's, and the plant has no right-half-plane zero. Boost. Q1 stays on and Q2 off; only the output leg switches. It is a boost: \(V = V_{in}/(1 - D)\), with the right-half-plane zero. Buck-boost. Both legs switch together: G1 turns on Q1 and Q4, and the inductor receives the input; G2 turns on Q2 and Q3, and the inductor discharges into the output. From the volt-second balance, \(D\,V_{in} = D'\,V\), that is, \(V/V_{in} = D/D'\). The first two modes have lower losses, but the firmware must decide which mode it is in and switch modes when \(V_{in}\) crosses \(V\), where each one's duty reaches its limit. The third covers the whole range with a single duty, without transitions. The price is that all four switches commutate every period and the inductor carries the input and output currents added together, \(I = I_o/D'\). The lab's mode The lab's converter always runs in buck-boost mode: G1 drives Q1 and Q4, G2 drives Q2 and Q3. The simulated firmware is the same as the buck's and the boost's, in floating point, with one duty and one voltage loop; the Q15 version was not simulated. The small-signal model and every number on this site are for that mode.

title: Four-switch buck-boost
heading: The plant in buck-boost mode
summary: Two legs and one inductor that step the voltage down or up; the buck, boost and buck-boost modes, the plant that changes with the input and the mode the lab uses.
prereqs: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: With G1, the inductor sees \(+v_{in}\); with G2, \(-v\). The averaged cell becomes \(L\,di_L/dt = d\,v_{in} - d'\,v - R_l\,i_L\), and the capacitor receives \(d'\,i_L\), as in the boost. Linearizing with \(\hat v_{in} = 0\), \(\hat d\) switches the voltage \(V_{in} + V\) across the inductor, instead of the boost's \(V\): \[G_{vd}(s) = G_0\,\frac{\left(1 - \dfrac{s}{2\pi f_{\mathrm{RHP}}}\right)\left(1 + \dfrac{s}{\omega_{\mathrm{ESR}}}\right)}{1 + \dfrac{s}{Q\,\omega_0} + \dfrac{s^2}{\omega_0^2}}, \qquad G_0 = \frac{R\,\bigl(D'(V_{in} + V) - I\,R_l\bigr)}{R_l + D'^2 R}, \qquad \omega_0 = \sqrt{\frac{R_l + D'^2 R}{L\,C\,(R + R_{\mathrm{ESR}})}}, \qquad Q = \frac{\sqrt{L\,C\,(R + R_{\mathrm{ESR}})(R_l + D'^2 R)}}{L + C\left[R_l\,(R + R_{\mathrm{ESR}}) + D'^2 R\,R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\right]}\] Here \(R_l\) adds the inductor and the two switches always in series with it. The right-half-plane zero has the same origin as in the boost, the \(I(sL + R_l)\) term: \[f_{\mathrm{RHP}} = \frac{D'(V_{in} + V) - I R_l}{2\pi I L} \approx \frac{R\,D'^2}{2\pi L}\cdot\frac{V_{in} + V}{V}\] As in the boost, the resonance is that of the inductor seen through \(D'\), \(f_0 \approx D'/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})\). The ADC sample also reads the ESR term of Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost, and the switched response behaves, to first order, like a delay of \((1 + D/2)\,T_s\), as in the boost. The site uses the sampled-data model of the switched circuit.

title: Four-switch buck-boost
heading: The plant changes with the input
summary: Two legs and one inductor that step the voltage down or up; the buck, boost and buck-boost modes, the plant that changes with the input and the mode the lab uses.
prereqs: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: With the output fixed, the input sets \(D\): from \(V/(V_{in} + V)\), 0.57 at 9 V to 0.44 at 15 V, without losses. Hence: The resonance rises with \(D'\), about 30 % from 9 to 15 V. The DC gain hardly changes: without losses, \(G_{vd}(0) = (V_{in} + V)/D'\), and both quantities grow together. The right-half-plane zero comes down when the input falls and when the load rises. The worst case is the minimum input with the maximum load. A fixed compensator must work at all these points; how to choose it is in Robust design across the operating range.

title: Four-switch buck-boost
heading: In the converters
summary: Two legs and one inductor that step the voltage down or up; the buck, boost and buck-boost modes, the plant that changes with the input and the mode the lab uses.
prereqs: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: The lab's buck-boost goes from 8–16 V to 12 V, at 100 kHz, with L = 22 µH, C = 100 µF and \(R_l\) = 15 mΩ + 2 × 10 mΩ = 35 mΩ. The scenarios cover 9 to 15 V and 1 to 3 A. The full averaged model gives: Point \(D\) \(I\) \(f_0\) DC gain \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}\) 9 V, 3 A (4 Ω) 0.583 7.20 A 1.45 kHz 46.6 (33.4 dB) 8.5 kHz 12 V, 1 A (12 Ω) 0.503 2.01 A 1.70 kHz 47.4 (33.5 dB) 42.6 kHz 12 V, 2 A (6 Ω) 0.506 4.05 A 1.70 kHz 46.9 (33.4 dB) 20.9 kHz 12 V, 3 A (4 Ω) 0.509 6.11 A 1.69 kHz 46.3 (33.3 dB) 13.7 kHz 15 V, 3 A (4 Ω) 0.452 5.47 A 1.89 kHz 47.2 (33.5 dB) 19.3 kHz From 12 to 12 V at 2 A, the inductor carries 4.05 A, twice the output current: that is the cost of buck-boost mode. The model was checked in QSPICE at 12 V and 1 A, 12 V and 2 A, and 9 V and 3 A: it stayed within 0.2 dB and 0.7° of the switched circuit from 300 Hz to 7 kHz (Measuring the loop gain by injecting into the duty). The full example is in Four-switch buck-boost 8–16 V → 12 V: worked example. Input from 9 to 15 V with the output at 12 V: the input crosses the output, the duty goes from about 0.59 to 0.46 (a little above the lossless duties), and the mode does not change. Exercise From the approximation, compute \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}\) at 12 V and 3 A, using \(D' = 0.491\). Compare with the table.

title: The buck inductor: core losses, Dowell and saturation
heading: The buck inductor: core losses, Dowell and saturation
summary: How the current ripple becomes core loss through the iGSE, why copper loses more at high frequency than its DC resistance suggests, and how to check saturation, with three designs of the lab's 22 µH inductor.
text: The lab model reduces the inductor to an inductance and a resistance, \(R_L\). A real inductor has a core that loses energy every flux cycle, a winding whose resistance rises with frequency, and a current above which the inductance drops. This note handles the three effects with the magnetics functions of the author's catalog.

title: The buck inductor: core losses, Dowell and saturation
heading: The flux in the core
summary: How the current ripple becomes core loss through the iGSE, why copper loses more at high frequency than its DC resistance suggests, and how to check saturation, with three designs of the lab's 22 µH inductor.
text: With \(N\) turns on a core of effective area \(A_e\), Faraday's law gives \(v_L = N A_e\,dB/dt\). Since \(v_L = L\,di_L/dt\), the flux swing follows the current swing: \[\Delta B = \frac{L\,\Delta i_L}{N A_e}, \qquad B_{\mathrm{peak}} = \frac{L\,I_{\mathrm{peak}}}{N A_e}\] The DC part of \(B\) spends no energy in the core, but brings it closer to saturation. The AC part, \(\Delta B\), is the one that loses.

title: The buck inductor: core losses, Dowell and saturation
heading: Core losses
summary: How the current ripple becomes core loss through the iGSE, why copper loses more at high frequency than its DC resistance suggests, and how to check saturation, with three designs of the lab's 22 µH inductor.
text: The Steinmetz equation describes a material's loss per volume under sinusoidal flux: \(P_v = k\,f^{\alpha}\,B_{\mathrm{peak}}^{\beta}\), with \(k\), \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) fitted to the manufacturer's curves. The buck's flux is triangular: it rises during \(DT_s\) and falls during \((1 - D)\,T_s\). The improved generalized Steinmetz equation (iGSE) uses the rate \(dB/dt\) of each segment and, for the triangular wave, becomes \[P_v = k_i\,f^{\alpha}\,\Delta B^{\beta}\,\left[D^{1-\alpha} + (1 - D)^{1-\alpha}\right]\] where \(k_i\) follows from \(k\), \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), with no new measurement. The loss is \(P_v\) times the effective volume \(V_e\). With \(\alpha\) near 1, as in powdered irons, the waveform correction almost vanishes; it weighs more in materials with a larger \(\alpha\) and a duty ratio near 0 or 1.

title: The buck inductor: core losses, Dowell and saturation
heading: Winding losses
summary: How the current ripple becomes core loss through the iGSE, why copper loses more at high frequency than its DC resistance suggests, and how to check saturation, with three designs of the lab's 22 µH inductor.
text: At high frequency, the current crowds near the conductor's surface, within a depth \[\delta = \sqrt{\frac{\rho}{\pi f \mu_0}}\] That is the skin effect. In a winding of several layers, the field of the neighboring layers induces circulating currents in each wire: the proximity effect. Dowell's model joins both into a factor \(F_R = R_{ac}/R_{dc}\): \[F_R = \Delta\left[M(\Delta) + \tfrac23\,(p^2 - 1)\,D(\Delta)\right], \qquad \Delta = d/\delta\] with \(p\) layers and Dowell's functions \(M\) and \(D\), which tend to 1 when \(\Delta\) is large. In the buck, only the ripple, of RMS value \(\Delta i_L/\sqrt{12}\), is AC. The copper loss is \((I_{L,\mathrm{rms}}^2 - \Delta i_L^2/12)\,R_{dc} + (\Delta i_L^2/12)\,F_R\,R_{dc}\). The \(p^2\) term is what makes the second layer expensive.

title: The buck inductor: core losses, Dowell and saturation
heading: Saturation
summary: How the current ripple becomes core loss through the iGSE, why copper loses more at high frequency than its DC resistance suggests, and how to check saturation, with three designs of the lab's 22 µH inductor.
text: In a gapped ferrite core, the inductance is nearly constant until \(B_{\mathrm{peak}}\) approaches \(B_{\mathrm{sat}}\), and then it collapses. In a powder core, the gap is distributed, and the permeability falls gradually with the magnetic field, \(N I/l_e\). In both cases, the check is made at the peak current and at the working temperature: \(B_{\mathrm{sat}}\) falls with temperature.

title: The buck inductor: core losses, Dowell and saturation
heading: In the converters
summary: How the current ripple becomes core loss through the iGSE, why copper loses more at high frequency than its DC resistance suggests, and how to check saturation, with three designs of the lab's 22 µH inductor.
text: The lab's buck has L = 22 µH and \(R_L\) = 30 mΩ, with no core loss, at 200 kHz. The three designs below use Magmattec powdered-iron toroids from the author's catalog (geometry, \(A_L\), and the Steinmetz coefficients and permeability roll-off fitted to the curves in the data sheets of materials 034 and 002), round wire, and the winding at 60 °C, where \(\delta\) = 0.159 mm. Values at 2 A, with \(\Delta i_L\) = 1.28 A: Design \(N\), wire \(\Delta B\) Core \(R_{dc}\) (20 °C) \(F_R\) Copper Total 034 (\(\mu\) = 33), T26/14/11 24, 0.8 mm, 1 layer 17.8 mT 473.5 mW 28.5 mΩ 5.0 154.4 mW 627.9 mW 002 (\(\mu\) = 10), T26/14/11 41, 1.0 mm, 2 layers 10.4 mT 24.8 mW 31.1 mΩ 18.8 236.5 mW 261.3 mW 002 (\(\mu\) = 10), T33/19/11 45, 1.0 mm, 1 layer 9.0 mT 24.4 mW 35.0 mΩ 6.3 196.5 mW 220.9 mW Two approximations in the copper pull in opposite directions. Dowell's \(F_R\) above does not use the 0.886 factor for round wire nor the layer's porosity, which puts it about 11 % high. The catalog's mean turn length, 35.4 mm, is below the perimeter of the T33/19/11's cross-section, 36 mm; with the 1 mm wire, it would be about 39 mm, and \(R_{dc}\) is about 10 % low. The material decides the core. The 034 gives the lab's \(R_L\) with few turns, but at 200 kHz it loses almost half a watt in the core, more than all the copper. The 002 is made for this frequency: with less permeability, it needs more turns, which also reduce \(\Delta B\), and it loses 19 times less. With \(\alpha\) = 1.04, the iGSE stays within 0.5 % of the sinusoidal Steinmetz. The second layer is expensive. On the T26/14/11, the 41 turns do not fit in one layer: \(F_R\) goes from 6.3 to 18.8, and the AC part of the copper loss reaches 92.4 mW, against 34.7 mW in the single-layer design. The larger toroid, T33/19/11, fits everything in one layer and is the chosen design; stranded insulated wire is the other way out. Saturation. In the 034, the permeability falls to 98.7 % at 2 A DC (22.7 µH) and only reaches 80 % at 13.4 A. In the 002, it does not fall up to the 2.64 A peak, and \(B_{\mathrm{peak}}\) = 18.5 mT against a \(B_{\mathrm{sat}}\) of 450 mT at 100 °C. The chosen design has 22.3 µH with no current and 35 mΩ, a little above the lab's \(R_L\). Thermal design and part selection for the buck computes its temperature rise, and Losses of the synchronous buck uses its core loss. Exercise With the input at 18 V, what is the core loss of the chosen design? Use \(A_e\) = 69.8 mm² and the fact that the loss grows with \(\Delta B^{2.11}\) (the \(\beta\) of material 002). Exercise In the two-layer design, why does the AC copper loss triple, if the AC current is the same?

title: Sizing L and C
heading: Sizing L and C
summary: How to choose the buck's inductor and capacitor from the ripple specifications, the capacitor's RMS current and the load step.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: This procedure uses the equations of Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM backwards: it starts from the specifications and arrives at L and C. At the end, we check the lab's buck.

title: Sizing L and C
heading: 1. Choose the current ripple and compute L
summary: How to choose the buck's inductor and capacitor from the ripple specifications, the capacitor's RMS current and the load step.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: Define the relative ripple \(r = \Delta i_L / I_{o,\max}\). Values from 20 % to 40 % are the usual starting point: less calls for a large, slow inductor; more raises the peak, the core losses and the capacitor's RMS current. From the ripple equation, \[L = \frac{V_o\,(1 - D)}{r\,I_{o,\max}\,f_s}\] Use the highest input voltage: \(1 - D\) grows with \(V_{in}\), and so does the ripple. Saturation Check the peak \(I_{o,\max} + \Delta i_L/2\) against the inductor's saturation current, not only against its rated current. The inductance of many powdered-iron inductors drops 20 % to 30 % with current, and the ripple rises in the same proportion.

title: Sizing L and C
heading: 2. Compute C and the maximum ESR from the voltage ripple
summary: How to choose the buck's inductor and capacitor from the ripple specifications, the capacitor's RMS current and the load step.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: With the specified output ripple \(\Delta v_o\), split the budget between the two parts: \[C \ge \frac{\Delta i_L}{8\,f_s\,\Delta v_o}, \qquad R_{\mathrm{ESR}} \le \frac{\Delta v_o}{\Delta i_L}\] With ceramic capacitors, the ESR is a few milliohms and the capacitive part dominates. With electrolytics, the ESR usually dominates, and the capacitance ends up well above the minimum. Remember that the parts are out of phase: requiring each one below \(\Delta v_o\) already leaves some margin. Ceramic capacitance under bias An X5R or X7R ceramic loses a good part of its capacitance with the applied DC voltage. Use the manufacturer's curve at the output voltage, not the rated value.

title: Sizing L and C
heading: 3. Check the capacitor's RMS current
summary: How to choose the buck's inductor and capacitor from the ripple specifications, the capacitor's RMS current and the load step.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: The buck's output capacitor carries the triangular part of \(i_L\): \[I_{C,\mathrm{rms}} = \frac{\Delta i_L}{\sqrt{12}}\] Compare it with the capacitor's rated RMS current (or that of the bank), at the working temperature. The input capacitor carries a pulsed current, much larger: RMS current in the buck's capacitors.

title: Sizing L and C
heading: 4. Check the load step and the resonance
summary: How to choose the buck's inductor and capacitor from the ripple specifications, the capacitor's RMS current and the load step.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: Ripple rarely sets C. In a load step \(\Delta I\), the capacitor supplies the difference until the loop reacts, and the loop reacts in about \(1/(2\pi f_c)\). A first-order estimate of the dip is \[\Delta V \approx \frac{\Delta I}{2\pi\,f_c\,C}\] where \(f_c\) is the crossover frequency of the loop gain. Finally, compute the resonance \(f_0 = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})\) of the plant: it must lie well below \(f_s/2\) and preferably below \(f_c\), because the compensator will have to cancel its pole pair.

title: Sizing L and C
heading: 5. The calculation in Python
summary: How to choose the buck's inductor and capacitor from the ripple specifications, the capacitor's RMS current and the load step.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: from math import pi, sqrt vin, vo, fs = 24.0, 9.0, 200e3 # input, output, switching io_max = 2.0 # maximum load current (A) r = 0.4 # desired ripple: 40 % of io_max dv_max = 0.010 * vo # output ripple: 1 % of Vo D = vo / vin L = vo * (1 - D) / (r * io_max * fs) # from the current ripple di = vo * (1 - D) / (L * fs) C = di / (8 * fs * dv_max) # capacitive part only esr_max = dv_max / di # ESR part only print(f"D = {D:.3f}, L >= {L*1e6:.1f} uH, C >= {C*1e6:.1f} uF, ESR <= {esr_max*1e3:.0f} mOhm") # check against the lab's buck L, C, esr = 22e-6, 47e-6, 5e-3 di = vo * (1 - D) / (L * fs) print(f"di = {di:.3f} A ({di/io_max:.0%} of {io_max} A), peak {io_max + di/2:.2f} A") print(f"dv_C = {di/(8*fs*C)*1e3:.1f} mV, dv_ESR = {esr*di*1e3:.1f} mV, " f"I_C,rms = {di/sqrt(12):.2f} A, f0 = {1/(2*pi*sqrt(L*C))/1e3:.2f} kHz") The output: D = 0.375, L >= 35.2 uH, C >= 5.6 uF, ESR <= 112 mOhm di = 1.278 A (64% of 2.0 A), peak 2.64 A dv_C = 17.0 mV, dv_ESR = 6.4 mV, I_C,rms = 0.37 A, f0 = 4.95 kHz

title: Sizing L and C
heading: In the converters
summary: How to choose the buck's inductor and capacitor from the ripple specifications, the capacitor's RMS current and the load step.
prereqs: Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: The lab's buck uses L = 22 µH and C = 47 µF, with an ESR of 5 mΩ. L: at 2 A, the 1.28 A ripple is 64 % of the current, well above the procedure's 40 %, and at 1 A it exceeds 100 %. The small inductor lets the current change fast, at \((V_{in} - V_o)/L = 0.68\) A/µs, which helps in the load step; the price is a 2.64 A peak and more core loss (The buck inductor: core losses, Dowell and saturation). C: for 1 % ripple, 5.6 µF would do with the 35 µH inductor (8.9 µF with the 22 µH one). The 47 µF come from the load step: with \(f_c\) = 8 kHz and a 1 A step, \(\Delta V \approx 1/(2\pi\cdot 8\,\text{kHz}\cdot 47\,\text{µF}) = 0.42\) V. In the simulation with the 2p2z, the output drops to 8.59 V, a 0.41 V dip. RMS current: 0.37 A, comfortable for any 47 µF ceramic. Resonance: \(1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})\) = 4.95 kHz (4.96 kHz in the model with losses, at 9 Ω), below the 8 kHz crossover and far below \(f_s/2\) = 100 kHz. Load step from 1 to 2 A with the 2p2z: the dip depends on \(C\) and on \(f_c\) Exercise Redo the buck's L for 40 % ripple at 2 A, given that the input may rise to 28 V. Exercise If the 1 A step's specification were a dip of at most 0.25 V, with the same 8 kHz crossover, what C would be needed? In the author's handbook Modelagem de Conversores Chaveados: do modelo à bancada virtual (in Portuguese): the same filter sizing, together with the control loop.

title: Gvg, Zout and the three ports of the plant
heading: Gvg, Zout and the three ports of the plant
summary: Besides the duty, the output responds to the input, through Gvg, and to the load current, through Zout; in the buck, Gvg(0) = D, in the boost, 1/D' and with no right-half-plane zero, and QSPICE confirms both models.
prereqs: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: The plant has three inputs. The controller moves the duty; the input voltage and the load current are disturbances, which the loop only corrects. At the output, the three add up: \[\hat v_o = G_{vd}\,\hat d + G_{vg}\,\hat v_{in} - Z_{out}\,\hat i_o\] \(G_{vd}\) is in The buck's transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\) and Transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\) of the boost. \(G_{vg}\) is the transfer function from the input to the output, with the duty fixed. \(Z_{out}\) is the output impedance: the drop at the output per ampere drawn by an extra current source in parallel with the load.

title: Gvg, Zout and the three ports of the plant
heading: In the buck
summary: Besides the duty, the output responds to the input, through Gvg, and to the load current, through Zout; in the buck, Gvg(0) = D, in the boost, 1/D' and with no right-half-plane zero, and QSPICE confirms both models.
prereqs: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: In the averaged model, the switch node is the source \(V_{in}\hat d + D\,\hat v_{in}\) that drives the LC filter (The averaged switch model). Both inputs go through the same filter, so \[G_{vg}(s) = \frac{D}{V_{in}}\,G_{vd}(s), \qquad G_{vg}(0) = D\,\frac{R}{R + R_s} = \frac{V_o}{V_{in}}\] with the same poles and the same ESR zero. At DC, \(G_{vg}\) is the ratio \(V_o/V_{in}\) itself, with the steady-state duty, which already covers the loss in \(R_s\). For \(Z_{out}\), set the other two inputs to zero: with \(\hat d = \hat v_{in} = 0\), the switch node carries no perturbation, a ground for the signal, and the output sees the inductor in parallel with the capacitor and the load: \[Z_{out}(s) = (R_s + sL) \parallel Z_o, \qquad Z_o = R \parallel \left(R_{\mathrm{ESR}} + \frac{1}{sC}\right)\] At low frequency, \(Z_{out} \approx R_s\); near \(f_0\), the LC parallel resonates, and the peak is close to \(Q\sqrt{L/C}\); above, the capacitor is left.

title: Gvg, Zout and the three ports of the plant
heading: In the boost
summary: Besides the duty, the output responds to the input, through Gvg, and to the load current, through Zout; in the buck, Gvg(0) = D, in the boost, 1/D' and with no right-half-plane zero, and QSPICE confirms both models.
prereqs: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: The averaged equations of Transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\) of the boost, with \(\hat d = 0\) and the input perturbation, become \[(sL + R_l)\,\hat i_L = \hat v_{in} - D'\hat v, \qquad \hat v = Z_o\,(D'\,\hat i_L - \hat i_o)\] and, eliminating \(\hat i_L\), \[G_{vg}(s) = \frac{D'\,Z_o}{sL + R_l + D'^2 Z_o}, \qquad Z_{out}(s) = Z_o \parallel \frac{sL + R_l}{D'^2}\] At \(s = 0\), without losses, \(G_{vg}(0) = 1/D'\): the derivative of \(V = V_{in}/D'\) with \(D\) fixed. The denominator is that of \(G_{vd}\): the same poles, at \(f_0 \approx D'/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})\). The numerator lacks the term \(-I(sL + R_l)\), which comes from \(\hat d\) multiplying the inductor current (The right-half-plane zero). That is why \(G_{vg}\) has no right-half-plane zero: only the ESR's. A rise of the input raises the inductor current, and the output starts rising at once, without the initial swing the wrong way that the duty causes. In the output impedance, the inductor appears again as \(L/D'^2\), and the losses as \(R_l/D'^2\): at low frequency, \(Z_{out} \approx R_l/D'^2\), sixteen times \(R_l\) with \(D' \approx 0.25\).

title: Gvg, Zout and the three ports of the plant
heading: The measurement in QSPICE
summary: Besides the duty, the output responds to the input, through Gvg, and to the load current, through Zout; in the buck, Gvg(0) = D, in the boost, 1/D' and with no right-half-plane zero, and QSPICE confirms both models.
prereqs: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: The ports are measured like the loop gain in Measuring the loop gain by injecting into the duty. The simulated firmware block (scenario.cpp) adds a small sine to the input voltage, for \(G_{vg}\), or to the load's conductance, for \(Z_{out}\): a current \(V\,g\,\sin\omega t\) in parallel with the load. Every period, at the ADC sample's instant, it records the output, not quantized, and the input or the injected current. The ratio of the Fourier components of the two, with a Hann window over 40 cycles after 30 ms, is the transfer function. In open loop, the duty is held at the model's steady-state value (in the buck, the lossless \(V_o/V_{in}\)), plus the dead time's share: G1 turns on only a dead time after the start of the period. In closed loop, the 2p2z runs, and the model is the open-loop one divided by \(1 + T\) (equation Sensitivity), at the run's mean duty. Every point was measured again at half the amplitude, and none changed by more than 0.17 dB and 0.9°: the response is linear. The model compared is the switched circuit sampled at the ADC's instant, like that of Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost, with the duty fixed. At low frequency it is the averaged model above. In the buck the two coincide; in the boost, the averaged one lags the phase of \(G_{vg}\) by 2° to 7° from 1 to 5 kHz, and QSPICE sides with the sampled one. title: Gvg, Zout and the three ports of the plant
heading: In the converters
summary: Besides the duty, the output responds to the input, through Gvg, and to the load current, through Zout; in the buck, Gvg(0) = D, in the boost, 1/D' and with no right-half-plane zero, and QSPICE confirms both models.
prereqs: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: Buck. From 24 V to 9 V, with 22 µH, 47 µF and 9 Ω: \(G_{vg}(0) = 9/24 = 0.375\) (−8.5 dB), with a peak of 2.66 (8.5 dB) at the resonance, at 4.93 kHz. \(Z_{out}\) goes from 39.8 mΩ at DC to 4.8 Ω at the resonance, close to \(Q\sqrt{L/C} = 7.1 \times 0.68\) Ω. In closed loop, the 2p2z brings \(G_{vg}\) to −13.6 dB at 1 kHz and \(Z_{out}\) from 149 to 80 mΩ. Near the crossover, \(|1 + T| < 1\): above 7 kHz, the closed-loop \(Z_{out}\) exceeds the open-loop one, with a peak of 0.98 Ω at 7.5 kHz. Boost. From 12 V to 48 V, at 1 A: \(G_{vg}(0) = 4.00\) (12.0 dB), with a peak of 16.8 (24.5 dB) at 680 Hz. \(Z_{out}\) is 0.37 Ω at DC, at the ADC's instant, and 9.7 Ω at the resonance. The loop crosses low, at 1.5 kHz, and corrects little: in closed loop, \(G_{vg}\) still reaches 1.87 (5.4 dB) at 1 kHz, and \(Z_{out}\) 1.8 Ω at 1.3 kHz. On the input step from 12 to 10 V, the output sags to 45.3 V (Synchronous boost 12 V → 48 V: worked example). Input feedforward attacks \(G_{vg}\) by another path, without waiting for the loop (Input feedforward). title: Input feedforward
heading: Input feedforward
summary: The firmware measures the input and recomputes the duty before the output moves: in the buck, d = u·Vin0/vin normalizes the loop gain and nearly cancels Gvg; in the buck-boost, the law V/(vin + V) corrects only the slow part.
prereqs: Gvg, Zout and the three ports of the plant
Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: A change of the input reaches the output through \(G_{vg}\) (\(G_{vg}\), \(Z_{out}\) and the three ports of the plant). The loop reacts only after the output moves, and in closed loop what is left is \(G_{vg}/(1 + T)\) (equation Sensitivity). But the firmware already measures the input, for the protections. With that measurement, it can correct the duty before the error shows up: this is input feedforward.

title: Input feedforward
heading: The idea
summary: The firmware measures the input and recomputes the duty before the output moves: in the buck, d = u·Vin0/vin normalizes the loop gain and nearly cancels Gvg; in the buck-boost, the law V/(vin + V) corrects only the slow part.
prereqs: Gvg, Zout and the three ports of the plant
Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: Add to the duty a term proportional to the input, \(\hat d = \hat d_{\mathrm{loop}} + F\,\hat v_{in}\). The output becomes \[\hat v_o = (G_{vg} + F\,G_{vd})\,\hat v_{in} + G_{vd}\,\hat d_{\mathrm{loop}}\] and the input drops out with \(F = -G_{vg}/G_{vd}\). In the buck, \(G_{vg} = (D/V_{in})\,G_{vd}\): both go through the same LC filter, and \(F = -D/V_{in}\) is just a gain. Its large-signal form is the steady state's, \(d = V_o/v_{in}\). With a compensator designed at the nominal input \(V_{in0}\), whose output is the duty \(u\) it asks for there, the law becomes \[d = u\,\frac{V_{in0}}{v_{in}}\] The product \(d\,v_{in}\), the switch node's average, is \(u\,V_{in0}\) for any input. It is the same as making the PWM carrier proportional to the input. The law has a second effect. The buck's plant is proportional to \(V_{in}\) (equation \(G_{vd}(s)\) of the buck), and the law divides the duty by \(v_{in}\): the loop gain no longer depends on the input.

title: Input feedforward
heading: What is left: the delay
summary: The firmware measures the input and recomputes the duty before the output moves: in the buck, d = u·Vin0/vin normalizes the loop gain and nearly cancels Gvg; in the buck-boost, the law V/(vin + V) corrects only the slow part.
prereqs: Gvg, Zout and the three ports of the plant
Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: The input is sampled together with the output, and the new duty takes effect only in the next period, at the falling edge: the same delay \(t_d = (1 + D)\,T_s\) as the loop's (Computation and PWM delay). The switch node is left with \(D\,\hat v_{in}(t) - D\,\hat v_{in}(t - t_d)\), and \[G_{vg,\mathrm{ff}}(s) = G_{vg}(s)\,\bigl(1 - e^{-s t_d}\bigr), \qquad \bigl|1 - e^{-j2\pi f t_d}\bigr| = 2\sin(\pi f t_d) \approx 2\pi f\,t_d\] The rejection is perfect at DC and gets 20 dB per decade worse. It holds while \(2\pi f t_d \ll 1\), that is, for slow changes such as a ramp of the source.

title: Input feedforward
heading: In the buck-boost
summary: The firmware measures the input and recomputes the duty before the output moves: in the buck, d = u·Vin0/vin normalizes the loop gain and nearly cancels Gvg; in the buck-boost, the law V/(vin + V) corrects only the slow part.
prereqs: Gvg, Zout and the three ports of the plant
Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: In the four-switch buck-boost, \(V/V_{in} = D/D'\), and the steady-state law is \(d = V/(v_{in} + V)\). With the compensator designed at \(V_{in0}\), \(V\) is the output that \(u\) would give there, \(V_{in0}\,u/(1 - u)\): \[d = \frac{V_{in0}\,u}{V_{in0}\,u + v_{in}\,(1 - u)}\] Here \(F = -G_{vg}/G_{vd}\) is not a gain: \(G_{vd}\) has the right-half-plane zero, and \(G_{vg}\) does not (\(G_{vg}\), \(Z_{out}\) and the three ports of the plant). The steady-state law cancels the input only at DC. Nor does it normalize the loop gain: the DC gain, about \((V_{in} + V)^2/V_{in}\), hardly changes from 9 to 15 V, but the gain above the resonance changes with the input (Robust design across the operating range). In the boost, \(F = -G_{vg}/G_{vd}\) would have a pole at the right-half-plane zero of \(G_{vd}\): an unstable filter. Only the steady-state law is left, \(d = 1 - v_{in}/V\).

title: Input feedforward
heading: In the firmware
summary: The firmware measures the input and recomputes the duty before the output moves: in the buck, d = u·Vin0/vin normalizes the loop gain and nearly cancels Gvg; in the buck-boost, the law V/(vin + V) corrects only the slow part.
prereqs: Gvg, Zout and the three ports of the plant
Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: #define DMIN 0.0f #define DMAX 0.9f /* buck; 0.8f in the buck-boost */ #define VIN_FLOOR 1.0f /* an invalid reading below this */ /* Buck: u is the duty the 2p2z asks for, designed at vin0. With d = u·vin0/vin, the product d·vin stays at u·vin0. */ float ff_buck(float u, float vin, float vin0) { return u * (vin0 / vin); } float ff_buck_inv(float d, float vin, float vin0) { return d * (vin / vin0); } /* Buck-boost: d = Vo/(vin + Vo), with Vo = vin0·u/(1 − u), the output u would give at vin0; top and bottom multiplied by (1 − u). */ float ff_buckboost(float u, float vin, float vin0) { float vc = vin0 * u; return vc / (vc + vin * (1.0f - u)); } float ff_buckboost_inv(float d, float vin, float vin0) { float vd = vin * d; return vd / (vd + vin0 * (1.0f - d)); } float duty_clamp(float d) { if (!(d >= DMIN)) d = DMIN; if (d > DMAX) d = DMAX; return d; } typedef struct { float a2, b0, b1, b2, u1, u2, e1, e2, vin0; } ctrl_t; /* One step of the buck's interrupt: vout and vin sampled on the same trigger, e = vref − vout. Returns the d that goes to the CCR. */ float isr_buck(ctrl_t *c, float e, float vin) { if (!(vin >= VIN_FLOOR)) return DMIN; /* NaN or no input: no pulse */ float u = c->u1 + c->a2 * (c->u1 - c->u2) + c->b0 * e + c->b1 * c->e1 + c->b2 * c->e2; float d = duty_clamp(ff_buck(u, vin, c->vin0)); u = ff_buck_inv(d, vin, c->vin0); /* the u of the applied d: no windup */ c->u2 = c->u1; c->u1 = u; c->e2 = c->e1; c->e1 = e; return d; } The 2p2z's states keep \(u\), not \(d\): the law stays outside the compensator, and the velocity form of The 2p2z in C, in the interrupt does not change. The limit applies to \(d\), and \(u\) is recomputed from the limited \(d\). With the input below \(V_{in0}\), \(d\) reaches DMAX while \(u\) is still DMAX\(\cdot v_{in}/V_{in0}\); a \(u\) limited only at DMAX would keep growing, and the loop would be slow to leave the limit (Anti-windup and duty saturation). In the buck-boost, the step is the same, with ff_buckboost and ff_buckboost_inv. Both samples come from the same ADC trigger, so the input and the output are from the same instant. An invalid input reading turns the pulse off instead of dividing by zero.

title: Input feedforward
heading: In the converters
summary: The firmware measures the input and recomputes the duty before the output moves: in the buck, d = u·Vin0/vin normalizes the loop gain and nearly cancels Gvg; in the buck-boost, the law V/(vin + V) corrects only the slow part.
prereqs: Gvg, Zout and the three ports of the plant
Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: The laws were simulated in the QSPICE firmware block, with the input read at the sample's instant, not quantized. These runs are not among the oscilloscope's scenarios. Buck. From 24 V to 9 V, the input drops to 18 V at 20 V/ms. Without feedforward, with the 2p2z, the output sags to 7.89 V and comes back within ±2 % only after 1.06 ms. With it, the output stays between 8.94 and 9.09 V; with the PID, between 8.95 and 9.07 V. The recorded scenario below comes from another version of the block and sags to 7.87 V. Buck with the 2p2z, input from 24 to 18 V, without feedforward: the output sags 1.1 V. The loop gain stays where it was designed. Without the law, the crossover falls from 8.0 kHz at 24 V to 7.2 kHz at 18 V; with it, it stays at 8.0 kHz at both. The phase margin goes from 41.3° at 24 V to 39.5° at 18 V: the loop is the same, and at 8 kHz the delay \((1 + D)\,T_s\) takes 21.6° with \(D = 0.5\), against 19.8° with 0.375. Without the law, the margin at 18 V would be 42.1°, because the crossover moves down. The law scales the whole \(u\), which already carries the dead time and the losses: in steady state, \(u = 0.388\), against \(V_o/V_{in} = 0.375\). The switch node sees \(u\) less the dead time, and the law corrects too much, by about \((DT/T_s)/D\), 2.7 %. At low frequency, the law alone leaves \(-(DT/T_s)\,\hat v_{in}\) at the switch node, and the rest is left to the loop. With this term, the model gives −39.3 dB at 1 kHz and −33.3 dB at 2 kHz; QSPICE measures −39.2 and −33.3 dB, against −13.6 and −12.6 dB without the law. Buck-boost. From 9 to 15 V at 10 V/ms, with 12 V and 2 A. Without the law, with the 2p2z, the output rises to 13.68 V. With it, the output stays between 11.82 and 12.23 V. Buck-boost with the 2p2z, input from 9 to 15 V, without feedforward: the output rises to 13.68 V. At 12 V and 1 kHz, the closed loop lets −5.9 dB through without the law and −22.8 dB with it, in QSPICE; the model gives −5.8 and −22.9 dB. The loop gain hardly changes. With \(V_{in0}\) = 12 V and 2 A, the law lowers it by 0.22 dB at 9 V, and the crossover goes from 2.44 to 2.41 kHz; at 15 V, from 3.53 to 3.51 kHz. In the step run, \(V_{in0}\) = 9 V, and at 15 V the law raises the gain by 0.11 dB. Exercise In the buck, the 2p2z asks for \(u = 0.375\), designed at 24 V. What duty does the law apply with the input at 18 V? And the product \(d\,v_{in}\)? title: The right-half-plane zero
heading: The right-half-plane zero
summary: In the boost and the buck-boost, raising the duty first pulls the output down; this right-half-plane zero, at R·D'²/L, limits the crossover frequency.
prereqs: Right-half-plane zero: the effect on the loop
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: In the buck, raising the duty raises the voltage applied to the LC filter, and the output rises. In the boost, the same action has two opposite effects. The main switch stays on longer, the inductor builds up more current, and the output will rise; but while the switch is on, the inductor is cut off from the output. At first, the inductor current is still the same, but it reaches the output during a smaller fraction of the period, \(D' - \hat d\): the output receives \(I\hat d\) less and falls. Only later, when the inductor current grows, does it rise. A response that starts in the opposite direction to where it ends is the signature of a right-half-plane zero.

title: The right-half-plane zero
heading: The boost's plant
summary: In the boost and the buck-boost, raising the duty first pulls the output down; this right-half-plane zero, at R·D'²/L, limits the crossover frequency.
prereqs: Right-half-plane zero: the effect on the loop
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: From the averaged model in continuous conduction, with the losses \(R_l\) of the inductor and one switch, the capacitor with its ESR and the load \(R\), the transfer function from the duty to the output is \[G_{vd}(s) = G_0\,\frac{\left(1 - \dfrac{s}{2\pi f_{\mathrm{RHP}}}\right)\left(1 + \dfrac{s}{\omega_{\mathrm{ESR}}}\right)}{1 + \dfrac{s}{Q\,\omega_0} + \dfrac{s^2}{\omega_0^2}}, \qquad G_0 = \frac{R\,(D'V - I\,R_l)}{R_l + D'^2 R}, \qquad \omega_0 = \sqrt{\frac{R_l + D'^2 R}{L\,C\,(R + R_{\mathrm{ESR}})}}, \qquad Q = \frac{\sqrt{L\,C\,(R + R_{\mathrm{ESR}})(R_l + D'^2 R)}}{L + C\left[R_l\,(R + R_{\mathrm{ESR}}) + D'^2 R\,R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\right]}\] The numerator vanishes when \(D'V = I(sL + R_l)\). With \(I = V/(RD')\), the inductor current, the zero sits at \(s = +2\pi f_{\mathrm{RHP}}\): \[f_{\mathrm{RHP}} = \frac{R\,D'^2 - R_l}{2\pi L} \approx \frac{R\,D'^2}{2\pi L}\] Right-half-plane zero A zero at \(s = +2\pi f_{\mathrm{RHP}}\), with \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}} > 0\). Like an ordinary zero, it makes the magnitude rise by 20 dB per decade above \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}\); but, like a pole, it lags the phase by up to \(90^\circ\). In a step, it makes the response start in the wrong direction.

title: The right-half-plane zero
heading: Why it limits the crossover
summary: In the boost and the buck-boost, raising the duty first pulls the output down; this right-half-plane zero, at R·D'²/L, limits the crossover frequency.
prereqs: Right-half-plane zero: the effect on the loop
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: An ordinary zero in the left half-plane helps the compensator: it gives gain and phase lead. The right-half-plane zero gives the gain and takes the phase, like a delay. The compensator cannot cancel it, because that would take a pole in the right half-plane, an unstable controller (Pole-zero cancellation and its risks). What is left is to cross well below it: at \(f_c\), it already takes \(\arctan(f_c/f_{\mathrm{RHP}})\), and this lag adds to the firmware's (Computation and PWM delay). Rules of thumb say to cross between a third and a fifth of the zero in the worst case: at \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}/3\), it takes 18.4° of phase; at \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}/5\), 11.3°. Neither is a limit: what decides is the margin at the worst corner, adding up the zero, the delay and the lead the compensator still gives there (Robust design across the operating range). With the \(3f_0\) floor of the type III recipe, the ceiling makes a window, which can be empty (The boost's crossover window). And the worst case is the maximum load with the minimum input: smaller \(R\) and \(D'\), lower zero. Unlike the buck's, the boost's plant changes a lot with the operating point, and the margins must be checked at all of them (Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins). Loop gain of the boost with the 2p2z: the crossover stays at 1.5 kHz, well below the right-half-plane zero More gain does not make the boost faster With a slow boost, the temptation is to raise the gain. Near the zero, the phase falls fast (26.6° at \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}/2\), 45° at it), the margin disappears, and the loop starts ringing on the load step, precisely where the current is highest and the zero lowest. In the Root locus (qualitative reading), the extra gain carries a branch toward the right half-plane.

title: The right-half-plane zero
heading: In the converters
summary: In the boost and the buck-boost, raising the duty first pulls the output down; this right-half-plane zero, at R·D'²/L, limits the crossover frequency.
prereqs: Right-half-plane zero: the effect on the loop
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: The boost goes from 12 V to 48 V, with 100 kHz, 33 µH and 100 µF. With the site's model, which includes the losses: Load \(D\) \(I_L\) \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}\) 1 A (48 Ω) 0.752 4.03 A 14.1 kHz 2 A (24 Ω) 0.754 8.14 A 6.9 kHz Doubling the load halves the zero: \(R\) halves, and \(D'\) hardly changes. The LC resonance, seen through \(D'\), is at \(D'/(2\pi\sqrt{LC}) = 690\) Hz. The boost's four designs show the limit: 2p2z: crosses at 1.5 kHz, \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}/4.6\) at 2 A (at 10 V and 2 A, at 1.27 kHz, \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}/3.7\)), between the 1/5 and 1/3 rules; MF of 45° at 1 A and 41° at 2 A. Aggressive: crosses at 4 kHz, with a MF of 19° at 1 A, but only 0.5° at 2 A, when the zero comes down to 6.9 kHz. Unstable: crosses near 8 kHz, above the zero at 2 A; MF of −20° at 1 A. Boost, load step from 1 to 2 A with the 2p2z Boost, the same step with the aggressive design: the ringing lasts milliseconds Boost with the unstable design: the loop oscillates before any step In the four-switch buck-boost, in buck-boost mode, the structure is the same: the duty switches the voltage \(V_d = V_{in} + V\) across the inductor, instead of \(V\), and the numerator becomes \(D'(V_{in} + V) - I(sL + R_l)\). From 12 to 12 V, the zero is at 21 kHz at 2 A and 13.7 kHz at 3 A, and the 2p2z crosses at 3 kHz. At 9 V and 3 A, the scenarios' worst corner, the zero comes down to 8.5 kHz, and the crossover must be chosen for that point (Robust design across the operating range). The full examples are in Synchronous boost 12 V → 48 V: worked example and Four-switch buck-boost 8–16 V → 12 V: worked example. The ADC does not read the average In the boost, the ADC samples just before the main switch turns on, when the capacitor carries the whole inductor current, and the sample includes an ESR term (Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost). The site's model accounts for it, and with it the zero of the plant the ADC sees is higher (about 8.4 kHz at 2 A). For design, the zero of the average, lower, is the conservative reference. title: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
heading: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
summary: The boost's plant in CCM has a DC gain of about V/D', a pair of poles that comes down with D' and a right-half-plane zero; the ADC also sees an ESR term and the firmware's delay.
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: In the buck, the duty only multiplies the input, and the plant is \(V_{in}\) times the LC filter (The buck's transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\)). In the boost, the averaged cell multiplies the state variables: the switch node is \(d'\,v\) and the current delivered to the output is \(d'\,i_L\), with \(d' = 1 - d\) (The averaged switch model). The plant inherits three differences from this: the gain depends on \(D'\), so does the resonance, and a right-half-plane zero appears.

title: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
heading: From the averaged model to the plant
summary: The boost's plant in CCM has a DC gain of about V/D', a pair of poles that comes down with D' and a right-half-plane zero; the ADC also sees an ESR term and the firmware's delay.
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: With \(R_l\) the inductor's resistance plus one switch's, the averaged equations of the inductor and the capacitor, perturbed and linearized with \(\hat v_{in} = 0\), become \[(sL + R_l)\,\hat i_L = V\hat d - D'\hat v, \qquad \hat v = Z_o\,(D'\,\hat i_L - I\,\hat d)\] with \(Z_o = R \parallel (R_{ESR} + 1/sC)\) and \(I\) the average inductor current. The first term of each equation comes from \(d\) multiplying \(v\) and \(i_L\): these are the \(V\hat d\) and \(I\hat d\) terms the buck does not have. Eliminating \(\hat i_L\): \[G_{vd}(s) = G_0\,\frac{\left(1 - \dfrac{s}{2\pi f_{\mathrm{RHP}}}\right)\left(1 + \dfrac{s}{\omega_{\mathrm{ESR}}}\right)}{1 + \dfrac{s}{Q\,\omega_0} + \dfrac{s^2}{\omega_0^2}}, \qquad G_0 = \frac{R\,(D'V - I\,R_l)}{R_l + D'^2 R}, \qquad \omega_0 = \sqrt{\frac{R_l + D'^2 R}{L\,C\,(R + R_{\mathrm{ESR}})}}, \qquad Q = \frac{\sqrt{L\,C\,(R + R_{\mathrm{ESR}})(R_l + D'^2 R)}}{L + C\left[R_l\,(R + R_{\mathrm{ESR}}) + D'^2 R\,R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\right]}\]

title: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
heading: DC gain, resonance and Q
summary: The boost's plant in CCM has a DC gain of about V/D', a pair of poles that comes down with D' and a right-half-plane zero; the ADC also sees an ESR term and the firmware's delay.
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: At \(s = 0\), \(Z_o = R\) and, without losses, \(G_{vd}(0) = V/D'\). At 48 V with \(D' \approx 0.25\), that gives about 190 V per unit of duty: eight times the gain of the lab's buck. The denominator is the LC filter with the inductor seen through \(D'^2\), as an inductance \(L/D'^2\). The pair of poles lies at \[f_0 \approx \frac{D'}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}\] and comes down when the input falls and \(D'\) shrinks. The exact \(f_0\) and \(Q\) are in (1): the damping comes from the load, \(1/(RC)\), from the losses in the inductor, \(R_l/L\), and from the ESR, which the \(Q\) formula includes. Effective inductance In the boost's averaged model, the inductor \(L\) seen from the output is \(L/D'^2\). With \(D' = 0.25\), the lab's 33 µH behave as 530 µH in the output filter: the resonance is four times lower than \(1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})\).

title: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
heading: The right-half-plane zero
summary: The boost's plant in CCM has a DC gain of about V/D', a pair of poles that comes down with D' and a right-half-plane zero; the ADC also sees an ESR term and the firmware's delay.
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: The numerator vanishes at \(s = +2\pi f_{\mathrm{RHP}}\): \[f_{\mathrm{RHP}} = \frac{R\,D'^2 - R_l}{2\pi L} \approx \frac{R\,D'^2}{2\pi L}\] Above \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}\), the magnitude stops falling at 40 dB per decade and the phase keeps falling: the zero adds up to \(-90^\circ\) to the \(-180^\circ\) of the pair of poles. The physics and the limit it puts on the crossover are in The right-half-plane zero. The ESR zero, in the left half-plane, lies at \(1/(2\pi R_{ESR} C)\) = 159 kHz, above the switching frequency, as in the buck (The ESR zero).

title: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
heading: The plant the ADC sees
summary: The boost's plant in CCM has a DC gain of about V/D', a pair of poles that comes down with D' and a right-half-plane zero; the ADC also sees an ESR term and the firmware's delay.
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: The controller does not see \(G_{vd}\). The sample is taken just before G1 turns on and also reads an ESR drop the average does not have (Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost), and the computed duty only applies in the next period (Computation and PWM delay). To first order, the plant the controller sees is \(G_{vd}\) plus the ESR term, times a delay of \((1 + D/2)\,T_s\). The site uses the sampled-data model of the switched circuit, with no fitted factor, and it was checked in QSPICE by adding a small sine to the duty in the firmware (Measuring the loop gain by injecting into the duty): at 1 and 2 A (48 and 24 Ω), it stayed within 0.2 dB and 1.4° of the switched circuit from 300 Hz to 7 kHz, across the resonance. The boost's plant at 1 A: the resonance peak near 690 Hz and, above it, the phase that keeps falling through the right-half-plane zero and the digital loop's delay.

title: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
heading: In the converters
summary: The boost's plant in CCM has a DC gain of about V/D', a pair of poles that comes down with D' and a right-half-plane zero; the ADC also sees an ESR term and the firmware's delay.
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: In the lab's boost, from 12 V to 48 V, with L = 33 µH, C = 100 µF, \(R_l\) = 15 mΩ + 10 mΩ = 25 mΩ and an ESR of 10 mΩ, the full averaged model gives: Point \(D\) \(f_0\) \(Q\) DC gain \(f_{\mathrm{RHP}}\) 12 V, 1 A (48 Ω) 0.752 690 Hz 4.4 190 (45.6 dB) 14.1 kHz 12 V, 2 A (24 Ω) 0.754 687 Hz 3.6 189 (45.5 dB) 6.9 kHz 10 V, 2 A (24 Ω) 0.797 570 Hz 3.0 225 (47.0 dB) 4.7 kHz Doubling the load hardly changes the gain and the resonance, but halves the zero. Lowering the input from 12 to 10 V moves everything: \(D'\) falls from 0.246 to 0.203, the resonance comes down 17 %, the gain rises 1.5 dB and the zero comes down by another third. At 1.5 kHz, the 2p2z's crossover, the plant is 34.1 dB at 1 A: that is what the compensator must attenuate there. The full example is in Synchronous boost 12 V → 48 V: worked example. In the four-switch buck-boost, the plant has the same form, with \(V_{in} + V\) in place of \(V\). title: The buck's transfer function Gvd(s)
heading: The buck's transfer function Gvd(s)
summary: The buck's plant in CCM, from duty ratio to output voltage, is a second-order system with the LC resonance, a load-dependent Q and the ESR zero.
prereqs: Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: The linearized averaged model replaced the switch pair by a source \(\hat v_{sw} = V_{in}\,\hat d\) that drives the output filter. The plant is therefore \(V_{in}\) times that filter's transfer function.

title: The buck's transfer function Gvd(s)
heading: From the circuit to the transfer function
summary: The buck's plant in CCM, from duty ratio to output voltage, is a second-order system with the LC resonance, a load-dependent Q and the ESR zero.
prereqs: Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: The inductor and the series resistance form \(Z_L = sL + R_s\), with \(R_s = R_L + R_{on}\). The capacitor with its ESR, in parallel with the load, forms \(Z_o = (R_{\mathrm{ESR}} + 1/sC)\parallel R\). The plant is a voltage divider: \[G_{vd}(s) = V_{in}\,\frac{Z_o}{Z_L + Z_o} = V_{in}\,\frac{R\,(1 + s R_{\mathrm{ESR}} C)}{\alpha_2 s^2 + \alpha_1 s + \alpha_0}\] with \[\alpha_2 = LC\,(R + R_{\mathrm{ESR}}), \qquad \alpha_0 = R + R_s\] \[\alpha_1 = L + C\left[R R_{\mathrm{ESR}} + R_s(R + R_{\mathrm{ESR}})\right]\] Arranged in the canonical second-order form: \[G_{vd}(s) = \frac{\hat v_o(s)}{\hat d(s)} = G_0\;\frac{1 + s/\omega_{\mathrm{ESR}}}{1 + \dfrac{s}{Q\,\omega_0} + \dfrac{s^2}{\omega_0^2}}, \qquad G_0 = V_{in}\,\frac{R}{R + R_s}\] It has three ingredients: the DC gain \(V_{in}R/(R + R_s) \approx V_{in}\), the LC's complex pole pair and the ESR zero.

title: The buck's transfer function Gvd(s)
heading: The resonance and the Q
summary: The buck's plant in CCM, from duty ratio to output voltage, is a second-order system with the LC resonance, a load-dependent Q and the ESR zero.
prereqs: Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: The pole pair sits at the filter's resonance, with a quality factor set by the damping: \[\omega_0 = \sqrt{\frac{R + R_s}{L\,C\,(R + R_{\mathrm{ESR}})}}, \qquad f_0 = \frac{\omega_0}{2\pi}, \qquad Q = \frac{\sqrt{L\,C\,(R + R_{\mathrm{ESR}})(R + R_s)}}{L + C\left[R\,(R_s + R_{\mathrm{ESR}}) + R_s R_{\mathrm{ESR}}\right]}\] Quality factor \(Q\) measures how lightly damped the pole pair is. On the Bode plot, the magnitude rises \(20\log_{10} Q\) dB (the rule, good from \(Q \approx 3.3\) on) above the DC gain at \(f_0\), and the phase drops 180° over a band about \(f_0/Q\) wide. In time, the response rings at \(f_0\) and decays with a time constant \(Q/(\pi f_0)\). Two sources of damping add like conductances: the load in parallel with the capacitor, with \(Q_R = R/Z_0\), and the series resistances, with \(Q_s = Z_0/(R_s + R_{\mathrm{ESR}})\). Hence the dependence on the load: heavy load (small R) damps more, and \(Q\) falls; light load (large R) damps less, and \(Q\) rises up to the limit \(Z_0/(R_s + R_{\mathrm{ESR}})\), set by the losses alone; the DC gain and \(f_0\) barely change with the load. Above \(f_0\), the magnitude falls 40 dB per decade and the phase stays near −180°. This is the phase the compensator must lift, with zeros near the resonance, for there to be phase margin at crossover (see Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins and The 2p2z compensator). The buck's plant: resonant peak near 5 kHz and a 40 dB per decade roll-off; the phase includes the digital loop's (1+D)Tₛ delay. The peak depends on the load Design the compensator at the lightest load the converter will see. That is where the resonant peak is highest, and where the loop gain may cross 0 dB again with little phase.

title: The buck's transfer function Gvd(s)
heading: The ESR zero
summary: The buck's plant in CCM, from duty ratio to output voltage, is a second-order system with the LC resonance, a load-dependent Q and the ESR zero.
prereqs: Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: The factor \(1 + s/\omega_{\mathrm{ESR}}\) in the numerator is the ESR zero: above \(f_{\mathrm{ESR}}\), the capacitor becomes a resistor, and the magnitude stops falling at 40 dB per decade. With ceramic capacitors, this zero lies above the switching frequency and does not help the control.

title: The buck's transfer function Gvd(s)
heading: The plant the digital loop sees
summary: The buck's plant in CCM, from duty ratio to output voltage, is a second-order system with the LC resonance, a load-dependent Q and the ESR zero.
prereqs: Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: \(G_{vd}(s)\) is an analog plant. In the microcontroller, the ADC samples the output and the new duty only applies in the next period. The plant seen by the controller is \(G_{vd}(s)\,e^{-s(1+D)T_s}\); the delay does not change the magnitude, but it removes phase, more so at higher frequencies (see Computation and PWM delay). The widget above already shows this delay in the phase.

title: The buck's transfer function Gvd(s)
heading: In the converters
summary: The buck's plant in CCM, from duty ratio to output voltage, is a second-order system with the LC resonance, a load-dependent Q and the ESR zero.
prereqs: Second-order pole pair and quality factor Q
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: In the lab's buck, with L = 22 µH, C = 47 µF, \(R_s\) = 40 mΩ and ESR = 5 mΩ: Load \(f_0\) \(Q\) Peak above the DC gain 4.5 Ω (2 A) 4.97 kHz 4.6 13.3 dB 9 Ω (1 A) 4.96 kHz 7.1 17.0 dB 18 Ω (0.5 A) 4.95 kHz 9.6 19.7 dB 90 Ω (0.1 A) 4.95 kHz 13.6 22.7 dB The DC gain is \(24\cdot 9/9.04 = 23.9\), or 27.6 dB, at any of these loads. At 8 kHz, the 2p2z's crossover, the plant is 23.4 dB: the compensator must attenuate 23.4 dB there. The ESR zero is at 677 kHz, out of reach. In the boost, the gain and the resonance change with the operating point, because the inductor is seen through \(D'\), and the right-half-plane zero appears (Transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\) of the boost).
