title: Thermal design and part selection for the buck
heading: Thermal design and part selection for the buck
summary: From loss to junction temperature through the thermal resistance, with the iteration that couples RDS(on) and temperature, and the criteria for choosing the MOSFETs, inductor and capacitors of the lab's buck.
prereqs: RMS current in the buck's capacitors
text: The budget of Losses of the synchronous buck says how many watts each part dissipates. What remains is the temperature that takes it to, and whether each part handles the voltage, the current and the heat with margin. This procedure does both for the lab's buck.

title: Thermal design and part selection for the buck
heading: 1. From loss to temperature
summary: From loss to junction temperature through the thermal resistance, with the iteration that couples RDS(on) and temperature, and the criteria for choosing the MOSFETs, inductor and capacitors of the lab's buck.
prereqs: RMS current in the buck's capacitors
text: Heat leaves the MOSFET's junction for the ambient through a chain of thermal resistances in series: junction to case (\(R_{\theta JC}\)), case to heat sink (\(R_{\theta CS}\)) and heat sink to air (\(R_{\theta SA}\)). In steady state, \[T_j = T_a + P\,(R_{\theta JC} + R_{\theta CS} + R_{\theta SA})\] In a surface-mount MOSFET, the "heat sink" is the board's copper. The data sheet then gives the total resistance, \(R_{\theta JA}\), measured on a standard board. The number only holds for that copper area. Junction temperature The junction temperature \(T_j\) is the temperature of the silicon. It is what the data sheet limits, not the case temperature. The thermal resistance \(R_\theta\), in °C/W, is the temperature rise per watt dissipated.

title: Thermal design and part selection for the buck
heading: 2. The iteration
summary: From loss to junction temperature through the thermal resistance, with the iteration that couples RDS(on) and temperature, and the criteria for choosing the MOSFETs, inductor and capacitors of the lab's buck.
prereqs: RMS current in the buck's capacitors
text: \(R_{DS(on)}\) grows with temperature. More loss heats the junction, which raises \(R_{DS(on)}\), which raises the loss. The author's thermal model solves the coupling by fixed-point iteration: start with \(T_j = T_a\); compute \(R_{DS(on)}(T_j)\) and the losses; compute the new \(T_j\) from the thermal network; repeat until the change falls below 0.001 °C. For silicon MOSFETs, the model's law is \(R_{DS(on)}(T_j) = R_{DS(on)}(25\,°\text{C})\,[(T_j + 273)/298]^2\). When the data sheet has the curve of \(R_{DS(on)}\) against temperature, the exponent comes from it. If the loss is too large for the network, the iteration diverges: that is thermal runaway. The inverse calculation says how much can be dissipated: \(P_{\max} = (T_{j,\max} - T_a)/R_{\theta JA}\).

title: Thermal design and part selection for the buck
heading: 3. The selection criteria
summary: From loss to junction temperature through the thermal resistance, with the iteration that couples RDS(on) and temperature, and the criteria for choosing the MOSFETs, inductor and capacitors of the lab's buck.
prereqs: RMS current in the buck's capacitors
text: MOSFET. a rated \(V_{DS}\) of at least \(1.2\,V_{in,\max}\), plus the switching voltage spike (Dead time and switching in the synchronous buck); a continuous current above the peak \(I_o + \Delta i_L/2\), at the working temperature; the lowest \(R_{DS(on)}\,Q_g\) product: a low \(R_{DS(on)}\) cuts conduction, but a high \(Q_g\) raises the gate loss and slows switching. Inductor. The inductance at the peak current with at least 20 % margin to saturation, or to the permeability drop in a powder core, and the temperature rise from copper and core losses (The buck inductor: core losses, Dowell and saturation). Capacitors. A rated voltage of at least 1.2 times the maximum voltage across the capacitor, a rated RMS current above the one computed in RMS current in the buck's capacitors, and the capacitance checked at the working voltage, because a ceramic loses capacitance under DC bias.

title: Thermal design and part selection for the buck
heading: In the converters
summary: From loss to junction temperature through the thermal resistance, with the iteration that couples RDS(on) and temperature, and the criteria for choosing the MOSFETs, inductor and capacitors of the lab's buck.
prereqs: RMS current in the buck's capacitors
text: The lab's buck goes from 24 V to 9 V, up to 2 A. The ambient is assumed to be 40 °C. MOSFETs. Both switches are Alpha & Omega's AO4262E (data sheet Rev.1.0, January 2016), 60 V, in an SO-8 package, with an \(R_{\theta JA}\) of 59 °C/W typical and 75 °C/W maximum in steady state, on 1 in² of 2 oz copper (\(R_{\theta JL}\) of 16 °C/W typical and 24 °C/W maximum to the lead), and \(T_{j,\max}\) = 150 °C. The typical \(R_{DS(on)}\) goes from 5.2 mΩ at 25 °C to 8.3 mΩ at 125 °C, which gives an exponent of 1.62 in the law above; with 2, it would be 9.3 mΩ. The iteration, with 75 °C/W and the 2 A losses of Losses of the synchronous buck, converges in 3 steps: Switch Loss \(T_j\) \(R_{DS(on)}(T_j)\) High side (conduction, switching, \(C_{oss}\), \(Q_{rr}\)) 199.4 mW 55.0 °C 6.1 mΩ Low side (conduction, dead time) 37.3 mW 42.8 °C 5.7 mΩ The high side runs hotter: it is the one that turns on with loss, charges the node and recovers the low side's diode. With the upper bound of \(Q_{rr}\), it would reach 464.6 mW and 74.9 °C. In QSPICE, with the VDMOS model, which has less \(C_{oss}\), the high side dissipates 112.1 mW and the low side 33.1 mW through the drain: the order holds. The internal gate resistance (1.3 Ω, about 30 % of the gate energy with 3 Ω outside) adds 17.3 and 13.4 mW, 1 to 2 °C more; the budget counts that part in the gate, not in the switches. With \(T_j\) at 125 °C, each switch could dissipate \((125 - 40)/75 = 1.13\) W: the buck needs no heat sink, only copper on the board. Voltage. \(1.2\cdot 24 = 28.8\) V. The author's transient model, with the default parasitic inductance of 17 nH in the power loop and \(t_f\) = 7 ns, predicts \(di/dt\) = 0.38 A/ns at turn-off at 2.64 A and a spike of 6.4 V above the input: 30.4 V. A 40 V switch would keep less than 10 V of headroom; the 60 V one keeps almost 30 V. The peak current, 2.64 A, is far below the 13 A continuous the data sheet gives at 70 °C. Why not the catalog's MOSFET. The lowest voltage in the author's component catalog is Infineon's IMLT40R011M2H, a 400 V SiC part with 11.3 mΩ, a \(Q_g\) of 85 nC and 18 V on the gate (data sheet values, extracted in the catalog). The \(R_{DS(on)}\) is twice as large, and the \(R_{DS(on)}\,Q_g\) product is 960 mΩ·nC, against \(5.2\cdot 30 = 156\) mΩ·nC. The gate alone would take \(2\cdot 85\,\text{nC}\cdot 18\,\text{V}\cdot 200\,\text{kHz} = 0.61\) W, more than all the buck's estimated losses with the AO4262E, 0.58 W. Inductor. The powdered-iron core of The buck inductor: core losses, Dowell and saturation (T33/19/11, 45 turns) shows no permeability drop up to the 2.64 A peak. It loses 220.9 mW, copper and core together. The catalog's surface thermal model gives 51.7 °C/W for this toroid: a rise of 11.4 °C. Capacitors. At the input, a rated voltage of 35 V or more, an RMS current of 1.02 A (worst case, 18 V and 2 A) and at least 13.9 µF effective for 1 % ripple at 18 V (0.18 V). At the 9 V output, 16 V is enough, with 0.37 A RMS. Exercise If the ambient reaches 85 °C, what will the high-side switch's temperature be at 2 A, without redoing the iteration? Exercise Up to what total loss per switch does the 1 in² board keep \(T_j\) below 100 °C with a 60 °C ambient?

title: Buck power stage
heading: Buck power stage
summary: From the sized filter to the parts: the RMS current in the capacitors, the losses, the dead time, the inductor and the thermal design of the lab's buck.
text: This trail takes the buck from the sized filter to the chosen parts: how much current the capacitors carry, where power is lost, what happens in the dead time, how much the inductor loses in core and copper and when it saturates, and what temperature all that leads to. It starts from the first two steps of the From the analog buck to the digital loop trail, Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM and Sizing L and C. The worked example is the Synchronous buck 24 V → 9 V: worked example. RMS current in the buck's capacitors: the input capacitor carries a pulsed current, much larger than the output capacitor's, which sees only the inductor's ripple. Losses of the synchronous buck: the conduction, switching, dead-time, gate, inductor and capacitor losses, added up into a budget and an efficiency curve. Dead time and switching in the synchronous buck: the switch node during the dead time, why the high-side switch switches with loss and the low-side one does not, and how to choose the dead time. The buck inductor: core losses, Dowell and saturation: the ripple becomes core loss, copper loses more at high frequency, and saturation is checked against the peak current. Thermal design and part selection for the buck: from loss to junction temperature, and the criteria for choosing the MOSFETs, inductor and capacitors.

title: The 2p2z in C, in the interrupt
heading: The 2p2z in C, in the interrupt
summary: The buck's interrupt in C: read the ADC, compute the error, run the 2p2z difference equation, saturate and write the CCR, with protection against NaN, fault, double-buffered coefficients and ADC overrun.
text: This note brings together what the trail built. The 2p2z compensator becomes the difference equation below, and the saturation from Anti-windup and duty saturation sits at the output: \[u[k] = -a_1\,u[k-1] - a_2\,u[k-2] + b_0\,e[k] + b_1\,e[k-1] + b_2\,e[k-2]\]

title: The 2p2z in C, in the interrupt
heading: The sequence in each period
summary: The buck's interrupt in C: read the ADC, compute the error, run the 2p2z difference equation, saturate and write the CCR, with protection against NaN, fault, double-buffered coefficients and ADC overrun.
text: The timer triggers the ADC at the sampling instant. In the boost and buck-boost scenarios (scenario.cpp), SAMPLE_PHASE = 0; the buck's frames come from the older version of the qspice-wine live demo, which sampled at the period start, with one period of delay. On a board, see ADC trigger and sample instant. The ADC finishes the conversion and calls the interrupt. The interrupt computes the error and the new duty cycle, and saturates it. It writes the CCR. With preload on, the new value takes effect only at the next update event. Step 4 is what scenario.cpp imitates with s->duty = s->pending: the duty cycle computed from the sample of period \(k\) governs period \(k+1\). With trailing-edge PWM, the total delay is \((1 + D)\,T_s\), the subject of Computation and PWM delay. Preload off Do not turn preload off to gain a period. Without it (the PREEN bit of HRTIM_TIMxCR on the H7; OC1PE on a general-purpose timer), the new compare value takes effect at once. If it is written below the counter's current value, the effect depends on the timer: on a general-purpose timer in PWM mode, the output drops at once and the pulse comes out shortened; on the HRTIM, which turns on and off through events, the turn-off comparison has already passed, and the switch stays on until the next period's turn-off, a pulse that is too long, the dangerous case. The double pulse is the opposite case: a larger value written after the falling edge. Keep preload on and accept the one-period delay that the design in Computation and PWM delay already includes.

title: The 2p2z in C, in the interrupt
heading: Float variant (with FPU, as on the H7's Cortex-M7)
summary: The buck's interrupt in C: read the ADC, compute the error, run the 2p2z difference equation, saturate and write the CCR, with protection against NaN, fault, double-buffered coefficients and ADC overrun.
text: This is the logic of scenario.cpp, with the error in volts and the standard buck design coefficients. The routine adds what a board firmware needs and the simulator does not have: NaN: a comparison with NaN is false. The test !(x >= lo) catches NaN, and the routine never writes NaN to the states or to the CCR. Enable and fault: ctrl_enable and ctrl_fault. When disabled or faulted, the routine switches the outputs off through HRTIM_ODISR and clears the states. On the synchronous buck, that also switches the low-side switch off: it shuts the converter down, it does not ask for DMIN. Only the main loop re-enables, in this order: it clears ctrl_fault, sets ctrl_enable = 1 and writes HRTIM1->sCommonRegs.OENR = HRTIM_OENR_TA1OEN | HRTIM_OENR_TA2OEN. The states restart from DMIN, and the start follows Soft-start and pre-biasing; it is also worth clearing the ADC's OVR (ADC_ISR_OVR) at that moment. Double-buffered coefficients: the main loop writes to the inactive set and only then switches the index. The interrupt reads the index once. ADC overrun: with OVRMOD = 1, set at initialization, a lost conversion raises the OVR flag (Interrupt deadline and budget). With it, or with a full-scale code, the sample is not valid, and the routine holds the CCR and counts. Minimum compare: the HRTIM needs CMP1xR ≥ 3 (PWM timer and shadow registers). So DMIN = CMP_MIN/PWM_N = 0.0015, and the state saturates where the CCR does. The simulated scenarios use DMIN = 0; the board code uses the 3-count floor. #include <stdint.h> #include "stm32h7xx.h" /* or your MCU's CMSIS header */ #define PWM_N 2000u /* 400 MHz / 200 kHz: HRTIM counts per period */ #define ADC_MAX 4095u /* 12 bits: codes 0 to 4095 */ #define LSB (20.0f / 4095.0f) /* volts per code, range 0 to 20 V */ #define CMP_MIN 3u /* RM0433, table 308: CMP1xR >= 3 */ #define DMIN ((float)CMP_MIN / PWM_N) /* 0.0015: the state saturates where the CCR does */ #define DMAX 0.9f #define E_MAX 20.0f /* largest accepted error, in volts */ typedef struct { float b0, b1, b2, a2; } coef_t; /* a1 = -(1 + a2) */ static coef_t coef_buf[2] = { /* two sets: the active and the inactive one */ { 0.23114164f, -0.43413087f, 0.20384645f, 0.15183580f }, { 0.23114164f, -0.43413087f, 0.20384645f, 0.15183580f }, }; static volatile uint8_t coef_sel; /* index of the active set; the ISR and coef_update read it */ static volatile float vref = 9.0f; /* written by the main loop */ static volatile uint8_t ctrl_enable; /* 1: closed loop */ static volatile uint8_t ctrl_fault; /* 1: latched fault; only the main loop clears it */ static volatile uint32_t overrun_count, hold_count; /* diagnostics */ static float u1 = 0.375f, u2 = 0.375f, e1, e2; /* states; start at the steady-state duty */ /* Once, before the loop and with ADSTART = 0: enable the FPU (CP10 and CP11 with full access) and set OVRMOD = 1, so OVR rises at the first missed read. */ void ctrl_init(void) { SCB->CPACR |= (3UL << (10 * 2)) | (3UL << (11 * 2)); __DSB(); __ISB(); ADC1->CFGR |= ADC_CFGR_OVRMOD; } /* Main loop: write the inactive set, then switch the index. */ void coef_update(const coef_t *n) { uint8_t next = coef_sel ^ 1u; coef_buf[next] = *n; /* the ISR does not read this set */ __DMB(); /* the copy finishes before the switch */ coef_sel = next; } /* Disabled or faulted: outputs off and states cleared, no NaN. */ static void ctrl_safe(void) { u1 = u2 = DMIN; e1 = e2 = 0.0f; HRTIM1->sCommonRegs.ODISR = HRTIM_ODISR_TA1ODIS | HRTIM_ODISR_TA2ODIS; /* idle state */ } void ADC_IRQHandler(void) /* ADC1 and ADC2 share the vector (ADC_IRQn = 18) */ { const coef_t *c = &coef_buf[coef_sel]; /* read the index once per interrupt */ uint32_t raw = ADC1->DR; /* reading DR clears the end-of-conversion flag */ GPIOB->BSRR = GPIO_BSRR_BS0; /* measurement pin: high */ if (!ctrl_enable || ctrl_fault) { ctrl_safe(); } else if (ADC1->ISR & ADC_ISR_OVR) { /* overrun: the conversion was lost */ ADC1->ISR = ADC_ISR_OVR; /* clear the flag (write 1) */ overrun_count++; hold_count++; /* hold the previous duty cycle */ } else if (raw >= ADC_MAX) { /* full scale: input out of range */ hold_count++; } else { float e = vref - (float)raw * LSB; if (!(e >= -E_MAX && e <= E_MAX)) { /* NaN lands here: the comparison is false */ ctrl_fault = 1; ctrl_safe(); } else { float u = u1 + c->a2 * (u1 - u2) + c->b0 * e + c->b1 * e1 + c->b2 * e2; if (!(u >= DMIN)) u = DMIN; /* NaN and values below DMIN */ if (u > DMAX) u = DMAX; /* saturation: anti-windup */ u2 = u1; u1 = u; e2 = e1; e1 = e; uint32_t cmp = (uint32_t)(u * PWM_N + 0.5f); HRTIM1->sTimerxRegs[0].CMP1xR = cmp < CMP_MIN ? CMP_MIN : cmp; /* preload: takes effect in the next period */ } } GPIOB->BSRR = GPIO_BSRR_BR0; /* measurement pin: low */ } u1 + a2*(u1 - u2) is the same as -a1*u1 - a2*u2, because \(a_1 = -(1 + a_2)\): it is the velocity form, which computes the increment \(\Delta u\) and adds it to u1. Written this way, it does without \(a_1 = -1.15\), which does not fit Q15 in the fixed-point variant, and the integrator sits exactly at \(z = 1\). The reference can also gain a ramp, adding a limited step to vref at each interrupt: that is the subject of Soft-start and pre-biasing.

title: The 2p2z compensator
heading: The 2p2z compensator
summary: The two-pole, two-zero compensator, a digital relative of the type III, designed by its poles and zeros, and its relation with the PID; with the buck's default design.
prereqs: Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins
PI, phase lead and the type III
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
From the boost to the digital loop
text: The buck's plant, above the LC resonance, has a phase near \(-180^\circ\) (The buck's transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\)), and the digital delay takes even more (Computation and PWM delay). An integrator alone would add \(-90^\circ\) and leave no margin; the compensator needs one, to drive the steady-state error to zero, and two zeros, to give phase back at the crossover. That is the 2p2z: two poles, two zeros. \[C(z) = K\,\frac{(1 - z_1 z^{-1})(1 - z_2 z^{-1})}{(1 - z^{-1})(1 - p\,z^{-1})}, \qquad z_i = e^{-2\pi f_{zi} T_s}, \quad p = e^{-2\pi f_p T_s}\] The poles are the integrator, at \(z = 1\), and a real high-frequency pole \(p\): it is the digital version of the analog type III, which has two high-frequency poles.

title: The 2p2z compensator
heading: Design by poles and zeros
summary: The two-pole, two-zero compensator, a digital relative of the type III, designed by its poles and zeros, and its relation with the PID; with the buck's default design.
prereqs: Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins
PI, phase lead and the type III
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
From the boost to the digital loop
text: Each root has a job on the Bode plot of the loop gain: Integrator (\(z = 1\)): infinite gain at DC, zero steady-state error at the sample. Two zeros near or below the LC resonance: each gives back up to \(+90^\circ\). Below it, they already give almost all their lead when the plant's phase plunges. Lower zeros give more phase at \(f_c\), but they lower the gain between the integrator and the resonance, and the loop corrects errors in that band slowly. On the pair, the zeros would cancel it, with the risks of Pole-zero cancellation and its risks. High-frequency pole: limits the gain above the crossover, where there is only ripple and quantization noise (ADC quantization). If the ESR zero falls inside the band, the pole cancels it (The ESR zero). Gain \(K\): chosen last, so that \(|T| = 1\) at \(f_c\). The zeros and the pole go to \(z\) by matching (The bilinear (Tustin) transform and prewarping): \(z_i = e^{-2\pi f_{zi}T_s}\) and \(p = e^{-2\pi f_p T_s}\), with the frequencies in hertz. Expanding the numerator and the denominator, \[C(z) = \frac{b_0 + b_1 z^{-1} + b_2 z^{-2}}{1 + a_1 z^{-1} + a_2 z^{-2}},\] the firmware receives \(b_0 = K\), \(b_1 = -K(z_1+z_2)\), \(b_2 = K z_1 z_2\), \(a_1 = -(1+p)\) and \(a_2 = p\), and runs the difference equation \[u[k] = -a_1\,u[k-1] - a_2\,u[k-2] + b_0\,e[k] + b_1\,e[k-1] + b_2\,e[k-2]\] The figure draws the same equation in direct form I: each \(z^{-1}\) delays by one period, the gains \(b_0\), \(b_1\), \(b_2\), \(-a_1\) and \(-a_2\) multiply the samples, and \(\Sigma\) adds the five terms into \(u[k]\). Direct form I of the 2p2z: the input e[k] goes through two one-period delays (z⁻¹) and the output u[k] through two more; the gains b₀, b₁ and b₂ on the input and −a₁ and −a₂ on the output all feed the adder Σ, which gives u[k] This is the velocity form: the integrator lives in the two past \(u\) terms. Since the integrator at \(z = 1\) forces \(1 + a_1 + a_2 = 0\), the equation can be rewritten as \(u[k] - u[k-1] = a_2\,(u[k-1] - u[k-2]) + b_0\,e[k] + b_1\,e[k-1] + b_2\,e[k-2]\): the firmware computes the increment \(\Delta u\) and adds it to the previous duty. The code is in The 2p2z in C, in the interrupt; what happens when \(u\) saturates, in Anti-windup and duty saturation. Poles and zeros of the buck's 2p2z in the z-plane: integrator at z = 1, double zeros near 1, pole near the origin

title: The 2p2z compensator
heading: The relation with the PID
summary: The two-pole, two-zero compensator, a digital relative of the type III, designed by its poles and zeros, and its relation with the PID; with the buck's default design.
prereqs: Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins
PI, phase lead and the type III
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
From the boost to the digital loop
text: In \(s\), the prototype is \[C(s) = K_I\,\frac{(1 + s/\omega_{z1})(1 + s/\omega_{z2})}{s\,(1 + s/\omega_p)} = K_P + \frac{K_I}{s} + \frac{K_D\,s}{1 + s\,T_F},\] a PID with a filter on the derivative. Matching coefficients, with \(\tau_{zi} = 1/(2\pi f_{zi})\) and \(\tau_f = 1/(2\pi f_p)\): \(K_P = K_I(\tau_{z1} + \tau_{z2} - \tau_f)\), \(K_D = K_I(\tau_{z1} - \tau_f)(\tau_{z2} - \tau_f)\) and \(T_F = \tau_f\). It is the same linear controller; what changes is the way of designing (gains or roots) and the implementation: the PID keeps the integrator in a state of its own, which can be clamped, and the velocity form does not. Design by roots, implement as you like Zeros, pole and crossover lead straight to the Bode plot; the PID gains come out afterwards, from the formulas above.

title: The 2p2z compensator
heading: In the converters
summary: The two-pole, two-zero compensator, a digital relative of the type III, designed by its poles and zeros, and its relation with the PID; with the buck's default design.
prereqs: Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins
PI, phase lead and the type III
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
From the boost to the digital loop
text: The buck has its LC resonance at \(1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC}) = 4.95\) kHz, with 22 µH and 47 µF, and its ESR zero at 677 kHz, far above \(f_s/2\). The site's default 2p2z has double zeros at 2 kHz (0.4 of the resonance), a pole at 60 kHz and a crossover at 8 kHz: \(z_1 = z_2 = e^{-2\pi \times 2000 \times 5\ \text{µs}} = 0.9391\) and \(p = 0.1518\); \(K = b_0 = 0.2311\), \(b_1 = -0.4341\), \(b_2 = 0.2038\), \(a_1 = -1.1518\) and \(a_2 = 0.1518\); MF of 41° and MG of 13.9 dB at 1 A; 46° and 14.1 dB at 2 A; the equivalent PID has \(K_P = 0.0316\), \(K_I = 202\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\), \(K_D = 1.20\ \text{µs}\) and \(T_F = 2.65\ \text{µs}\) (per volt of error). At 8 kHz, the compensator's \(+52^\circ\) take the plant with the delay from \(-191^\circ\) to \(-139^\circ\): hence the 41°. In QSPICE, the load step from 1 to 2 A pulls the output down to 8.59 V; it overshoots to 9.14 V and stays within 50 mV of its final value from about 130 µs on. Reference step from 9 to 5 V with the buck's 2p2z In the boost, the recipe is the same: zeros at 500 Hz, below the 690 Hz resonance, a pole at 30 kHz and a crossover at 1.5 kHz, low because of the The right-half-plane zero. The coefficients are in the Synchronous boost 12 V → 48 V: worked example worked example. Exercise A colleague moves the buck's 2p2z to a direct-form firmware, which stores \(a_1\) and \(a_2\), and types \(a_1 = -1.1581\), instead of \(-1.1518\); the other values are right. (The site's firmware, in velocity form, stores only \(a_2 = p\) and is safe from this typo.) Without simulating, predict what happens to the integrator. Where does the pole it had at \(z = 1\) go? At what voltage does the output settle? Exercise Find the equivalent integral gain \(K_I\), by matching the 2p2z to \(K_I/s\) at low frequency. Exercise A 1 V error appears at once. How much does the duty change in the first period? title: ADC quantization
heading: ADC quantization
summary: The ADC reads the output in steps of q = VFS/(2N - 1): the step, the quantization noise and the reference written as a code decide what the loop can regulate.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: The digital controller doesn't see the output voltage: it sees an integer. In Sampling and the zero-order hold (ZOH), sampling made time discrete; here the A/D converter (ADC) makes the amplitude discrete, and everything the firmware knows about \(v_o\) goes through that rounding.

title: ADC quantization
heading: The step (LSB)
summary: The ADC reads the output in steps of q = VFS/(2N - 1): the step, the quantization noise and the reference written as a code decide what the loop can regulate.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: ADC step The step, or LSB (least significant bit), is the smallest change of the measured voltage that changes the code read. An \(N\)-bit ADC has \(2^N\) codes, from 0 to \(2^N - 1\): code 0 reads 0 V, the largest reads full scale, and between them the measuring range is divided into \(2^N - 1\) steps. The ADC pin only accepts 0 to \(V_{\mathrm{ADC}}\) (3.3 V in the reference configuration, within the 1.62 to 3.6 V \(V_{DDA}\) range of DS12110, table 174, silicon revision V; the input spans 0 to \(V_{REF+}\)). To measure a larger output, a resistive divider of ratio \(k_{\mathrm{div}}\) scales the voltage down, and the range referred to the output becomes \(V_{FS} = V_{\mathrm{ADC}}/k_{\mathrm{div}}\): \[q = \frac{V_{FS}}{2^{N} - 1} = \frac{V_{\mathrm{ADC}}}{(2^{N} - 1)\,k_{\mathrm{div}}}\] In the buck, \(V_{FS}\) = 20 V and \(N\) = 12 bits. The divider has \(k_{\mathrm{div}} = 3.3/20 = 0.165\), and \[q = \frac{20\ \text{V}}{4095} = 4.884\ \text{mV na saída} \qquad \left(\frac{3.3\ \text{V}}{4095} = 0.806\ \text{mV no pino}\right).\] Code \(k\) reads \(k \cdot 20/4095\) V: the largest, 4095, reads exactly 20 V. That is the scale of the buck's simulation firmware (buck_pid.cpp; scenario.cpp does the same in the boost and buck-boost, with each one's full scale), which rounds the sample to the nearest code. The range needs headroom above the nominal output, to see the overshoot and to protect against overvoltage, but every volt of headroom makes \(q\) coarser.

title: ADC quantization
heading: Quantization noise
summary: The ADC reads the output in steps of q = VFS/(2N - 1): the step, the quantization noise and the reference written as a code decide what the loop can regulate.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: When the voltage moves many steps between samples, the rounding error \(\varepsilon = v - q\cdot\text{código}\) spreads evenly between \(-q/2\) and \(q/2\). The variance of that uniform distribution is \[\sigma_\varepsilon^2 = \frac{1}{q}\int_{-q/2}^{q/2} \varepsilon^2\, d\varepsilon = \frac{q^2}{12}, \qquad \sigma_\varepsilon = \frac{q}{\sqrt{12}} \approx 0.29\,q .\] In the buck, \(\sigma_\varepsilon = 4.884/\sqrt{12} = 1.41\) mV rms. This white-noise model holds during transients. In steady state it fails: the output barely changes, and the quantization error becomes a fixed error, or a repeating pattern. The same goes for a measurement: a signal that moves the sample by less than one code is lost in the rounding, which is why the sine that measures the loop gain grows with frequency (Measuring the loop gain by injecting into the duty).

title: ADC quantization
heading: What the zero-error band means
summary: The ADC reads the output in steps of q = VFS/(2N - 1): the step, the quantization noise and the reference written as a code decide what the loop can regulate.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: For the controller, every output within a band of width \(q\) around the reference's code gives the same error. Inside that band the integrator has nothing to correct. The regulation's resolution is, at best, \(\pm q/2 = \pm 2.44\) mV at 9 V, or 0.03 %. That is resolution, not accuracy. The divider's tolerance and the ADC's gain and offset errors are worth tens of steps (see exercise 1). And the loop only settles inside the band if the duty has a level that puts the output there: if the digital PWM is coarser than the ADC, the output jumps over the band and the loop oscillates, which is the subject of DPWM resolution and limit cycles.

title: ADC quantization
heading: The reference as a code
summary: The ADC reads the output in steps of q = VFS/(2N - 1): the step, the quantization noise and the reference written as a code decide what the loop can regulate.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: The firmware compares numbers. If the reference is written in volts, it almost never coincides with a code. With \(q = 20/4095\) V, 9 V is \(9 \cdot 4095/20 = 1842.75\) codes: the ADC only reads 1842 (8.9963 V) or 1843 (9.0012 V), and the error is \(+3.66\) mV or \(-1.22\) mV, never zero. The integrator goes up and down between the two codes forever. Write the reference as a code Compute the reference once, as an integer: REF_CODE = 1843, the code nearest to 1842.75. The loop then regulates at \(1843 \cdot 20/4095 = 9.0012\) V, 1.2 mV above 9 V, a quarter of a step. The error becomes REF_CODE - adc, an integer that can be exactly zero. The sample's instant in the period, the edge's ringing and the sampling window with a resistive divider are in ADC trigger and sample instant, an optional detour that builds on the boost of Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost.

title: ADC quantization
heading: In the converters
summary: The ADC reads the output in steps of q = VFS/(2N - 1): the step, the quantization noise and the reference written as a code decide what the loop can regulate.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: Buck. \(q\) = 4.884 mV, against an output ripple of 17.6 mV peak to peak at 1 A (Duty ratio and ripple of the buck in CCM): 3.6 steps. In the QSPICE scenarios, the output's average sits about 5 mV above the samples, because the sample falls near the ripple's valley (Sampling and the zero-order hold (ZOH)). That is one ADC step of error, the same size as the zero-error band. Boost. The range is 60 V for a 48 V output, with 12 bits: \(q = 60/4095 = 14.65\) mV. The zero-error band, \(\pm q/2 = \pm 7.33\) mV, is 0.015 % of the output, a little more than half the buck's fraction. Buck-boost. 20 V and 12 bits, like the buck: \(q\) = 4.884 mV for a 12 V output. Exercise 1 The buck uses a divider with \(k_{\mathrm{div}} = 0.165\). With 1 % resistors, what is the worst error of the divider's ratio, and how much is it at 9 V, in volts and in ADC steps? Exercise 2 At the 5 V reference of the step scenario, which codes does the ADC read near equilibrium, and which errors does the buck's firmware (buck_pid.cpp), which compares volts, compute? And if the reference is written as a code, at which voltage does the loop regulate? Exercise 3 A colleague writes the buck's 9 V reference as REF_CODE = (int)(9.0f * 4095.0f / 20.0f); and regulates with the error REF_CODE - adc. At what voltage does the loop leave the output, and by how much does it miss the 9 V? What is wrong with the line? title: Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost
heading: Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost
summary: In the boost and the buck-boost, the sample taken just before G1 turns on sits above the output's average and reads an ESR term that changes the plant; and the switched response behaves, to first order, like a delay of (1 + D/2)·Tₛ, not (1 + D)·Tₛ.
prereqs: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: The ADC does not read the output's average over a period, which the averaged model describes: it reads the voltage at one instant, and its value there depends on the waveform. In the boost and the buck-boost, the difference is larger and changes with the duty and with the current: it becomes part of the plant.

title: Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost
heading: What the sample reads
summary: In the boost and the buck-boost, the sample taken just before G1 turns on sits above the output's average and reads an ESR term that changes the plant; and the switched response behaves, to first order, like a delay of (1 + D/2)·Tₛ, not (1 + D)·Tₛ.
prereqs: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: This site's firmware triggers the ADC at the start of each period, just before G1 turns on. In the boost, G1 is the main switch: until then, G2 was conducting, and the capacitor received the inductor current minus the load's. Two effects add up: The capacitor ripple. While G1 conducts, only the capacitor feeds the load, and the voltage falls by \(\Delta v_C = I_o D T_s/C\); while G2 conducts, it rises again. The sample catches the end of the rise, the peak: \(\Delta v_C/2\) above the average. The ESR drop. On average, the capacitor receives \(d'\,i_L - i_o = 0\). At the sampling instant, it receives \(i_L - i_o\): the whole inductor current, \(d\,i_L\) more than the average. The sample reads \(R_{ESR}\,d\,i_L\) more, minus the valley of the current ripple. The first effect is nearly constant and only shifts the regulated value: the loop regulates the sample, and the average sits below it. The second changes with \(d\) and with \(i_L\), and its linearization enters the plant: \[\hat v_s = \hat v + R_{ESR}\left(D\,\hat i_L + I\,\hat d\right)\] Plant seen by the ADC The transfer function from the duty to the sample, not to the average output. It is the one that enters the loop gain. In this site's boost and buck-boost, it is, to first order, \(G_{vd}\) plus the ESR term, times a delay of \((1 + D/2)\,T_s\). The \(R_{ESR}\,I\,\hat d\) term does not fall with frequency. Well above the resonance, the \(-I(sL + R_l)\) term leaves the average output at about \(-I\,Z_o\,\hat d\), which includes \(-I\,R_{ESR}\,\hat d\); the sample cancels that part, and the right-half-plane zero moves up. The plant seen by the ADC gains a little phase near the crossover, and a design made with the average stays on the conservative side.

title: Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost
heading: The effective delay
summary: In the boost and the buck-boost, the sample taken just before G1 turns on sits above the output's average and reads an ESR term that changes the plant; and the switched response behaves, to first order, like a delay of (1 + D/2)·Tₛ, not (1 + D)·Tₛ.
prereqs: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: The delay from the sample to the edge it moves is \((1 + D)\,T_s\) in the buck (Computation and PWM delay). In the boost and the buck-boost, the firmware has the same delay, but the switched circuit's response behaves, to first order, like a shorter delay: \[t_d \approx (1 + D/2)\,T_s\] Delaying G1's edge deprives the capacitor of the inductor current at its peak, not of its average. At the edge, the state is half a ripple away from the average (\(i_L\) at its peak, \(v_C\) at its valley), and the effect is that of a perturbation at the middle of G1's pulse, not at the edge. In the buck, the circuits of G1 and G2 have the same dynamics, the jump at the edge does not depend on the state, and \((1 + D)\,T_s\) is exact. The site does not use this approximate delay: in the boost's and buck-boost's Bode plots, the plant is the sampled-data model of the switched circuit, with no fitted factor. In each period, the state (\(i_L\), \(v_C\)) goes through the circuits of G1 and G2; the duty change enters as a jump at the falling edge, computed with the steady state there; the sample reads \(v_C\) plus the drop on the ESR, and the period of computation adds \(z^{-1}\). Against QSPICE (Measuring the loop gain by injecting into the duty), from 300 Hz to 7 kHz, this model stays within 0.2 dB and 1.4° in the boost (12 V at 1, 2 and 4 A) and within 0.2 dB and 0.7° in the buck-boost (12 V and 1 A, 12 V and 2 A, 9 V and 3 A). Almost all of the rest comes from the dead time, which the model leaves out. The \((1 + D/2)\,T_s\) is not a physical delay (the firmware's is still \((1 + D)\,T_s\)) and holds only for this firmware and this sample, at the period start. Another instant changes the offset, the ESR term and the delay (ADC trigger and sample instant). Phase margin of the boost's 2p2z at 1 A as a function of the delay: at 1.5 kHz, each period of delay costs only 5.4°.

title: Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost
heading: In the converters
summary: In the boost and the buck-boost, the sample taken just before G1 turns on sits above the output's average and reads an ESR term that changes the plant; and the switched response behaves, to first order, like a delay of (1 + D/2)·Tₛ, not (1 + D)·Tₛ.
prereqs: Transfer function Gvd(s) of the boost
trails: From the boost to the digital loop
text: Boost. At 1 A, the inductor current has a valley of 2.68 A, and at the sampling instant the ESR adds \(10\,\text{m}\Omega \times (2.68 - 1) = 17\) mV. The capacitor ripple is \(1\,\text{A} \times 0.752 \times 10\,\text{µs}/100\,\text{µF} = 75\) mV, and the peak sits 38 mV above the average. The sample should sit about 54 mV above the average. In QSPICE, with the samples regulated at 48.00 V, the output's average before the step is 47.95 V: Boost with the 2p2z, 1 A: before the step, the average sits about 50 mV below the regulated value. In the plant, the right-half-plane zero goes from 14.1 to 22.1 kHz at 1 A and from 6.9 to 8.4 kHz at 2 A. At the 2p2z's crossover, the ESR term adds 1.6° of margin, at 1 and at 2 A. The equivalent delay is \((1 + 0.752/2) \times 10\,\text{µs} = 13.8\) µs, and it costs 7.4° at 1.5 kHz. With \((1 + D)\,T_s\), it would cost 2.0° more. The sampled-data model, with both effects, gives 46.2° at 1 A and 41.5° at 2 A. In it, removing the ESR from the sample costs about 2°: the count is another one, with the inductor current at the sampling instant, not the term linearized around the average that gives the 1.6° in the averaged model. Buck-boost. At 12 V and 2 A, the capacitor ripple is \(2 \times 0.506 \times 10\,\text{µs}/100\,\text{µF} = 101.2\) mV, and the peak sits 50.6 mV above the average. The inductor current's valley is 2.67 A in the model, and the ESR adds another \(10\,\text{m}\Omega \times (2.67 - 2) = 6.7\) mV. In the scenarios, the average before the reference step is 11.95 V. The ESR term takes the zero from 20.9 to 28.9 kHz and adds 1.2° of margin to the 2p2z. Exercise What is the constant term \(R_{ESR}\,D\,I\) in the boost at 2 A, with \(D = 0.754\) and \(I = 8.14\) A? And the \(\Delta v_C/2\) share? Exercise How much phase separates the firmware's delay, \((1 + D)\,T_s\), from the equivalent delay \((1 + D/2)\,T_s\) at the buck-boost 2p2z's crossover, 3 kHz with \(D = 0.506\)? And at a 10 kHz crossover? In the author's handbook Modelagem de Conversores Chaveados: do modelo à bancada virtual (in Portuguese): the ADC sample instant and the ESR term.

title: ADC trigger and sample instant
heading: ADC trigger and sample instant
summary: From the timer's trigger to the instant the ADC actually samples, and where to put that instant in the period: the offset from the average, the ESR term in the plant and the (1 + D - ) Ts delay.
prereqs: Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost
text: The site's scenarios sample the output at the start of the period, just before G1 turns on. On a board, the sample instant is a choice: the timer triggers the ADC, the ADC takes a while to sample, and the point chosen changes the value read, the plant and the delay.

title: ADC trigger and sample instant
heading: The trigger
summary: From the timer's trigger to the instant the ADC actually samples, and where to put that instant in the period: the offset from the average, the ESR term in the plant and the (1 + D - ) Ts delay.
prereqs: Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost
text: The PWM timer triggers the ADC in hardware. Between the trigger and the result there are three times, on the H7: Trigger latency, \(t_{LATR}\). The trigger reaches the ADC 1.5 to 2.5 ADC cycles later, in asynchronous mode (CKMODE = 00; in the synchronous modes, up to 2.5, 2.5 and 2.25 cycles). Sampling window, \(t_S\). It comes from table 175 of DS12110 (silicon revision V), not from the register minimum: 8.5 cycles, 170 ns at 50 MHz, on a direct channel with a low-impedance source (Centered PWM on the H7: case B). Conversion. At 12 bits, \(8.5 + 0.5 + 12/2 = 15\) cycles: 300 ns with the ADC at 50 MHz, the maximum with BOOST = 11 (table 174). The effective sample instant is the end of the window, \(t_{LATR} + t_S\): 200 to 220 ns after the trigger, at 50 MHz. This delay does not enter \((1+D)\,T_s\) (Computation and PWM delay): in the worst case, it adds 0.63° at 8 kHz. The ADC clock is a design variable, up to 50 MHz. High-impedance divider The internal sampling capacitor, 4 pF (DS12110, table 174), charges through the divider during the window. Table 175 gives the minimum window for each external impedance and, at 12 bits, only goes up to 680 Ω (301 ns on a direct channel). With a 50 kΩ divider, the RC constant is 200 ns, more than the whole 170 ns window: the capacitor doesn't charge fully, and the code comes out low. To settle within half an LSB at 12 bits, the window needs \(\ln 2^{13} \approx 9.0\) RC constants: about 1.8 µs. At 50 MHz, the first SMP that covers it is 387.5 cycles (RM0433): 7.75 µs, more than the buck's 5 µs period. A longer window may not fit: the fix is a buffer. A capacitor at the pin only works with a low-impedance divider; with 50 kΩ, it cannot be large enough without putting the pole in the loop's band (Sensing and anti-aliasing filter).

title: ADC trigger and sample instant
heading: Where to sample
summary: From the timer's trigger to the instant the ADC actually samples, and where to put that instant in the period: the offset from the average, the ESR term in the plant and the (1 + D - ) Ts delay.
prereqs: Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost
text: With synchronous sampling, the ripple becomes a constant offset between the sample and the average, at any instant (Sampling and the zero-order hold (ZOH)). The loop regulates the sample, and the average is shifted. The offset depends on the instant, in the switched circuit's steady state: Sample offset (mV) Edge Middle of G1 Middle of G2 Buck, 9 V and 1 A −6.0 −9.2 +7.8 Boost, 1 A +52.9 −11.4 +37.3 Boost, 2 A +121.7 −21.4 +68.2 Buck-boost, 12 V and 2 A +51.6 −25.6 +31.8 "Peak and valley give the average" holds for \(i_L\), not for \(v_o\): no instant cancels the voltage offset. In the simulation, the edge is clean. On the board, right after the edge the measured voltage rings for tens to hundreds of nanoseconds, from the layout's parasitic inductances and the MOSFETs' capacitances: it is the worst instant. Trigger the ADC from a compare channel of the timer (PWM timer and shadow registers), away from the edges, and check it on the scope. In the boost and the buck-boost, "after the edge" is already the G1 interval. The sample loses the ESR term and jumps by \(R_{ESR}\) times the valley of \(i_L\): 27 mV at 1 A and 68 mV at 2 A, in the boost. In scenario.cpp, G2 turns off at \(t = 0\), and G2's body diode takes the current: a soft edge. G1 turns on 100 ns later against that diode, with reverse recovery: a hard edge. A trigger at the period start samples 200 to 220 ns later, already inside G1. Advance the trigger so the sample falls before G1 turns on, next to G2's turn-off, or sample inside G1 after the ringing and redo the plant.

title: ADC trigger and sample instant
heading: What changes in the plant
summary: From the timer's trigger to the instant the ADC actually samples, and where to put that instant in the period: the offset from the average, the ESR term in the plant and the (1 + D - ) Ts delay.
prereqs: Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost
text: At the edge, the sample reads the ESR term of Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost, and the right-half-plane zero seen by the ADC moves up: from 14.1 to 22.1 kHz at 1 A and from 6.9 to 8.4 kHz at 2 A, in the boost. In the middle of G1, the ESR carries the constant current \(-i_o\): the coefficient of \(\hat i_L\) changes sign, from \(+R_{ESR}\,D\) to \(-R_{ESR}\,D'\), that of \(\hat d\) does not change, and the zero goes back to the average's. Compared with the sample at the edge, the 2p2z's margin loses about 2° to this term, and the shorter delay gives back a part, which the notes do not compute. In exchange, the ADC trigger has to follow the duty, with a second compare channel of the timer, and less time is left for the computation. Designing with the average's zero stays on the conservative side.

title: ADC trigger and sample instant
heading: Delay with
summary: From the timer's trigger to the instant the ADC actually samples, and where to put that instant in the period: the offset from the average, the ESR term in the plant and the (1 + D - ) Ts delay.
prereqs: Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost
text: With preload kept, moving the sample shortens the delay. In scenario.cpp, which simulates the boost and the buck-boost, SAMPLE_PHASE = \(\varphi\) is the fraction of the period from the start to the sample: 0, the default and the value of every published scenario, is the edge; 0.5 is the middle of the period. The delay to the falling edge becomes \[t_d = (1 + D - \varphi)\,T_s,\] provided the computation ends before the update event. The models behind the Bode plots hold only with \(\varphi = 0\); another phase requires redoing the plant and recording the scenarios again. Updating the CCR in the same period, without preload, would also cut the delay, but the write can arrive after the counter has passed the new value, and on the HRTIM the switch stays on until the next period (The 2p2z in C, in the interrupt). Exercise 1 In the buck, the sample is at the period start (\(\varphi = 0\)). Suppose it moves to \(0.5\,T_s\), with preload kept and the computation still before \((k+1)T_s\). In the model, how much does the delay drop with \(D = 0.375\), and how much phase does the 2p2z gain at 8 kHz? Exercise 2 In the boost, a sample just after G1's edge is off by 27 mV at 1 A. A colleague estimates the error at 2 A as 54 mV, in proportion to the load. Does the estimate hold? title: Anti-windup and duty saturation
heading: Anti-windup and duty saturation
summary: When the duty hits its limit, the integrator must not keep accumulating error: the integrator clamp, the 2p2z velocity form and back-calculation.
text: The duty has limits, and the linear 2p2z compensator doesn't know it. This note shows, step by step, how to keep an integrator from accumulating error while the output is saturated.

title: Anti-windup and duty saturation
heading: 1. Saturate the duty
summary: When the duty hits its limit, the integrator must not keep accumulating error: the integrator clamp, the 2p2z velocity form and back-calculation.
text: Every controller ends with a clamp to \([d_{\min}, d_{\max}]\). In the buck, \(d_{\min}\) = 0 and \(d_{\max}\) = 0.9. Besides the physical limit between 0 and 1, a maximum below 1 leaves time for the driver's bootstrap capacitor to recharge and an off interval to measure current. With \(d_{\max} = 0.9\), the buck only delivers 15 V if the input is above about 17 V.

title: Anti-windup and duty saturation
heading: 2. Understand windup
summary: When the duty hits its limit, the integrator must not keep accumulating error: the integrator clamp, the 2p2z velocity form and back-calculation.
text: While the output is saturated, the loop is open: raising the command changes nothing. The integrator keeps adding the error, and that excess must be discharged later, with an error of the opposite sign, that is, with overshoot. The PID of scenario.cpp and buck_pid.cpp uses the simplest solution, the integrator clamp: the state is limited to the same range as the duty. integ += KI * T * err; if (integ < DMIN) integ = DMIN; /* anti-windup by clamping */ if (integ > DMAX) integ = DMAX; d = KP * err + integ + deriv; if (d < DMIN) d = DMIN; if (d > DMAX) d = DMAX; The clamp prevents the worst, but the integrator can still sit at \(d_{\max}\) when the operating point needs much less, and the output overshoots the reference while it unwinds. The "In the converters" section measures that overshoot in the boost.

title: Anti-windup and duty saturation
heading: 3. Or use the velocity form
summary: When the duty hits its limit, the integrator must not keep accumulating error: the integrator clamp, the 2p2z velocity form and back-calculation.
text: The 2p2z in C computes each duty from the two previous ones (equation Difference equation of the 2p2z) and stores the saturated ones. No state grows past the limits: the form is anti-windup by construction. It has one flaw, though. When a jump in the error saturates the duty, the next period's term \(b_1\,e[k-1]\) takes back the whole kick, which was never applied, and the duty plunges the other way.

title: Anti-windup and duty saturation
heading: 4. Back-calculation
summary: When the duty hits its limit, the integrator must not keep accumulating error: the integrator clamp, the 2p2z velocity form and back-calculation.
text: An alternative to the clamp is to feed back to the integrator the difference between the saturated and the computed command, with a time constant \(T_t\): \[x_I[k+1] = x_I[k] + K_I\,T_s\,e[k] + \frac{T_s}{T_t}\,\bigl(d_{\mathrm{sat}}[k] - d[k]\bigr).\] Outside saturation, the new term is zero. In saturation, it pulls the integrator to the value that keeps the command at the limit. A rule of thumb is \(T_t = \sqrt{T_i\,T_d}\), with \(T_i = K_P/K_I\) and \(T_d = K_D/K_P\). /* PID with back-calculation; deriv comes from the derivative term */ float pid_step(float e, float deriv) { float d = KP * e + integ + deriv; float dsat = d < DMIN ? DMIN : d > DMAX ? DMAX : d; integ += KI * T * e + (T / TT) * (dsat - d); /* back-calculation */ return dsat; } The most common trigger of saturation is the jump of the derivative term on a reference step, and computing the derivative on the measurement avoids it: see Derivative kick and derivative on the measurement.

title: Anti-windup and duty saturation
heading: In the converters
summary: When the duty hits its limit, the integrator must not keep accumulating error: the integrator clamp, the 2p2z velocity form and back-calculation.
text: Buck. The duty goes from 0 to 0.9. On the step from 9 to 5 V without slew, it stays at zero for one period, too short for windup: the integrator moves only \(K_I\,T_s\,e = 1309 \times 5\ \mu \times (-4) = -0.026\) (Derivative kick and derivative on the measurement). Boost. QSPICE simulations, with the netlist and firmware of the scenarios. The same PID (\(K_P\) = 0.0114, \(K_I\) = 18.2, \(K_D\) = 1.75 µs/V, \(T_F\) = 7.96 µs) runs with the integrator clamp and as a 2p2z in velocity form, with the same transfer function. Settling, here, means entering the ±2 % band around 48 V for good. Input dropout. At 6 V, not even \(d_{\max}\) = 0.85 is enough: the output stalls at 36.6 V, and the integrator sits on the clamp at 0.85, while the operating point at 12 V needs 0.76. The input then returns to 12 V at 10 V/ms. With the clamp, another 450 µs at the limit, 33.8 A in the inductor, a 56.0 V peak, and settling in 1.79 ms: that is windup. In velocity form, 240 µs at the limit, 21.5 A, a 50.4 V peak, and settling in 0.96 ms. This simulation is not among the site's scenarios. Reference step from 40 to 48 V, without slew. The derivative kick takes the duty to 0.85. With the clamp, four periods at 0.85, no overshoot, and settling in 1.0 ms. In velocity form, it is the flaw of section 3: the duty drops to 0.09 and stays at zero for two periods, the inductor current goes to −34.7 A, and the output plunges to 7.7 V. Even 3.6 ms after the step, it is at 46.6 V. Boost, reference step from 40 to 48 V without slew, PID with the integrator clamp: four periods at 0.85 and settling in 1.0 ms. The same step with the PID as a 2p2z in velocity form: the inductor current goes to −34.7 A and the output to 7.7 V. Buck-boost. The duty goes from 0 to 0.8. In the scenarios, only the unstable controller hits the limits; on the step from 12 to 8 V without slew, the PID takes the duty to 0.08, without saturating (Derivative kick and derivative on the measurement). Exercise In the buck, compute \(T_t = \sqrt{T_i T_d}\) for the original PID (\(K_P\) = 0.0565, \(K_I\) = 1309, \(K_D\) = 1.5 µs/V). How many switching periods is that? title: Computation and PWM delay
heading: Computation and PWM delay
summary: From the ADC sample to the PWM edge it moves, (1 + D) Ts go by in this firmware, and this delay costs 360 f (1 + D) Ts of phase at the crossover.
prereqs: Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
From the boost to the digital loop
text: In the analog loop, a change at the output reaches the PWM comparator almost at once. In the digital one, the information goes through a chain: the ADC converts, the interrupt computes, the PWM register is updated and only then does one edge of the pulse move. Each stage delays the response, and a pure delay \(t_d\) is \(e^{-s t_d}\): it does not change the magnitude of the loop gain, but it costs phase.

title: Computation and PWM delay
heading: The chain in this site's firmware
summary: From the ADC sample to the PWM edge it moves, (1 + D) Ts go by in this firmware, and this delay costs 360 f (1 + D) Ts of phase at the crossover.
prereqs: Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
From the boost to the digital loop
text: Period \(k\) starts at \(t = kT_s\): Sample and conversion. The timer triggers the ADC at \(kT_s\), at the period start (Sampling and the zero-order hold (ZOH)): that is what the buck's frames do and, with SAMPLE_PHASE = 0, the boost and buck-boost scenarios. The trigger latency and the sampling window add up to 200 to 220 ns, which do not enter \((1+D)T_s\): the trigger and the choice of instant are in ADC trigger and sample instant, an optional detour that builds on the boost of Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost. Computation. The end-of-conversion interrupt runs the PID or the 2p2z and writes the new duty cycle to the compare register (CCR). Update in the next period. With preload on, the new CCR only takes effect at the next update event, at \((k+1)T_s\). That guarantees a whole pulse with the old value, even if the computation is slow, provided it finishes before the update event, and it costs one period. The modulated edge. In trailing-edge PWM (sawtooth carrier), the switch turns on at the start of the period and off at \((k+1+D)T_s\). Only that edge depends on \(d\); the duty-cycle perturbation enters the plant there, \(DT_s\) after the start. Adding these up, the delay from the sample to the edge it moves is \[\varphi_d(f) = -360^\circ\, f\, t_d, \qquad t_d = (1 + D)\,T_s\] The term \(DT_s\) plays the role of the zero-order hold: instead of the ZOH's average half period, the modulator delays to the edge that actually moves. The PWM modulator also has a gain: in the HRTIM, \(d = \mathrm{CMP1xR}/2000\), with 2000 counts per period (400 MHz for 200 kHz), and each step is worth \(1/2000\). In this firmware the duty cycle is computed per unit, as in Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins, and \(G_{vd}\) already includes \(V_{in}\). The resolution of those steps is the subject of DPWM resolution and limit cycles. For those coming from the reference course There, the digital loop's delay is "ZOH, \(-\omega T_s/2\), plus \(z^{-1}\) when the update goes to the next cycle". The rule is the same as here: that ZOH is the modulator of the center-aligned PWM, and in the trailing-edge PWM it becomes the \(DT_s\) term (Notation in this course). In the buck, with \(D = 0.375\), "ZOH plus \(z^{-1}\)" counts \(1.5\,T_s\) instead of \(1.375\,T_s\): the 2p2z margin comes out at \(39.5^\circ\) with the pure delay (\(39.6^\circ\) with the ZOH's sinc) instead of \(41.3^\circ\), on the safe side because \(D < 0.5\). Do not add the ZOH's phase to \((1+D)\,T_s\): it is already inside the \(DT_s\) term. The note PWM update: trailing edge vs symmetric compares the timings in a timing diagram. Phase of the buck's loop gain near the crossover, and the phase margin against the delay, from 0 to 2Tₛ: each period of delay costs \(360^\circ \cdot f_c \cdot T_s\) /* ADC end-of-conversion interrupt, triggered by the timer at t = kTs. */ void ADC_IRQHandler(void) { float v = adc_read() * (VFS / 4095.0f); /* sample at kTs, in volts */ float d = control_step(vref - v); /* PID or 2p2z */ HRTIM1->sTimerxRegs[0].CMP1xR = (uint32_t)(d * 2000u); /* 400 MHz / 200 kHz; timer A; preload: takes effect at (k + 1)Ts */ }

title: Computation and PWM delay
heading: Other timings
summary: From the ADC sample to the PWM edge it moves, (1 + D) Ts go by in this firmware, and this delay costs 360 f (1 + D) Ts of phase at the crossover.
prereqs: Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
From the boost to the digital loop
text: Sample away from the period start. With preload kept, moving the sample shortens the delay to \((1 + D - \varphi)\,T_s\) (ADC trigger and sample instant). Center-aligned PWM. The centered pulse on the H7 (sample at the reset, load at the next reset) is in Centered PWM on the H7: case B, and its delay is not \((1+D)\,T_s\). Computation that misses the deadline. If the interrupt ends after the update event, the value only takes effect one period later: \((2+D)T_s\). Jitter and priorities The delay is only \((1+D)T_s\) if the control interrupt never misses its deadline. A higher-priority communication interrupt, slow flash access or a debugging printf can push the CCR write past the update event in some periods, and the loop then has a varying delay. Give the control the highest priority. The deadline and how to measure it are in Interrupt deadline and budget. Phase budget Before choosing \(f_c\), work out the phase the delay will cost. If it exceeds about 30°, the crossover is too high for the chosen timing.

title: Computation and PWM delay
heading: In the converters
summary: From the ADC sample to the PWM edge it moves, (1 + D) Ts go by in this firmware, and this delay costs 360 f (1 + D) Ts of phase at the crossover.
prereqs: Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
From the boost to the digital loop
text: For the buck, with \(D = 0.375\) and \(T_s = 5\ \text{µs}\) (200 kHz), \(t_d = 6.875\ \text{µs}\). At 8 kHz, the 2p2z crossover, the delay costs \(19.8^\circ\): \(14.4^\circ\) from the computation period and \(5.4^\circ\) from the \(DT_s\) term. At 18 kHz, \(44.6^\circ\); at 25 kHz, \(61.9^\circ\). That is the main reason the aggressive and unstable designs lose margin. The model with \((1+D)T_s\) was checked in QSPICE, adding a small sine wave to the duty cycle inside the firmware: from 500 Hz to 15 kHz, it stayed within 0.3 dB and 0.7° of the simulation (Measuring the loop gain by injecting into the duty). For the boost and the buck-boost, the firmware's delay is also \((1 + D)\,T_s\), but the switched circuit's response behaves, to first order, like a delay of \((1 + D/2)\,T_s\) (Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost). Delaying G1's edge deprives the capacitor of the inductor current at its peak, not of its average: it is as if the perturbation entered at the middle of G1's pulse. In the buck, the jump at the edge does not depend on the state, and \((1 + D)\,T_s\) is exact. The site does not use a fitted delay for these two: it uses the sampled-data model of the switched circuit, which stays within 0.2 dB and 1.4° of QSPICE from 300 Hz to 7 kHz. With the crossover at 1.5 kHz in the boost, the delay matters little; there the limit is the The right-half-plane zero. Exercise 1 At what frequency does the buck's \((1+D)T_s\) delay alone consume 45° of phase? Exercise 2 A higher-priority communication interrupt delays the control routine, and the CCR is written after the update event. What happens to the 2p2z margin? title: Derivative kick and derivative on the measurement
heading: Derivative kick and derivative on the measurement
summary: On a reference step, a derivative term computed on the error jumps in a single period and saturates the duty; differentiating the measurement takes the reference out of that term.
text: The saturation of Anti-windup and duty saturation needs a trigger. On a reference step, the fastest one is the PID's derivative term. This note shows the size of that jump, the derivative kick, and how to remove it without changing the loop's margins.

title: Derivative kick and derivative on the measurement
heading: 1. The kick
summary: On a reference step, a derivative term computed on the error jumps in a single period and saturates the duty; differentiating the measurement takes the reference out of that term.
text: The buck's PID (buck_pid.cpp) and that of scenario.cpp, in the boost and the buck-boost, compute the derivative on the error \(e = v_{ref} - v\), with a filter of time constant \(T_F\): \[d_D[k] = \frac{T_F\,d_D[k-1] + K_D\,\bigl(e[k] - e[k-1]\bigr)}{T_F + T_s}.\] Without a filter, with \(T_F = 0\), as in the buck's PID, this is \(K_D\,(e[k] - e[k-1])/T_s\). On a reference step \(\Delta\), the output has not changed yet, and the error jumps by \(\Delta\) from one sample to the next. In the first period, the derivative is \[d_D = \frac{K_D}{T_F + T_s}\,\Delta .\] Without a filter, the jump lasts one period: in the next one, the error barely changes, and the term returns to zero. With a filter, it decays by the factor \(p = T_F/(T_F + T_s)\) each period, the PID's pole. Added to the proportional term, \(K_P\,\Delta\), it usually exceeds the duty's limits.

title: Derivative kick and derivative on the measurement
heading: 2. Derivative on the measurement
summary: On a reference step, a derivative term computed on the error jumps in a single period and saturates the duty; differentiating the measurement takes the reference out of that term.
text: With a constant reference, \(e[k] - e[k-1] = -(v[k] - v[k-1])\). Differentiating the measurement instead of the error gives the same term, and the loop gain, from the sample to the duty, does not change: the margins stay the same. What changes is the reference's path, which now enters only through the proportional and integral terms. A reference step no longer produces a derivative kick: /* Derivative on the measurement, with the filter of scenario.cpp (TF = 0 in the buck) */ float derivative(float vmeas) { deriv = (TF * deriv - KD * (vmeas - vmeas_prev)) / (TF + T); /* no kick when vref changes */ vmeas_prev = vmeas; return deriv; } The result takes the place of deriv in the back-calculation PID of Anti-windup and duty saturation. The proportional term still jumps by \(K_P\,\Delta\). And the 2p2z, which does not separate the derivative from the other terms, jumps too: its \(b_0\,e[k]\) term acts in full in the first period (The 2p2z compensator). For both, the remedy is the reference ramp of Soft-start and pre-biasing, which keeps the error small during the transition.

title: Derivative kick and derivative on the measurement
heading: In the converters
summary: On a reference step, a derivative term computed on the error jumps in a single period and saturates the duty; differentiating the measurement takes the reference out of that term.
text: Buck. In the pid-vref-step scenario, the reference goes from 9 to 5 V without slew. The error jumps to −4 V, and the derivative term is \(K_D\,\Delta e/T_s = (1.5\ \mu/5\ \mu)\times(-4) = -1.2\). Added to \(K_P\,e = -0.23\) and to the integrator near 0.38, the command goes negative, and the duty is clamped to zero for one period. The low-side switch stays on for the whole period, and the inductor current goes negative, down to about −5 A: the high-side switch returns energy to the input. The duty then climbs back over about ten periods, and the output sinks to 4.30 V. Buck, reference step from 9 to 5 V without slew: the derivative kick sets the duty to zero for one period, and the inductor current goes to about −5 A. Boost. The boost's PID has a derivative filter, and the first period's kick is \(K_D/(T_F + T_s) = 0.097\) per volt of jump in the error. On the step from 48 to 40 V, that gives \(-0.78\), plus \(K_P\,e = -0.09\): the duty also goes to zero for one period, and the inductor current reaches −16 A. On the step back, from 40 to 48 V, the kick takes the duty to 0.85, and what follows depends on the firmware's form (Anti-windup and duty saturation). Boost, reference step from 48 to 40 V without slew: one period at zero duty, and the inductor current reaches −16 A. Buck-boost. Here the kick is \(K_D/(T_F + T_s) = 1.37/(5.31 + 10) \approx 0.090\) per volt. On the step from 12 to 8 V, that is \(-0.36\), plus \(K_P\,e = -0.07\), against an integrator near 0.52. The command drops to 0.09 for one period, without reaching zero; G1 conducts for 0.08 of the period, because the 100 ns dead time takes 0.01 off. The current reaches −4 A (Four-switch buck-boost 8–16 V → 12 V: worked example). Buck-boost, reference step from 12 to 8 V without a slew: the duty drops to 0.08 for one period, and the inductor current reverses down to −4 A. Exercise 1 On the buck's step from 9 to 5 V (\(K_P\) = 0.0565, \(K_I\) = 1309, \(K_D\) = 1.5 µs/V, no filter, \(T_s\) = 5 µs), what is the derivative term in the first period with the derivative on the error? And with the derivative on the measurement? Does the duty saturate in the second case? Exercise 2 In the boost (\(K_P\) = 0.0114, \(K_D\) = 1.75 µs/V, \(T_F\) = 7.96 µs, \(T_s\) = 10 µs), compute the kick per volt of jump in the error. On the step from 40 to 48 V, why does the duty saturate at 0.85, and for how many periods? Before the step, the integrator holds the steady-state command, 0.71. title: Discretization table
heading: Discretization table
summary: The six most used maps from s to z (forward and backward Euler, Tustin, prewarped Tustin, ZOH equivalent and matched pole-zero), with stability, DC gain, high-frequency behavior and when to use each.
text: A controller designed in \(s\) has to become a difference equation. The bilinear (Tustin) transform and prewarping introduced the bilinear transform, and Sampling and the zero-order hold (ZOH) introduced the zero-order hold. This table gathers those two and the other common methods, with \(T_s = 1/f_s\) the sampling period.

title: Discretization table
heading: The maps
summary: The six most used maps from s to z (forward and backward Euler, Tustin, prewarped Tustin, ZOH equivalent and matched pole-zero), with stability, DC gain, high-frequency behavior and when to use each.
text: Method Substitution or rule The left half of the \(s\) plane goes to DC gain High frequency When to use Forward Euler \(s \to \dfrac{z - 1}{T_s}\) the half plane \(\mathrm{Re}\,z < 1\): a stable pole can leave the unit circle kept (\(s = 0 \to z = 1\)) the axis \(s = j2\pi f\) becomes the line \(z = 1 + j2\pi f\,T_s\), outside the circle; the error grows with \(2\pi f\,T_s\) almost never in a compensator; only for dynamics very slow compared with \(f_s\) Backward Euler \(s \to \dfrac{1 - z^{-1}}{T_s}\) the disk of radius 1/2 centered at \(z = 1/2\): always stable, but too damped kept \(s \to \infty\) goes to \(z = 0\) a PID's integrator and derivative; simple filters Tustin (bilinear) \(s \to \dfrac{2}{T_s}\,\dfrac{z - 1}{z + 1}\) exactly the unit disk kept \(f \to \infty\) goes to \(z = -1\) (\(f_s/2\)); frequencies are compressed, \(f_d = \tfrac{1}{\pi T_s}\arctan(\pi f_a T_s)\) the default for compensators Prewarped Tustin \(s \to \dfrac{2\pi f_0}{\tan(\pi f_0 T_s)}\,\dfrac{z - 1}{z + 1}\) the unit disk kept like Tustin, but exact at \(f_0\) when one frequency must land in place: the crossover, a notch ZOH equivalent \(G(z) = (1 - z^{-1})\,\mathcal{Z}\{G(s)/s\}\) exact poles, \(z = e^{pT_s}\) kept exact for a staircase input; a strictly proper \(G\) ends up with \(b_0 = 0\), which adds one period of delay discretizing the plant seen by the PWM, not the compensator Matched pole-zero each pole and zero goes to \(z = e^{pT_s}\); zeros at infinity go to \(z = -1\); the gain is matched at DC or another frequency the unit disk (exact poles) matched the finite zeros are exact too; the phase of fast poles differs from the continuous one poles and zeros with a physical meaning, as in this course's 2p2z The methods agree when the singularity is slow compared with \(f_s\) and diverge as it approaches \(f_s/2\). The figure shows it on the buck's 2p2z. The buck's default 2p2z (zeros at 2 kHz, pole at 60 kHz, crossover at 8 kHz) discretized at 200 kHz: compare the discrete response with the continuous one near the fast pole.

title: Discretization table
heading: Reading the table
summary: The six most used maps from s to z (forward and backward Euler, Tustin, prewarped Tustin, ZOH equivalent and matched pole-zero), with stability, DC gain, high-frequency behavior and when to use each.
text: Stability: only forward Euler can make a stable pole unstable. A real pole at \(s = -2\pi f_p\) goes to \(z = 1 - 2\pi f_p T_s\), which leaves the circle when \(f_p > f_s/\pi\). DC gain: all of them keep the gain at \(z = 1\), which is why the integrator stays an integrator. Matched pole-zero keeps it because the gain is chosen to. Delay: the ZOH equivalent of a compensator without a direct term adds one period of delay. That is why it serves for the plant, in Sampling and the zero-order hold (ZOH), and not for the controller. Frequency warping: in Tustin, it is negligible below \(f_s/10\) and large near \(f_s/2\). Prewarping fixes one frequency only (see The bilinear (Tustin) transform and prewarping).

title: Discretization table
heading: In the converters
summary: The six most used maps from s to z (forward and backward Euler, Tustin, prewarped Tustin, ZOH equivalent and matched pole-zero), with stability, DC gain, high-frequency behavior and when to use each.
text: Buck. The default design at 200 kHz has zeros at 2 kHz and a pole at 60 kHz, and scenarios.json takes it to \(z\) by matched pole-zero: the pole goes to \(p = e^{-2\pi \cdot 60\,\text{k}\cdot T_s} = 0.1518\), which is \(a_2\), and \(a_1 = -(1 + p) = -1.1518\). The four substitution methods give, for the two singularities: Method zero at 2 kHz pole at 60 kHz Forward Euler 0.93717 −0.8850 Backward Euler 0.94088 0.3466 Tustin 0.93908 0.0296 matched 0.93910 0.1518 At the zero, at 1 % of \(f_s\), the four agree to two decimal places. The pole, at 30 % of \(f_s\), lands in four different places: forward Euler puts it near \(z = -1\), ringing at \(f_s/2\), and Tustin turns it into a pole that, seen in frequency, sits at 48.1 kHz instead of 60 kHz. The PID of scenario.cpp uses backward Euler: integ += KI * T * err adds the current error, and the derivative is \(K_D\,(e[k] - e[k-1])/T_s\), with its filter also discretized by backward Euler. Exercise 1 In the buck, above what frequency does a real pole of the compensator discretized by forward Euler become unstable? Exercise 2 By Tustin without prewarping, at what frequency does the 60 kHz pole appear? What constant replaces \(2/T_s\) so that it lands exactly at 60 kHz? Exercise 3 In a hypothetical case, the compensator of a converter that runs at \(f_s = 100\) kHz has a real pole at 60 kHz, and the firmware discretizes it by forward Euler. On the board, this pole's signal alternates in sign every sample and grows. What is the discrete pole, and by how much does it grow per period?
