title: DPWM resolution and limit cycles
heading: DPWM resolution and limit cycles
summary: The duty also moves in steps: when the step it causes at the output is larger than the ADC step, the loop has nowhere to settle and oscillates in a limit cycle.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
From the boost to the digital loop
text: In ADC quantization, the measurement of the output moved in steps. So does the actuator: the digital PWM (DPWM) only produces a finite number of duty values, and the two quantizers together can keep the loop from settling.

title: DPWM resolution and limit cycles
heading: The DPWM step
summary: The duty also moves in steps: when the step it causes at the output is larger than the ADC step, the loop has nowhere to settle and oscillates in a limit cycle.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
From the boost to the digital loop
text: The timer counts from 0 to the end of the period, and the output changes when the counter passes the compare value, the CCR (PWM update: trailing edge vs symmetric). The duty can only be \(\mathrm{CCR}/N_{\mathrm{PWM}}\): \[N_{\mathrm{PWM}} = \frac{f_{\mathrm{clk}}}{f_s}, \qquad \Delta D = \frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{PWM}}}, \qquad n_{\mathrm{PWM}} = \log_2 N_{\mathrm{PWM}}\] With the HRTIM at 400 MHz and \(f_s\) = 200 kHz, there are \(400/0.2 = 2000\) counts per period: \(\Delta D = 1/2000\), or \(\log_2 2000 = 11.0\) bits. In symmetric PWM, each half period has 1000 steps, 10.0 bits. Doubling \(f_s\) costs one bit. The STM32H7's HRTIM is a high-resolution timer. It counts on the CPU clock, at 400 MHz, only with the bit HRTIMSEL = 1 of RCC_CFGR (RM0433, section 8.7.7); with HRTIMSEL = 0, it runs at 200 MHz. The step is 2.5 ns, \(1/400\) MHz (RM0433, table 307). The reference clock tree is in Interrupt deadline and budget.

title: DPWM resolution and limit cycles
heading: The step at the output
summary: The duty also moves in steps: when the step it causes at the output is larger than the ADC step, the loop has nowhere to settle and oscillates in a limit cycle.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
From the boost to the digital loop
text: In steady state, changing the duty by \(\Delta D\) moves the output by \(|G_{vd}(0)|\,\Delta D\), with \(G_{vd}\) the plant of The buck's transfer function \(G_{vd}(s)\). In the buck, \(G_{vd}(0) \approx V_{in}\): \[\Delta V_{\mathrm{DPWM}} = \frac{24\ \text{V}}{2000} = 12.0\ \text{mV} \qquad \text{contra} \qquad q = 4.884\ \text{mV}.\] One HRTIM step moves the output about 2.5 ADC steps. Because it is larger than the zero-error band, 4.884 mV wide, a CCR value lands inside the band only in about 40 % of the positions of the reference (\(q/\Delta V_{\mathrm{DPWM}} = 0.41\)). In the others, the output jumps over the band. The buck's two quantizers: a 12-bit ADC and an 11-bit DPWM (2048 levels, 11.7 mV per step at the output; the HRTIM at 200 kHz has 2000). Change the resolutions and see when a DPWM level falls inside the zero-error band.

title: DPWM resolution and limit cycles
heading: Limit cycle
summary: The duty also moves in steps: when the step it causes at the output is larger than the ADC step, the loop has nowhere to settle and oscillates in a limit cycle.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
From the boost to the digital loop
text: Limit cycle A sustained periodic oscillation of a nonlinear system, with no external excitation. In a quantized loop, the output alternates between DPWM levels because none of them cancels the error read. The integrator accumulates the error and raises the duty one step; the output rises 12 mV and jumps over the 4.884 mV band; the error changes sign, the integrator goes down, and the story repeats. The linear analysis of Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins doesn't predict it: the loop oscillates even with good margins, with an amplitude of the order of the DPWM step. Peterchev and Sanders (2003) gave three conditions against steady-state limit cycles: a DPWM finer than the ADC, so that a DPWM level lies inside the zero-error band. They suggest one extra bit, which gives two DPWM levels per ADC level; an integrator with limited gain. Without it, a steady-state error remains outside the band; with too much gain, it can't adjust the duty in fine steps. With the variables normalized to \(V_{in}\), the integral gain lies between 0 and 1; no excess loop gain: the ADC acts as a gain that changes with amplitude (its describing function), and the loop with that gain must not pass through the −1 point. In practice, this asks for headroom in the gain margin. The first two, the static conditions: \[\Delta V_{\mathrm{DPWM}} = |G_{vd}(0)|\,\Delta D < q, \qquad 0 < k_i\,|G_{vd}(0)| \le 1\] They assume a zero-error band: with the reference between two codes, as in ADC quantization, the integrator hunts forever.

title: DPWM resolution and limit cycles
heading: Dither
summary: The duty also moves in steps: when the step it causes at the output is larger than the ADC step, the loop has nowhere to settle and oscillates in a limit cycle.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
From the boost to the digital loop
text: When resolution is short, the firmware alternates the CCR between two neighboring values over \(M\) periods. The LC filter takes the average, and the average duty moves in steps of \(\Delta D/M\). The price is a component at \(f_s/M\), which must fall well above the crossover and be attenuated by the LC. /* Dither over M = 4 periods. d4 is the duty in counts with 2 fraction bits (d * 2000 * 4). The bit-reversed order spreads the "high" periods. */ static const uint8_t threshold[4] = {0, 2, 1, 3}; static uint32_t k; uint32_t ccr_with_dither(uint32_t d4) { uint32_t base = d4 >> 2, frac = d4 & 3u; return base + (frac > threshold[k++ & 3u]); /* frac periods out of 4 get +1 */ } The integrator also needs resolution With \(k_i\,q/\Delta D \ll 1\), each sample moves the integrator by a fraction of a count. Stored in whole counts, the increment rounds to zero and the integrator never moves: an artificial dead band. Store the state in float or with fraction bits, as in Q15 fixed point.

title: DPWM resolution and limit cycles
heading: In the converters
summary: The duty also moves in steps: when the step it causes at the output is larger than the ADC step, the loop has nowhere to settle and oscillates in a limit cycle.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
From the boost to the digital loop
text: Buck. In this site's simulations, only the ADC is quantized, and the duty is a double: condition 1 holds by construction. On the STM32H7, the 12.0 mV at 200 kHz break the condition; the dither with \(M = 4\) (3.0 mV) meets it. Condition 2 holds with room to spare: in the PID, \(k_i = K_I T_s\) = 1309 × 5 µs = 0.0065 per volt, and \(k_i\,|G_{vd}(0)| = 0.16\); in the 2p2z, the integrator moves \((b_0 + b_1 + b_2)/(1 - a_2) = 1.01\times10^{-3}\) per volt and per sample, and the product is 0.024. That integrator moves only \(k_i\,q/\Delta D = 0.0099\) of a count per code of error and needs the resolution of the warning above. Boost. The static gain is much larger: \(V_{in}/(1-D)^2 \approx 12/0.248^2 \approx 195\) V without losses, and 190.4 V in the averaged model with losses, at 48 V and 1 A. At 100 kHz, the HRTIM makes 4000 counts, and each moves the output \(190.4/4000 = 47.6\) mV, more than three times \(q\) = 14.65 mV. Condition 1 asks for \(f_s < q\,f_{\mathrm{clk}}/|G_{vd}(0)| = 31\) kHz; with \(M = 4\) in the dither, the effective step drops to 11.9 mV, below \(q\). Exercise 1 With the HRTIM at 400 MHz and the 12-bit ADC, up to what switching frequency does the buck meet condition 1? And with one bit of headroom? Exercise 2 With the HRTIM at 400 MHz and 200 kHz, what \(M\) (a power of 2) does the dither need to meet condition 1 in the buck? At what frequency is the dither's component, and why does it matter little? Exercise 3 A 24 V buck at 200 kHz, with the HRTIM at 400 MHz and no dither, shows two alternating levels at the output, 12 mV apart. What is the cause, by condition 1, and which remedy of this note removes it? text: This is the final step of the digital control trail, a mini-project. You choose one of the two converters with a right-half-plane zero, the boost or the buck-boost, write its digital loop in C, and check the code against the numbers this site already records.

title: Mini-project: the firmware of one converter
heading: Checklist
summary: Write and check in C the digital loop of the boost or the buck-boost, with a checklist, two calculations with answers, and a delivery sheet with the expected values.
prereqs: The 2p2z in C, in the interrupt
Robust design across the operating range
text: Check each item in your code before running any simulation. Coefficients. \(b_0\), \(b_1\), \(b_2\) and \(p\) are those of the table in the last section, copied from scenarios.json with every digit. In the code, \(a_1 = -(1+p)\) and \(a_2 = p\) (The 2p2z compensator). State. The firmware stores the duty actually applied, after the limit, not the computed one. That prevents accumulation beyond the limit, but not the return of the kick: in the velocity form, the term \(b_1\,e[k-1]\) of the next period removes the jump that was never applied, and on the boost the duty drops to 0.09 and sits at zero for two periods (Anti-windup and duty saturation). Reference step. Change the reference along a ramp (Soft-start and pre-biasing) or move the derivative to the measurement (Derivative kick and derivative on the measurement), so the error does not jump. Limits and reference. The duty stays between 0 and \(D_{max}\), and REF_CODE is a rounded integer, not a truncated one (ADC quantization). Sample. The ADC triggers at the period start, just before G1 turns on, as in the scenarios; the coefficients hold for that instant. Sampling within G1 calls for redoing the plant (ADC trigger and sample instant). Start-up. The recorded scenarios begin in steady state; test start-up and protections separately.

title: Q15 fixed point
heading: Q15 fixed point
summary: The scale of the buck's 2p2z coefficients in fixed point: Qm.n formats, Q15 multiplication with rounding and saturation, and the coefficients in counts per code in Q3.12.
text: The 2p2z compensator has coefficients such as 0.23114 and −0.43413. In fixed point (fixed-point), each number becomes an integer with an implicit scale, and this note shows how that scale works. If the core has an FPU and measurement does not ask otherwise, the decision to use fixed point is in Floating point or fixed point.

title: Q15 fixed point
heading: The Q m . n format
summary: The scale of the buck's 2p2z coefficients in fixed point: Qm.n formats, Q15 multiplication with rounding and saturation, and the coefficients in counts per code in Q3.12.
text: Q\(m\).\(n\) format A signed integer \(X\) represents \(x = X/2^n\): \(n\) fraction bits and \(m\) integer bits beyond the sign, in \(1 + m + n\) bits in total. Q15 (or Q0.15) is the int16_t read as a fraction, from −1 to \(1 - 2^{-15}\), in steps of \(3.05\times10^{-5}\). \[x = \frac{X}{2^{n}}, \quad X \in \left[-2^{m+n},\; 2^{m+n}-1\right], \qquad Z = \left\lfloor \frac{X\,Y + 2^{n-1}}{2^{n}} \right\rfloor\] Q2.13 covers −4 to 4 in steps of \(1.22\times10^{-4}\): it trades resolution for headroom. The product of two Q15 numbers has 30 fraction bits and fits in 32 bits. To return to Q15, add half a step (\(2^{14}\)) and shift 15 bits: #include <stdint.h> static inline int16_t sat16(int32_t x) /* saturate instead of wrapping */ { return x > INT16_MAX ? INT16_MAX : x < INT16_MIN ? INT16_MIN : (int16_t)x; } static inline int16_t q15_mul(int16_t a, int16_t b) { int32_t p = (int32_t)a * b; /* Q30: the cast comes before the multiplication */ p += 1 << 14; /* round instead of truncating */ return sat16(p >> 15); /* -1 * -1 = +1 does not fit in Q15: saturate */ } Three pitfalls Overflow: without saturation, \(0.9 + 0.2\) in Q15 becomes \(-0.9\). A duty cycle that jumps from 0.9 to −0.9 is the worst possible error. On Cortex-M3, M4 and M7, the CMSIS provides __SSAT(x, 16), which saturates in one instruction. Truncation: p >> 15 without the half step always rounds down, a bias that the integrator accumulates. Shifting negatives: in C99, >> of a negative number is implementation-defined. On GCC for ARM it is arithmetic; check your compiler. To add several products, use a 64-bit accumulator. Each Q15 × Q15 product already takes 31 bits, and two of them added together can overflow 32 bits. On the Cortex-M4 and M7, the SMLAL instruction multiplies and accumulates into 64 bits. On the M4 it takes one cycle (Cortex-M4 TRM, table 3-1); the M7 issues one such operation, 32 × 32 + 64 → 64 bits, per cycle, with a two-cycle result latency (Cortex-M7 TRM, section 1.2.1). The M0 has no such instruction, and the compiler emulates the operation in several.

title: Q15 fixed point
heading: The buck's 2p2z coefficients
summary: The scale of the buck's 2p2z coefficients in fixed point: Qm.n formats, Q15 multiplication with rounding and saturation, and the coefficients in counts per code in Q3.12.
text: The standard design (crossover at 8 kHz, double zeros at 2 kHz, pole at 60 kHz) has, in duty cycle per volt of error, \(b_0 = 0.23114\), \(b_1 = -0.43413\), \(b_2 = 0.20385\) and, in the denominator, \(a_1 = -(1 + p) = -1.15184\) and \(a_2 = p = 0.15184\). The \(a_i\) tie \(u\) to \(u\) and do not depend on units. In the difference equation, \(a_1\) exceeds 1 in magnitude and does not fit Q15. There are two options: Velocity form: rewrite the equation as \(u[k-1] + a_2\,(u[k-1] - u[k-2]) + \dots\), so that only \(a_2\) must be stored, in Q15: 4975. The \(a_1\) is implicit, \(-(2^{15} + 4975)/2^{15}\), and exact. Format with headroom for both: in Q1.14, which runs from −2 to almost 2, \(a_1\) = −18872 and \(a_2\) = 2488. In both cases, \(a_1\) and \(a_2\) share the same format. Because \(2^n\) is an integer, rounding both with the same scale keeps \(1 + a_1 + a_2 = 0\) exact, and the integrator stays at \(z = 1\). With \(a_1\) in Q1.14 and \(a_2\) in Q15, the sum would be \(-3.05\times10^{-5}\), and the integrator would move to \(z = 1.000036\), outside the unit circle. Units matter too. The firmware receives ADC codes and writes HRTIM counts. Multiplying the coefficients by \(N_{\mathrm{PWM}}\,q = 2000 \times 4.884\ \text{mV} = 9.77\) gives values in counts per code: \(2.258\), \(-4.241\) and \(1.991\). Now all three exceed 1 in magnitude, and the format needs headroom: \(|b_1| = 4.24\) does not fit Q2.13 (±4), but fits Q3.12 (±8). The equation's states also keep the 12 fraction bits: without them, the integrator's steps, hundredths of a count, would round to zero, as DPWM resolution and limit cycles warns. The script below quantizes the coefficients and measures the effect: import numpy as np fs, q, N = 200e3, 20/4095, 2000 # 400 MHz / 200 kHz: counts per period b = np.array([0.23114164, -0.43413087, 0.20384645]); p = 0.15183580 a1, a2 = -(1 + p), p # denominator 1 + a1 z^-1 + a2 z^-2 K = N * q # from duty cycle/volt to counts/code ki = b.sum() / (1 - a2) # integrator step per sample for n in (15, 14): # a1 and a2 on the same scale: 1 + a1 + a2 = 0 exactly A1, A2 = round(a1 * 2**n), round(a2 * 2**n) print(f"a in Q{15 - n}.{n}", A1, A2, 2**n + A1 + A2) # Q0.15: -37743 does not fit int16 for name, n, scale in [("Q15 d/V", 15, 1), ("Q2.13 d/V", 13, 1), ("Q4.11 d/V", 11, 1), ("Q3.12 cnt/code", 12, K), ("Q4.11 cnt/code", 11, K)]: B = np.round(b * scale * 2**n) # the integers written to the firmware bq = B / 2**n / scale a2q = np.round(a2 * 2**15) / 2**15 # a2 in Q15: 4975; a1 = -(1 + a2) implicit f = np.abs(np.log(np.roots(bq))) * fs / (2 * np.pi) print(name, B.astype(int), np.round(f), f"{100 * (bq.sum() / (1 - a2q) / ki - 1):+.1f} %") Format, units \(b_0\), \(b_1\), \(b_2\) zeros (were 2 kHz double) integral gain phase margin exact — 2000 and 2000 Hz — 41.3° Q15, duty/V 7574, −14226, 6680 1904 and 2094 Hz −0.3 % 41.3° Q2.13, duty/V 1894, −3556, 1670 complex pair, 2135 Hz +13.9 % 41.1° Q4.11, duty/V 473, −889, 417 686 and 3325 Hz −43 % 41.7° Q3.12, counts/code (2000 steps) 9248, −17369, 8156 complex pair, 2020 Hz +2.0 % 41.3° Q4.11, counts/code (2000 steps) 4624, −8685, 4078 1815 and 2184 Hz −0.9 % 41.3° The pole, with \(a_2\) = 4975 in Q15, moves from 60 000 to 60 002 Hz; with \(a_2\) = 2488 in Q1.14, to 59 996 Hz. The margins come from the buck model in tools/qspice_loop_check.py. The phase of \(C(z)\) at 8 kHz changes by −0.03° in Q3.12 and +0.02° in Q4.11, against the exact coefficients, and the 41.3° margin does not change to the first decimal. The table has two lessons: The margin barely changes. Near the crossover, an error of \(10^{-4}\) in a coefficient of 0.4 is negligible. The integrator and the double zero change a lot. The integral gain is proportional to \(b_0 + b_1 + b_2 = 8.6\times10^{-4}\), a sum of nearly equal numbers that cancel. A double zero is ill-conditioned: an error \(\delta\) in the coefficients separates it by about \(\sqrt{\delta}\). That is why the scale matters: the integral-gain error falls from 13.9 % in Q2.13 per volt to 2.0 % in Q3.12 per code.

title: Q15 fixed point
heading: In the converters
summary: The scale of the buck's 2p2z coefficients in fixed point: Qm.n formats, Q15 multiplication with rounding and saturation, and the coefficients in counts per code in Q3.12.
text: Buck. In Q3.12, the coefficients in counts per code stay within 2.0 % of the exact integral gain and keep the 41.3° margin; the code is in Floating point or fixed point. The aggressive design, with \(b_1 = -15.4\) counts per code, needs Q4.11 (±16); the unstable one, with −21.2, does not fit even there. Changing the design may need another format: the code must check the range before writing. Boost. The standard 2p2z has \(b_0 = 0.165\), \(b_1 = -0.319\) and \(b_2 = 0.155\) per volt: again, a small sum next to each term. Exercise 1 In Q15, what integer represents \(a_2 = 0.15184\)? And \(a_1 = -1.15184\)? What is the largest rounding error of a coefficient in Q2.13? Exercise 2 The ADC error runs from −4095 to 4095 codes, and the largest coefficient in Q3.12, in counts per code, is \(|b_1|\) = 17369. Does one product fit in 32 bits? And the sum of the three terms \(b_i\,e\)? In the author's handbook Modelagem de Conversores Chaveados: do modelo à bancada virtual: the fixed-point arithmetic of the compensator.

title: Floating point or fixed point
heading: Floating point or fixed point
summary: Between `float` and fixed point, the core decides first: without an FPU, fixed point is the output; with an FPU, the choice is a design one, and only a cycle measurement justifies it.
text: The 2p2z compensator equation can run on floating-point numbers, which the core computes with the coefficients as they are, or on fixed-point integers, each with an implicit scale (Q15 fixed point). The choice depends first on what the core has in hardware, and then on what measurement shows.

title: Floating point or fixed point
heading: By the core's hardware
summary: Between `float` and fixed point, the core decides first: without an FPU, fixed point is the output; with an FPU, the choice is a design one, and only a cycle measurement justifies it.
text: With a single-precision FPU (Cortex-M4F, M33 and others): use float. On the M4F, an addition or a multiplication takes 1 cycle, and a multiply-accumulate 3 (Cortex-M4 TRM, table 7-1); for the M33, see the core's manual. The 24-bit mantissa is enough for this loop. With a double-precision FPU (the H7's Cortex-M7, PM0253): float and double both run in hardware, and choosing between them and fixed point is a design decision. Fixed point saves cycles only if measurement shows it. This note has no such measurement for the H7, and claims no speed-up without a number. Without an FPU (Cortex-M0 and M0+): each float operation becomes a library call, typically tens of cycles. With a 5 µs period and a 64 MHz core, there are only 320 cycles per period, and fixed point is used there. Hidden double precision On a single-precision FPU (M4F, M33), 0.5 is a double, and x * 0.5 is computed in software. Write 0.5f, and compile with -Wdouble-promotion so the compiler points at the cases. On the H7 double precision also runs in the FPU, but promotion still changes the result type: write 0.5f to keep float.

title: Floating point or fixed point
heading: Measure before switching
summary: Between `float` and fixed point, the core decides first: without an FPU, fixed point is the output; with an FPU, the choice is a design one, and only a cycle measurement justifies it.
text: Fixed point is not justified by the mere existence of an FPU. On the H7, the fixed-point variant comes in only if measuring the float routine shows that it does not fit the deadline with the margin the design needs. The measurement is the one in Interrupt deadline and budget: an output pin and the DWT cycle counter, on production code. With the number in hand, the decision is a margin calculation. Fixed point has costs of its own, which the FPU does not remove: Scale: each quantity has a format, and the coefficient range is checked before the coefficients are written (Q15 fixed point). Fraction bits in the states: the states keep the 12 fraction bits. Without them, the integrator's steps, hundredths of a count, would round to zero, as DPWM resolution and limit cycles warns. Saturation: every sum that can leave the range saturates, because an integer wrap-around sends the duty cycle from its maximum to a negative value.

title: Floating point or fixed point
heading: Fixed-point variant
summary: Between `float` and fixed point, the core decides first: without an FPU, fixed point is the output; with an FPU, the choice is a design one, and only a cycle measurement justifies it.
text: The error stays in ADC codes, the duty cycle in HRTIM counts with 12 fraction bits, and the coefficients in Q3.12, as in Q15 fixed point. The numbers are for 2000 counts per period: #define FRAC 12 #define REF_CODE 1843 /* 9 V * 4095 / 20 V = 1842.75 */ static const int32_t b0q = 9248, b1q = -17369, b2q = 8156; /* Q3.12: |b1| = 4.24 does not fit Q2.13 */ static const int32_t a2q = 4975; /* a2 = p in Q15; a1 = -(1 + a2) */ static const int32_t UMIN = 3 << FRAC; /* CMP1xR >= 3 (RM0433, table 308) */ static const int32_t UMAX = 1800 << FRAC; /* 0.9 * 2000 counts */ static int32_t uq1 = 750 << FRAC, uq2 = 750 << FRAC; /* 0.375 * 2000 */ static int32_t eq1, eq2; void ADC_IRQHandler(void) { int32_t e = REF_CODE - (int32_t)ADC1->DR; /* error in codes: can be 0 */ int64_t d = (int64_t)a2q * (uq1 - uq2); /* up to 3.7e10: only this product needs 64 bits */ int32_t acc = uq1 + (int32_t)((d + (1 << 14)) >> 15) + b0q * e + b1q * eq1 + b2q * eq2; /* sum below 1.6e8: fits 32 bits */ if (acc < UMIN) acc = UMIN; /* saturate in Q12 counts */ if (acc > UMAX) acc = UMAX; uq2 = uq1; uq1 = acc; eq2 = eq1; eq1 = e; HRTIM1->sTimerxRegs[0].CMP1xR = (uint32_t)((acc + (1 << (FRAC - 1))) >> FRAC); /* timer A */ } Only the product \(a_2\,(u[k-1] - u[k-2])\) needs 64 bits: with \(u\) up to \(1800 \times 4096 \approx 7.4\times10^{6}\) and \(a_2\) = 4975, it reaches \(3.7\times10^{10}\). The \(b_i\,e\) terms, with \(|e| \le 4095\), add up to at most \((9248 + 17369 + 8156) \times 4095 = 1.42\times10^{8}\), far from \(2^{31}\), as the exercise in Q15 fixed point shows. This matters on a core without a 64-bit multiply, such as the Cortex-M0+, where each int64_t multiplication becomes a library call (__aeabi_lmul). In C11, >> of a negative int64_t is implementation-defined; on GCC for ARM it is arithmetic; check your compiler. And this variant lacks the guards of the float routine: enable, fault and the ADC's OVR flag would have to be added the same way.

title: Floating point or fixed point
heading: In the converters
summary: Between `float` and fixed point, the core decides first: without an FPU, fixed point is the output; with an FPU, the choice is a design one, and only a cycle measurement justifies it.
text: Buck. At 200 kHz, the period has 2000 HRTIM counts at 400 MHz, that is, 2000 core cycles. That is the deadline the routine must meet, and the measurement in Interrupt deadline and budget says whether it does. In the standard design the coefficients in counts per code fit Q3.12, and the code above is the fixed-point counterpart of the float routine in The 2p2z in C, in the interrupt. The integer reference 1843 regulates at \(1843 \times 20/4095 = 9.0012\) V. Boost. At 100 kHz, the period has 4000 cycles, twice the buck's deadline; the margin grows by more than that, because the routine takes the same time. The coefficient scale changes with the ADC range, 60 V, as Q15 fixed point shows. Exercise 1 A Cortex-M0+ at 64 MHz, with no FPU, drives the buck at 200 kHz. How many cycles are there per period? Why is the float variant risky? Exercise 2 A Cortex-M4F program writes float x = y * 0.5;. Which part makes the operation run in double precision in software, and what does the compiler warn about with the right option?

title: Centered PWM on the H7: case B
heading: Centered PWM on the H7: case B
summary: Centered pulse from two comparators of the up-counter, sample at the reset and load at the next reset: the delay to the pulse center is 1.5 Ts, whatever D.
prereqs: PWM update: trailing edge vs symmetric
text: The STM32H7 HRTIM has no up-down counting mode, the one that centers the pulse in symmetric PWM. The reference manual (RM0433) gives only the up-counter, so the centered pulse comes from two of its comparators: CMP1 sets the output and CMP2 resets it. Each period, the CPU recalculates both from \(D\): \[c_1 = \frac{(1-D)\,T_s}{2}, \qquad c_2 = \frac{(1+D)\,T_s}{2}, \qquad c_1 + c_2 = T_s.\] For \(D = 0.375\) and \(T_s = 5\ \text{µs}\), \(c_1 = 1.5625\ \text{µs}\) and \(c_2 = 3.4375\ \text{µs}\). The center of the pulse stays at \(T_s/2\) for any \(D\), because the two edges move in opposite directions.

title: Centered PWM on the H7: case B
heading: Case B: the sequence
summary: Centered pulse from two comparators of the up-counter, sample at the reset and load at the next reset: the delay to the pulse center is 1.5 Ts, whatever D.
prereqs: PWM update: trailing edge vs symmetric
text: The figure shows two periods, \(k\) and \(k+1\), with time counted from the sample (the reset of period \(k\)). The other timings are in PWM update: trailing edge vs symmetric. The counter climbs from 0 to PER and restarts at every period. The ADC is triggered by the period event: the sample falls on the reset of period \(k\). CMP2 does not trigger the sample. The CPU converts, computes \(D\) and writes CMP1 and CMP2 into the preload. The update event at the next reset, that of \(k+1\), copies both values into the active registers. In period \(k+1\), CMP1 sets the output at \(1.5625\ \text{µs}\) and CMP2 resets it at \(3.4375\ \text{µs}\): the pulse is centered at \(2.5\ \text{µs}\). Illustrative timing diagram of the symmetric PWM, case B, the H7 reference: up-counter, ADC sample at the reset of period k, computation in the CPU, write to the preload of CMP1 and CMP2, update event at the reset of k+1 and the pulse centered in period k+1. Below, the inductor current and its average: the current equals the average at the reset (midpoint of the fall) and at the pulse center (midpoint of the rise). The widths of the conversion and computation bars are illustrative.

title: Centered PWM on the H7: case B
heading: The delay is 1.5·Tₛ for any D
summary: Centered pulse from two comparators of the up-counter, sample at the reset and load at the next reset: the delay to the pulse center is 1.5 Ts, whatever D.
prereqs: PWM update: trailing edge vs symmetric
text: From the sample to the update event there is one period, \(T_s\); from there to the pulse center, half a period, \(T_s/2\). The total, \(1.5\,T_s\), does not depend on \(D\), because the center does not move when \(D\) changes. It is the "ZOH plus \(z^{-1}\)" count of PWM update: trailing edge vs symmetric, with \(1.5\,T_s\) as the nominal value. The effective sample falls at the end of the sampling window, \(t_{LATR} + t_S\) after the reset. With the ADC at 50 MHz, tLATR is 1.5 to 2.5 cycles (30 to 50 ns), and the window is 8.5 cycles (170 ns, see below): the sample falls \(200\) to \(220\ \text{ns}\) after the reset, and the delay to the pulse center is between \(7.28\) and \(7.30\ \text{µs}\). The window is not the register minimum, 1.5 cycles (30 ns; DS12110, table 174, silicon revision V). At 12 bits, table 175 (p. 276) asks for at least 53 ns on a direct channel, 80 ns on a fast channel and 129 ns on a slow channel, even with \(R_{AIN}\) = 47 Ω. They hold up to 125 °C, with 47 pF on the board and \(V_{DDA}\) = 1.6 V. The H7's SMP field only takes 1.5, 2.5, 8.5, 16.5, 32.5, 64.5, 387.5 and 810.5 cycles (RM0433, section 25.4.13). With a direct channel and a source of \(R_{AIN} \le 47\) Ω (the divider with a buffer), as this note assumes, 2.5 cycles (50 ns) are not enough, and the smallest value that works is 8.5 cycles. Same symbol, another \(T_s\) The last row of the table in PWM update: trailing edge vs symmetric also says \(1.5\,T_s\), but there \(T_s\) is the sampling period of the double update, \(T_{PWM}/2\), and the delay is \(0.75\,T_{PWM}\). Here, \(T_s = T_{PWM}\).

title: Centered PWM on the H7: case B
heading: Computation budget
summary: Centered pulse from two comparators of the up-counter, sample at the reset and load at the next reset: the delay to the pulse center is 1.5 Ts, whatever D.
prereqs: PWM update: trailing edge vs symmetric
text: The write to the preload has to arrive before the update event, that is, within \(T_s\) after the sample. In that interval fit the latency of the ADC trigger from the HRTIM, the conversion and the computation: the budget is \(T_s\) minus those three. None of them is measured yet. The latency and the conversion come from the ADC datasheet (DS12110, table 174, silicon revision V), since RM0433 does not give the latency; the computation has to be measured in the H7 firmware. That is why the figure has no numbers on those bars.

title: Centered PWM on the H7: case B
heading: The current and the sample
summary: Centered pulse from two comparators of the up-counter, sample at the reset and load at the next reset: the delay to the pulse center is 1.5 Ts, whatever D.
prereqs: PWM update: trailing edge vs symmetric
text: The inductor current equals its average at two instants of each period: at the reset, which falls at the midpoint of the fall, and at the pulse center, which falls at the midpoint of the rise. With the trigger latency and the 8.5-cycle window, the sample falls 200 to 220 ns after the reset, still on the fall, whose slope is \(9\ \text{V}/22\ \text{µH} = 0.409\ \text{A/µs}\): the sample sits 82 to 90 mA below the average (model result). The dead time of 50 ns in the model shifts the pulse center by about +25 ns and the current at the reset by about +10 mA, measured in QSPICE (the model gives +9 mA), and the current at \(T/2\) falls by about 17 mA; the figure does not show this effect. The output voltage does not fare as well: in the buck example with \(D = 0.375\), the reset falls at the peak of the \(v_C\) ripple, and the sampled voltage deviates from the average by +7.84 mV at the reset and by −9.21 mV at the pulse center, measured in QSPICE (the ideal model gives +7.79 mV and −9.21 mV), where the steady-state average sits 8.7 mV below the reference; the ideal model does not predict this offset, which comes from the losses and the dead time, and it does not change the offsets relative to the average; the figure does not draw it. The trigger latency still needs a measurement on the board.

title: Centered PWM on the H7: case B
heading: In the converters
summary: Centered pulse from two comparators of the up-counter, sample at the reset and load at the next reset: the delay to the pulse center is 1.5 Ts, whatever D.
prereqs: PWM update: trailing edge vs symmetric
text: In the course's buck, with 200 kHz, the period is \(T_s = 5\ \text{µs}\). With \(D = 0.375\), the delay to the pulse center is \(7.5\ \text{µs}\). The 2p2z margin with this delay has not been recalculated yet (see the open items) and is not the trailing-edge margin of PWM update: trailing edge vs symmetric. Exercise With \(D = 0.75\), at which instants do CMP1 and CMP2 fire in period \(k+1\)? Where is the center of the pulse, and how wide is the pulse?

title: Centered PWM on the H7: case B
heading: Open items
summary: Centered pulse from two comparators of the up-counter, sample at the reset and load at the next reset: the delay to the pulse center is 1.5 Ts, whatever D.
prereqs: PWM update: trailing edge vs symmetric
text: These figures need validation before they count as fact: the ADC trigger latency (tLATR of 1.5 to 2.5 cycles with CKMODE = 00) and the conversion time (DS12110, table 174), the sampling window (table 175, which depends on the channel and on the source impedance), the computation time measured on the H7, the comparison and preload rules, which are inferred from RM0433, and the voltage offset and the margin with case B, measured in QSPICE. Under the H7 migration rule, an independent reviewer checks the numbers before publication.

title: Interrupt deadline and budget
heading: Interrupt deadline and budget
summary: The control routine must write the CCR before the update event that copies it; the budget is the period minus the trigger, conversion, entry and computation, and only a measurement with a pin or the DWT, on production code, says whether it fits.
text: The control routine runs in an interrupt, and its write to the CCR must arrive before the update event that copies it into the active register (PWM timer and shadow registers). If it arrives in time, the delay is the one in Computation and PWM delay. If not, the value only takes effect a period later.

title: Interrupt deadline and budget
heading: The deadline
summary: The control routine must write the CCR before the update event that copies it; the budget is the period minus the trigger, conversion, entry and computation, and only a measurement with a pin or the DWT, on production code, says whether it fits.
text: At 200 kHz, the period is 5 µs. The HRTIM counts on the core clock (HRTIMSEL = 1, as in DPWM resolution and limit cycles), at 400 MHz, so the period has 2000 cycles. The sample is taken at the start of the period (as in the buck's frames), and the write to the CCR must fit before it ends: \[T_s \ge t_{\text{trigger}} + t_{\text{conversion}} + t_{\text{entry}} + t_{\text{computation}} + t_{\text{write}}\] Each term is counted from the start of the period. If the sum exceeds \(T_s\), the update event comes first, and the delay becomes \((2+D)\,T_s\). In the reference configuration, the CPU runs at 400 MHz and the AXI bus at 200 MHz (HPRE = 1000b, divide by 2), the VOS1 ceilings for silicon revision V (DS12110 revision 11, table 112). The HRTIM runs at 400 MHz, with D1CPRE = 0xxx (no division) and HRTIMSEL = 1; with HRTIMSEL = 0, it runs at 200 MHz.

title: Interrupt deadline and budget
heading: What consumes the deadline
summary: The control routine must write the CCR before the update event that copies it; the budget is the period minus the trigger, conversion, entry and computation, and only a measurement with a pin or the DWT, on production code, says whether it fits.
text: Trigger and conversion. The trigger reaches the ADC 1.5 to 2.5 ADC cycles after the timer, and a 12-bit conversion, with the 8.5-cycle window, takes 15 cycles: 300 ns with the ADC at 50 MHz (ADC trigger and sample instant). Interrupt entry. On the Cortex-M4 it takes at most 12 cycles with zero-wait-state memory (Cortex-M4 TRM, section 3.9.1); the Cortex-M7 manual gives no figure, and it must be measured. It does not include two things, and the real entry is longer when they occur: FPU lazy stacking. Entry stores the eight words of the basic frame (xPSR, PC, LR, R12 and R0 to R3). With the FPU in use, S0 to S15 and FPSCR are not stored yet: the core reserves the space, under the ASPEN and LSPEN bits of the FPCCR register (PM0253, section 4.7.2), and stores those registers only at the routine's first floating-point instruction. The cost falls inside the routine, and only a worst-case measurement shows it. Flash wait states. Code and constants read from flash cost wait states on every read. In the reference, the flash needs 2 wait states at VOS1 with the AXI at 200 MHz and WRHIGHFREQ = 10 (RM0433, table 17): three AXI clock cycles per read, or six CPU cycles at 400 MHz. Computation. The 2p2z equation has four multiplications and five additions or subtractions, plus saturation and the write. What that costs in cycles depends on the core and the FPU, and only measurement gives the number. Fast code On the STM32H7, the routine can run from ITCM (0x0000 0000, 64 KB, RM0433 section 2.4), with zero wait states (section 2.1.2), and the state can sit in DTCM (0x2000 0000, 128 KB, section 2.4). static alone puts nothing there: the routine and the state need their own sections, with __attribute__((section(...))) and matching sections in the linker script, and the routine must be copied to ITCM at start-up. Do not call library functions inside it. Outside the TCMs, the default memory map already puts SRAM in the data cache, with a write-back policy (PM0253, table 17): with the cache on, it goes through it with no setup at all, and the MPU changes those attributes.

title: Interrupt deadline and budget
heading: Measuring
summary: The control routine must write the CCR before the update event that copies it; the budget is the period minus the trigger, conversion, entry and computation, and only a measurement with a pin or the DWT, on production code, says whether it fits.
text: Measure with the production code, with the flash and cache as they will be on the board. There are two tools. GPIO pin. The pair of BSRR writes in the The 2p2z in C, in the interrupt code makes a pulse whose width is the interrupt's duration. On the oscilloscope, alongside the PWM, you see the latency from the start of the period and the variation from one period to the next, the jitter. DWT cycle counter. On Cortex-M3, M4 and M7, the DWT counts clock cycles in CYCCNT (Cortex-M7 TRM, table 11-1). The M0 and M0+ have no such counter; there, use the pin. On the Cortex-M7, and so on every STM32F7 and H7, the DWT has a software lock, DWT_LAR, that the M4 lacks: write DWT->LAR = 0xC5ACCE55 before enabling the counter. The LAR field exists only in CMSIS core_cm7.h, and on an M4 that line does not compile. static uint32_t worst; /* worst measured case, in cycles */ void measure_init(void) /* once, at initialization */ { CoreDebug->DEMCR |= CoreDebug_DEMCR_TRCENA_Msk; DWT->LAR = 0xC5ACCE55; /* unlock the DWT: Cortex-M7 only */ DWT->CYCCNT = 0; DWT->CTRL |= DWT_CTRL_CYCCNTENA_Msk; } void ADC_IRQHandler(void) { uint32_t t0 = DWT->CYCCNT; /* at the start of the interrupt */ /* ... control routine ... */ uint32_t dt = DWT->CYCCNT - t0; /* at the end; unsigned subtraction survives the wrap */ if (dt > worst) worst = dt; /* keep the worst case, not the average */ } The DWT measures only from the routine's entry to its end. The trigger, the conversion and the interrupt entry are outside it, and the deadline includes all three. To measure from the start of the period, read the HRTIM counter at the end of the routine: it already counts from the start of the period.

title: Interrupt deadline and budget
heading: Interrupt overrun
summary: The control routine must write the CCR before the update event that copies it; the budget is the period minus the trigger, conversion, entry and computation, and only a measurement with a pin or the DWT, on production code, says whether it fits.
text: There is an overrun when the routine ends after the update event. The write misses the event, the value takes effect a period later, and the delay goes from \((1+D)\,T_s\) to \((2+D)\,T_s\). The usual overrun shows only on the pin, when the routine's pulse runs past the update event's instant, or on the counter. The ADC's OVR flag only catches a delay of about a whole period, or a blocked interrupt, and only in the right mode. With the default, OVRMOD = 0, DR is an eight-entry FIFO. After one missed read, the routine reads the previous sample and stays one sample late, with no end; OVR only rises after eight accumulated missed reads, when the FIFO is full (RM0433, section 25.4.27, p. 962). With OVRMOD = 1 (bit 12 of ADC_CFGR), OVR rises at the first missed read, and DR holds the latest conversion (RM0433, section 25.4.27). The routine in The 2p2z in C, in the interrupt uses that mode and handles the case. Exercise Suppose, for the exercise only, that the trigger and the conversion take 0.5 µs together, and that the interrupt entry plus the computation take 1.8 µs, in a 5 µs period. Is there room left for the write to the CCR? How much?

title: Measuring the loop gain by injecting into the duty
heading: Measuring the loop gain by injecting into the duty
summary: A sine added to the duty in the firmware gives the loop gain as -C/U; the amplitude has to grow with frequency so the ADC sample moves several codes, and a second measurement at half the amplitude shows whether the point is linear.
prereqs: Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
From the boost to the digital loop
text: The site's models were checked against the switched circuit in QSPICE, with the scenarios' firmware. This note shows how: where the sine goes in, how the loop gain comes out, and the two precautions that separate a reliable measurement from one that only measures the ADC's rounding.

title: Measuring the loop gain by injecting into the duty
heading: The injection
summary: A sine added to the duty in the firmware gives the loop gain as -C/U; the amplitude has to grow with frequency so the ADC sample moves several codes, and a second measurement at half the amplitude shows whether the point is linear.
prereqs: Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
From the boost to the digital loop
text: Inside the interrupt, the firmware adds a small sine \(x\) to the duty \(c\) the controller computed, and the PWM uses \(u = c + x\). The sine goes around the loop: it moves the output, the ADC sample, the error and, one period later, \(c\) itself. With \(T = \beta\,G_c\,G_m\,G_{vd}\) and the error defined as reference minus sample, the part of \(c\) at the sine's frequency is \(\hat c = -T\,\hat u\), and \[T = -\frac{C}{U},\] with \(C\) and \(U\) the Fourier components of \(c\) and \(u\) at the injected frequency. Since both signals are read at the same point in the firmware, the computation and PWM delays enter the measurement with no extra care. The same computation with the sample \(V\) in place of \(C\) gives the plant as the ADC sees it, \(V/U\), without the compensator. In the lab, tools/qspice_loop_check.py records \(c\), \(u\) and the sample every period, waits 30 ms for the LC resonance, which rings for tens of milliseconds in open loop, and computes \(C\) and \(U\) over 40 whole cycles of the sine, with a Hann window against the leakage of that ringing. On a board, the procedure is the same: the firmware injects and records \(c\) and \(u\), and the computation is done offline. In the published scenarios, the injection never happens. TEST_MODE, a netlist parameter of the block (default 0), must be 1 for the injection to act; tools/qspice_loop_check.py sets it, and the published scenarios leave it at 0.

title: Measuring the loop gain by injecting into the duty
heading: The amplitude grows with frequency
summary: A sine added to the duty in the firmware gives the loop gain as -C/U; the amplitude has to grow with frequency so the ADC sample moves several codes, and a second measurement at half the amplitude shows whether the point is linear.
prereqs: Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
From the boost to the digital loop
text: The sine has to be small so as not to leave the linear regime, but the ADC sample only moves in steps of \(q = V_{FS}/(2^N - 1)\) (ADC quantization). Above the resonance, the plant falls, and a fixed amplitude that is enough at low frequency ends up moving the sample by less than one code: what gets measured then is the rounding, not the plant. The way out is to choose, at each frequency, the amplitude that, according to the model, moves the sample by about 10 codes: \[a(f) = \min\!\left(0.06,\ \max\!\left(0.004,\ \frac{10\,q}{|P(f)|}\right)\right),\] with \(P\) the plant from the duty to the sample, in volts per unit of duty. The floor, 0.004, keeps the sine small near the resonance, where a large one would reverse the inductor current at light load; the ceiling is 0.06, or less when the applied duty, which swings by \(a/|1+T|\), would come close to its limits: it may use at most 80 % of its distance to \(D_{min}\) or \(D_{max}\). In the boost at 10 V input, from 5.5 to 7 kHz, 0.06 would take the duty to 0.87, above the 0.85 limit.

title: Measuring the loop gain by injecting into the duty
heading: The linearity check
summary: A sine added to the duty in the firmware gives the loop gain as -C/U; the amplitude has to grow with frequency so the ADC sample moves several codes, and a second measurement at half the amplitude shows whether the point is linear.
prereqs: Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
From the boost to the digital loop
text: In a linear system, the gain does not depend on the amplitude. So each frequency is measured again with half the sine: if \(T\) changes by more than 0.5 dB or 3°, the point is not linear and must not be used to check the model. The check catches the inductor current nearly reversing, the duty touching its limits and the sample moving only a few codes.

title: Measuring the loop gain by injecting into the duty
heading: In the converters
summary: A sine added to the duty in the firmware gives the loop gain as -C/U; the amplitude has to grow with frequency so the ADC sample moves several codes, and a second measurement at half the amplitude shows whether the point is linear.
prereqs: Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
From the boost to the digital loop
text: Boost (\(q\) = 14.65 mV). At 1 A, the plant is 9.8 dB at 5.5 kHz and 5.7 dB at 7 kHz, about 3.1 and 1.9 V per unit of duty. With the old fixed sine of 0.004, the sample moved 0.84 and 0.52 code, and at half amplitude the response vanished: the check flagged −68 and −59 dB. With the growing amplitude, 0.047 at 5.5 kHz and 0.06 at 7 kHz (8 codes), the points pass the check, and the model stays within 0.2 dB and 1.4° of QSPICE from 300 Hz to 7 kHz, at 12 V and 1, 2 and 4 A. Buck-boost (\(q\) = 4.884 mV). At 12 V and 1 A, the 0.004 sine moved the sample 2.4 codes at 7 kHz, and half the amplitude changed the gain by 0.9 dB. With 0.016, the change drops to 0.01 dB. At 12 V and 1 A, 12 V and 2 A, and 9 V and 3 A, the sampled-data model of Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost stays within 0.2 dB and 0.7° of QSPICE from 300 Hz to 7 kHz. The averaged model with the fitted delay \((1 + 0.6\,D)\,T_s\), which the site used before, stayed within 0.45 dB and 1.9°. Buck (\(q\) = 4.884 mV). From 500 Hz to 15 kHz, the model with the \((1 + D)\,T_s\) delay stays within 0.3 dB and 0.7° of QSPICE. At 30 kHz, the amplitude that would give 10 codes is above the ceiling; with 0.06, the magnitude matches the model (0.07 dB), but half the amplitude still changes the phase by 4.6°, and the point still fails. The cause is not the ADC: with 0.06, the inductor current swings by 0.41 A, more than the ripple's valley, 0.36 A, and briefly changes sign; the dead time then adds to the duty. With half the sine, the current does not reverse, and the measurement is within 0.3 dB and 0.7° of the model. No amplitude gives both enough codes and a current that does not reverse, so the point stays out of the validation. With the fixed sine, the magnitude there was 1.4 dB off. Exercise 1 In the boost at 2 A, the model gives \(|P|\) = 10.89 dB at 5.5 kHz. What amplitude does the rule choose? How many codes did the fixed 0.004 sine move? Exercise 2 In the buck, the plant is −3.46 dB at 30 kHz. What amplitude would the rule ask for, which one does it use, and how many codes does the sample move with the full sine and with half of it? In the author's handbook Modelagem de Conversores Chaveados: do modelo à bancada virtual (in Portuguese): loop measurement by sine sweep, the lab's reference method; Middlebrook injection is also covered there.

title: Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins
heading: Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins
summary: The loop gain T = β Gc Gm Gvd, the crossover frequency and the phase and gain margins, and what they predict about overshoot and ringing.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
From the boost to the digital loop
text: A voltage loop reads the output, compares it with the reference and corrects the duty. A signal that goes once around the loop passes through four blocks in series: the controller \(G_c\), the modulator \(G_m\), the plant \(G_{vd}\) from the small-signal note and the sensor's feedback \(\beta\). Their product is the loop gain: \[G_{vd}(s) = \frac{\hat v_o(s)}{\hat d(s)} = G_0\;\frac{1 + s/\omega_{\mathrm{ESR}}}{1 + \dfrac{s}{Q\,\omega_0} + \dfrac{s^2}{\omega_0^2}}, \qquad G_0 = V_{in}\,\frac{R}{R + R_s}\] \[T(s) = \beta\,G_c(s)\,G_m\,G_{vd}(s)\] Loop gain \(T(s)\) is the gain of one full turn around the loop. With the loop closed, the output follows the reference by \(T/(1+T)\), and a disturbance at the output is divided by \(1 + T\). Where \(|T| \gg 1\), the output follows the reference; where \(|T| \ll 1\), the loop does nothing. Stability is analyzed on \(T\), not on the closed loop.

title: Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins
heading: Crossover and margins
summary: The loop gain T = β Gc Gm Gvd, the crossover frequency and the phase and gain margins, and what they predict about overshoot and ringing.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
From the boost to the digital loop
text: Crossover frequency \(f_c\): where \(|T| = 1\) (0 dB). In order of magnitude, it is the closed loop's bandwidth; the higher it is, the faster the loop corrects. Phase margin (MF): \(180^\circ + \angle T(j2\pi f_c)\). It is how much extra phase lag the loop still tolerates at \(f_c\) before it oscillates. Gain margin (MG): \(-|T|_{\mathrm{dB}}\) at the frequency where the phase crosses \(-180^\circ\). It is how much the gain can still rise. Both measure the distance from \(T\) to the point \(-1\), where \(1 + T = 0\) and the loop oscillates by itself. At the crossover, \(|1 + T| = 2\sin(\mathrm{MF}/2)\), so the closed loop peaks near \(f_c\) at about \[\left|\frac{T}{1+T}\right|_{f_c} = \frac{1}{2\sin(\mathrm{MF}/2)}.\] In the time domain, with an MF of 60° there is no peak, the overshoot is small and the ringing dies out in a few cycles of \(f_c\); with 30°, the peak is close to 6 dB, and every step rings near \(f_c\). A rough rule for the damping of the pole pair near the crossover is \(\zeta \approx \mathrm{MF}/100\) (From margin to damping: the ζ ≈ MF/100 rule and where it fails); with the 2p2z, it misses by up to 11 % in the boost (12 V, 1 and 2 A), up to 24 % in the buck-boost (12 V at 1 and 2 A, 9 V at 3 A) and 31 % in the buck; at other points of the buck-boost, by more: 27 % at 8 V and 3 A, 36.5 % at 9 V and 1 A. In all three converters, this pair rules the load step, but it is not dominant: there is also a slow real pole, near 470 Hz in the buck, 200 Hz in the boost and 330 Hz in the buck-boost, which makes the tail and sets the settling when the reference changes. Loop gain of the buck with the default 2p2z: crossover, phase margin and gain margin

title: Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins
heading: Why fc cannot rise at will
summary: The loop gain T = β Gc Gm Gvd, the crossover frequency and the phase and gain margins, and what they predict about overshoot and ringing.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
From the boost to the digital loop
text: Three things limit the crossover of a converter controlled by a microcontroller: Sampling. The firmware sees the output once per period (Sampling and the zero-order hold (ZOH)). Nothing above \(f_s/2\) can be controlled, and well before that the averaged model loses accuracy. Delay. The duty computed from a sample only moves the output \((1+D)\,T_s\) later (Computation and PWM delay). This delay leaves \(|T|\) alone, but takes a phase that grows linearly with \(f\), and above the LC resonance the buck's phase is already near \(-180^\circ\). At \(f_s/10\), the buck's delay costs \((1+D)\cdot 36^\circ\) (49.5°), more than the compensator gives back (The 2p2z compensator): in practice, \(f_c\) seldom goes above \(f_s/10\). The buck's 2p2z crosses at \(f_s/25\), where the delay costs 19.8°. The right-half-plane zero, in the boost and the buck-boost: it adds phase lag like a pole while it raises the gain, and \(f_c\) must stay well below it (The right-half-plane zero). The margin at one operating point only \(G_{vd}\) changes with the load, the input voltage and the duty. Check the margins in the worst case; in the boost, the worst case is the maximum load with the minimum input. Move the crossover In the plot above, take the crossover from 8 to 18 and then to 25 kHz, with the same zeros and pole. The phase margin falls as the delay uses up the phase: these are, roughly, the aggressive and unstable designs of the table below.

title: Loop gain, crossover frequency and margins
heading: In the converters
summary: The loop gain T = β Gc Gm Gvd, the crossover frequency and the phase and gain margins, and what they predict about overshoot and ringing.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
From the boost to the digital loop
text: The buck goes from 24 V to 9 V, with 200 kHz, 22 µH and 47 µF. The site's four controllers, at 1 A (9 Ω), by the model validated in QSPICE (Measuring the loop gain by injecting into the duty): Design \(f_c\) MF MG Closed-loop peak Original PID 8.9 kHz 25° 11.6 dB 7.6 dB 2p2z 8.0 kHz 41° 13.9 dB 3.3 dB Aggressive 18 kHz 16° 2.7 dB 12.9 dB Unstable 25 kHz −18° −3.2 dB — The peak formula gives 3.0 dB for the 2p2z and 11.4 dB for the aggressive design, close to the model. In the unstable one, the phase crosses \(-180^\circ\) at 19.2 kHz, below the crossover, with \(|T| > 1\): linear analysis predicts an oscillation near 19 kHz. In the simulation, held in check only by the duty's limits, it settles between 20 and 24 kHz. Load step with the 2p2z: MF of 41°, little ringing The same step with the aggressive design: MF of 16°, damped ringing Unstable design: the loop oscillates before any step In the boost, from 12 V to 48 V, the 2p2z crosses at only 1.5 kHz, with an MF of 46° at 1 A and 41° at 2 A: the limit there is the right-half-plane zero, not the delay (Synchronous boost 12 V → 48 V: worked example). In the Four-switch buck-boost 8–16 V → 12 V: worked example, the 2p2z crosses at 3 kHz with an MF of 42.6° at 12 V and 2 A; with the input and the load, the crossover goes from 2.4 to 3.6 kHz, and the margin from 39° to 44° (Robust design across the operating range). Exercise With the 2p2z's phase margin of 41°, estimate the closed-loop peak in dB. Exercise The buck's delay is \((1+D)\,T_s\), with \(D = 0.375\) and \(T_s = 5\ \text{µs}\). How much phase does it take at 8 kHz and at 18 kHz? Exercise Without looking at the captions above, predict from the closed-loop peak and the phase margin in the table which rings more on the load step, the 2p2z or the aggressive design. Then check the scenarios. In the author's handbook Modelagem de Conversores Chaveados: do modelo à bancada virtual (in Portuguese): the loop frequency response, with the same definitions.

title: PWM timer and shadow registers
heading: PWM timer and shadow registers
summary: The PWM timer counts up to the period and compares with the CCR; the new value enters through the preload, at the update event. Edge, center, dead time and minimum pulse decide what the duty cycle becomes on the board, and DMIN = 0 in the model hides those limits.
prereqs: PWM update: trailing edge vs symmetric
text: A digital PWM is a timer that counts clock pulses, and the output switches when the count passes the compare value. What comes out on the board also depends on the instant the new value takes effect and on the limits of the switch and the driver.

title: PWM timer and shadow registers
heading: Counter, ARR and CCR
summary: The PWM timer counts up to the period and compares with the CCR; the new value enters through the preload, at the update event. Edge, center, dead time and minimum pulse decide what the duty cycle becomes on the board, and DMIN = 0 in the model hides those limits.
prereqs: PWM update: trailing edge vs symmetric
text: On a general-purpose timer, the counter counts from 0 up to the value in the ARR register and returns to zero, so the period has ARR + 1 counts. A compare register, the CCR, says at which count the output changes. With the trailing edge, the output switches on at the start of the period and off at the CCR. The duty cycle is \(d = \mathrm{CCR}/N_{\mathrm{PWM}}\), with \(N_{\mathrm{PWM}}\) counts per period, as in DPWM resolution and limit cycles. In the HRTIM, those roles belong to PERxR and CMP1xR. On the H7 reference, the HRTIM counts at 400 MHz: at 200 kHz there are 2000 counts per period, each 2.5 ns long; on a general-purpose timer, that is ARR = 1999. The HRTIM period and compare values must be at least 3 periods of the \(f_{\mathrm{HRTIM}}\) clock: with CKPSC = 101, CMP1xR ≥ 3 (RM0433, table 308). The CMP1xR = 0 that DMIN = 0 asks for is out of range: clamp it to 3 and, to switch the output off, use HRTIM_ODISR, which takes it to its idle state. Another compare channel, placed at a chosen count, triggers the ADC conversion. In the HRTIM, the registers HRTIM_ADC1R to HRTIM_ADC4R select those events (RM0433, section 37.3.18); in HRTIM_ADC1R, for timer A, they are the bits AD1TAC2 to AD1TAC4, AD1TAPER and AD1TARST. CMP1 of timers A to E cannot trigger the ADC; the master timer's CMP1 can (AD1MC1).

title: PWM timer and shadow registers
heading: Preload and update event
summary: The PWM timer counts up to the period and compares with the CCR; the new value enters through the preload, at the update event. Edge, center, dead time and minimum pulse decide what the duty cycle becomes on the board, and DMIN = 0 in the model hides those limits.
prereqs: PWM update: trailing edge vs symmetric
text: Without preload, a write to the CCR takes effect at once, and what comes out depends on the timer. On a general-purpose timer in level PWM mode, a new CCR below the current count drops the output at once, and the pulse comes out short; a larger CCR written after the fall turns the output back on, and the pulse comes out doubled. In the HRTIM, the output is set and reset by events: a CMP below the count misses the reset event, and the switch stays on until the next period's reset. That is the dangerous case. With preload (PREEN in HRTIM_TIMxCR on the H7; OC1PE on a general-purpose timer), the write goes to the shadow register, and the update event copies the value into the active register. In the HRTIM, the transfer needs an enabled update source, such as the TxRSTU or TxREPU bits in HRTIM_TIMxCR (HRTIM_TIMCR_TRSTU and HRTIM_TIMCR_TREPU in CMSIS), or a software update, the TASWU bit in HRTIM_CR2 for timer A (RM0433, section 37.3.10). A value written at \(kT_s\) takes effect in the next period: this is the one-period delay of Computation and PWM delay. In trailing-edge PWM, the update event is the start of the period, and only the falling edge moves. In center-aligned PWM, it is the peak, the valley or both, and both edges move (PWM update: trailing edge vs symmetric); the H7 HRTIM counter only counts up, so the centered pulse comes from two comparators (Centered PWM on the H7: case B). The ARR also has preload.

title: PWM timer and shadow registers
heading: Dead time
summary: The PWM timer counts up to the period and compares with the CCR; the new value enters through the preload, at the update event. Edge, center, dead time and minimum pulse decide what the duty cycle becomes on the board, and DMIN = 0 in the model hides those limits.
prereqs: PWM update: trailing edge vs symmetric
text: In a synchronous buck, the two switches are complementary, with a dead time between them so that they never conduct together (Synchronous buck 24 V → 9 V: worked example already mentions it). It delays the turn-on of each switch: the high side conducts for \(DT_s - t_{dt}\), and the low side for \((1-D)\,T_s - t_{dt}\). The average voltage loses a term proportional to \(f_s\,t_{dt}\), with a sign that depends on the direction of the current.

title: PWM timer and shadow registers
heading: Bootstrap recharge
summary: The PWM timer counts up to the period and compares with the CCR; the new value enters through the preload, at the update event. Edge, center, dead time and minimum pulse decide what the duty cycle becomes on the board, and DMIN = 0 in the model hides those limits.
prereqs: PWM update: trailing edge vs symmetric
text: The high-side switch's driver usually feeds the gate from a bootstrap capacitor, recharged only while the low-side switch conducts. The recharge window in each period may stand for the upper duty-cycle limit. With DMAX = 0.9 and the dead time of 50 ns, \((1 - \mathrm{DMAX})\,T_s - t_{dt} = 0.5 - 0.05 = 0.45\) µs of low-side conduction remains in the buck. The recharge time comes from the driver's datasheet.

title: PWM timer and shadow registers
heading: Minimum pulse and DMIN = 0
summary: The PWM timer counts up to the period and compares with the CCR; the new value enters through the preload, at the update event. Edge, center, dead time and minimum pulse decide what the duty cycle becomes on the board, and DMIN = 0 in the model hides those limits.
prereqs: PWM update: trailing edge vs symmetric
text: There is a shortest pulse that the timer and the driver can deliver: if \(DT_s\) does not exceed the dead time, the high-side switch never conducts, and the driver has its own minimum response time, which comes from its datasheet. The averaged model and the clamp at DMIN = 0 have no lower limit: a request for \(10^{-3}\) passes as a real output. The switched simulation already swallows pulses shorter than the dead time: with \(D = 10^{-3}\), 5 ns against 50 ns, G1 never turns on, as on a board. The driver's own minimum pulse is not modeled.

title: PWM timer and shadow registers
heading: In the converters
summary: The PWM timer counts up to the period and compares with the CCR; the new value enters through the preload, at the update event. Edge, center, dead time and minimum pulse decide what the duty cycle becomes on the board, and DMIN = 0 in the model hides those limits.
prereqs: PWM update: trailing edge vs symmetric
text: Buck. At 200 kHz, 2000 counts per period. DMAX may stand for the bootstrap recharge; DMIN stands for no minimum pulse at all. Boost. At 100 kHz, the period has 4000 counts. The controlled switch, G1, is on the ground side. The high-side one, G2, which rectifies, uses a bootstrap recharged while G1 conducts: that imposes a minimum duty cycle on the synchronous boost. The range from 0 to 0.85 does not include the minimum pulse either. Exercise 1 With 2000 counts per period, how many counts is a request of \(10^{-3}\), how long does the pulse last at 400 MHz, and why does the board not deliver it, with a dead time of 50 ns? Exercise 2 With DMAX = 0.9, \(T_s = 5\) µs and a dead time of 50 ns, how much time per period is left with the low-side switch on? And if the driver needs more than that to recharge the bootstrap?

title: PWM update: trailing edge vs symmetric
heading: PWM update: trailing edge vs symmetric
summary: How a digital PWM takes the new duty from the CCR's preload to the edge it moves, and the delay that follows, td = tc + tm: "half-period ZOH plus z-1" and "(1 + D) Ts" are the same model for different PWMs; adding the two counts the modulator twice.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: In a digital PWM, the firmware does not move the edge: it writes the new duty to the CCR's preload (the shadow register), and a timer update event copies it to the active register (PWM timer and shadow registers). In a trailing-edge PWM, with a sawtooth, the update is the counter reset; in a symmetric PWM, with a triangle, it is the peak, the valley or both. Only then does the edge move, and the loop's delay is the time from the sample to that edge. Trailing-edge PWM (top) and symmetric PWM (bottom): carrier, CCR, gate, sample, write to the CCR and update event; with the step, the edges that sample k moves and the delays t_c, t_m and t_d, in Tₛ The reference course counts this delay as "ZOH, \(-\omega T_s/2\), plus \(z^{-1}\) when the update goes to the next cycle". This site counts \((1 + D)\,T_s\) (Computation and PWM delay). Both counts are right, each for its own PWM; the error is to mix them.

title: PWM update: trailing edge vs symmetric
heading: One delay, two parts
summary: How a digital PWM takes the new duty from the CCR's preload to the edge it moves, and the delay that follows, td = tc + tm: "half-period ZOH plus z-1" and "(1 + D) Ts" are the same model for different PWMs; adding the two counts the modulator twice.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: With one update per period, the delay to the plant is \[t_d = t_c + t_m,\] where \(t_c\) runs from the sample to the update event, when the new duty takes effect, and \(t_m\) from there to the edge it moves (or to the midpoint of the two, when both move). In small signals, the edge shifted by \(\hat d\,T_s\) adds to the switched voltage a pulse of height \(V_{in}\) and width \(\hat d\,T_s\): to first order, an impulse at the edge's instant. So the modulator acts as a pure delay \(t_m\), with exact phase in the baseband; the folded terms are negligible in the buck up to about \(f_s/10\). In an analog PWM, the edge follows the instantaneous modulating signal, and \(t_m\) does not exist: the modulator is only the gain \(1/V_M\).

title: PWM update: trailing edge vs symmetric
heading: Trailing edge, update in the next period
summary: How a digital PWM takes the new duty from the CCR's preload to the edge it moves, and the delay that follows, td = tc + tm: "half-period ZOH plus z-1" and "(1 + D) Ts" are the same model for different PWMs; adding the two counts the modulator twice.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: This site's firmware: sample at \(kT_s\), CCR preload, switch on at the start of the period. Then \(t_c = T_s\), and only the falling edge moves, \(DT_s\) after the start: \(t_m = DT_s\). Splitting off the half period, \[(1+D)\,T_s = \underbrace{T_s}_{z^{-1}} + \underbrace{T_s/2}_{\text{ZOH}} + \underbrace{(D-\tfrac12)\,T_s}_{\text{edge position}}.\] The "ZOH" is already inside the \(DT_s\) term. With \(D = 0.5\), both counts give \(1.5\,T_s\); with \(D < 0.5\), "ZOH plus \(z^{-1}\)" counts too much delay and stays on the safe side; with \(D > 0.5\), it counts too little and is optimistic. With a leading edge, \(t_m = (1-D)\,T_s\), and the error flips.

title: PWM update: trailing edge vs symmetric
heading: Symmetric PWM, update at the peak or valley
summary: How a digital PWM takes the new duty from the CCR's preload to the edge it moves, and the delay that follows, td = tc + tm: "half-period ZOH plus z-1" and "(1 + D) Ts" are the same model for different PWMs; adding the two counts the modulator twice.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: With a triangle carrier and the load at a peak or a valley, the two edges it moves lie symmetric about the carrier's next extreme, \(T_s/2\) after the load, for any \(D\). So \(t_m = T_s/2\): the other course's "ZOH" is the modulator, not one more block. The on pulse is centered on the valley, so sampling there is away from the switching edges. Three timings: Computation and update \(t_c\) \(t_d\) sample at the valley, no preload (immediate write) the computation \(T_s/2\) sample at the valley, load at the peak (preload) \(T_s/2\) \(T_s\) load at the next peak or valley \(T_s\) \(1.5\,T_s\) In the first row, the load is the write itself: \(t_m = T_s/2 - t_c\), and the sum stays \(T_s/2\) if the write lands before the falling edge, \(DT_s/2\) after the valley. At small \(D\) there is hardly any time, and a late write delays or loses the edge; that is why the preload is the usual setup. In the middle row, the sample at the valley and the load at the next peak give \(t_c = T_s/2\); the edges' midpoint comes \(T_s/2\) later, and \(t_d = T_s\). With double update, at every peak and valley, \(T_s = T_{PWM}/2\). Each load moves one edge only, \((1-D)\,T_s\) or \(DT_s\) after it, in turn; the mean is \(T_s/2\), and the last row holds: \(t_d = 1.5\,T_s = 0.75\,T_{PWM}\). In the other rows, \(T_s = T_{PWM}\). The H7's centered pulse, from the up-counter, two comparators and a load at the next reset, has a delay of \(1.5\,T_s\) and is in Centered PWM on the H7: case B. Counting twice Adding the ZOH (\(T_s/2\)) to \((1 + D)\,T_s\) gives \((1.5 + D)\,T_s\): the modulator goes in twice, as the ZOH and as \(DT_s\). In the symmetric PWM, the same error is adding a "PWM delay" of \(T_s/2\) to the ZOH. Count \(t_c\) once and \(t_m\) once. Phase of the buck's loop gain with the 2p2z and phase margin against D, for four ways of counting the delay; the dotted line is the exact sampled-data model of the trailing edge

title: PWM update: trailing edge vs symmetric
heading: In the converters
summary: How a digital PWM takes the new duty from the CCR's preload to the edge it moves, and the delay that follows, td = tc + tm: "half-period ZOH plus z-1" and "(1 + D) Ts" are the same model for different PWMs; adding the two counts the modulator twice.
trails: From the analog buck to the digital loop
text: In the buck, with 24 V and 9 V, \(D = 0.375\) and \(t_d = 1.375\,T_s = 6.875\ \text{µs}\). The 2p2z has a \(41.3^\circ\) margin at the 8 kHz crossover, the last of the loop's three (Feedback and margins), and the exact sampled-data model gives \(41.4^\circ\). "ZOH plus \(z^{-1}\)" uses \(1.5\,T_s\), takes \(1.8^\circ\) more and gives \(39.6^\circ\) with the ZOH's sinc, as in the figure; with the pure delay, \(39.5^\circ\), as in Computation and PWM delay. With a symmetric PWM updated in the same cycle, only the ZOH, it would be \(53.9^\circ\). Adding the ZOH to \((1 + D)\,T_s\) would give \(34.2^\circ\). In QSPICE, from 2 to 15 kHz, the \((1 + D)\,T_s\) model stays within \(0.7^\circ\) of the measurement, and "ZOH plus \(z^{-1}\)" is off by up to \(3.2^\circ\) on the safe side (Measuring the loop gain by injecting into the duty). In the boost and the buck-boost, the firmware's delay is also \((1 + D)\,T_s\), but the switched response behaves, to first order, like \((1 + D/2)\,T_s\), and the site uses the circuit's sampled-data model (Sampling instant and the ESR in the boost). That is why the figure compares only the buck. Exercise Predict, before moving anything: which of the four curves in the right panel do not depend on \(D\)? At what \(D\) does the \((1 + D)\,T_s\) curve meet the \(T_s + T_s/2\) one? Exercise With \(D = 0.375\), the right margin is \(41.3^\circ\). Predict the double-counting margin, knowing that each period costs \(360^\circ \times 8000 \times 5\ \text{µs} = 14.4^\circ\) at 8 kHz. Then highlight \((1.5 + D)\,T_s\) in the figure. Exercise A buck with the same \(V_{in}\), \(D = 0.75\) (the buck's averaged stage does not depend on \(D\)) and the same firmware is designed with "ZOH plus \(z^{-1}\)". Is the count safe or optimistic, and by how much at 8 kHz? Check with the \(D\) control.
